(uncertain).** In the only trial (43 people with at least a year of training, 8 weeks), progressing load or reps gave similar results: rectus femoris thickness +2.8 mm favouring reps (95% CI -0.5 to 5.8), Smith-machine squat 1RM +2.0 kg favouring load (-2.4 to 7.8) [@Plotkin2022_loadVsRepProgression]. The 2009 ACSM consensus advises novices to use 8-12RM loads 2-3 days a week and add 2-10% once they exceed the target by 1-2 reps, which is double progression [@ACSM2009_progression_models]. No trial has compared schemes in true novices.

**4. Autoregulation and RIR (uncertain).** Autoregulated and percentage-based loading gave similar 1RM gains (6 studies; mean difference 2.07 kg, -0.32 to 4.46) [@Hickmott2022_autoregulation], and RPE- and percentage-based loads produced similar 1RM and muscle-thickness gains in 21 lifters (squat +17.1 vs +13.9 kg, not significant) [@Helms2018_RPEvsPercent]. People under-predicted their [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] by 0.95 reps on average (0.17 to 1.73; [[term:i2|I²]] 97.9%), more accurately near failure and in sets of 12 reps or fewer [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy].

**5. Deloads and short breaks (uncertain).**

| Trial | Who | Design | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pancar 2026 | 19 untrained men | One limb did 1 session of 2 sets in weeks 4 and 8 | Same thickness and 10RM; all CIs include zero [@Pancar2026_deloadUntrained] |
| Coleman 2024 | 39 trained lifters | Full week off after week 4 of 9 | Same growth; squat 1RM -3.6 kg (95% CrI -10.4 to 3.2) [@Coleman2024_deloadRCT] |
| Ogasawara 2013 | 14 untrained men | Three 6-week blocks with 3-week breaks vs 24 weeks continuous | Same 24-week growth and strength; rapid regain [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous] |

The Delphi consensus defines deloads but supplies no outcome data [@Bell2023_deloadDelphi].

**6. What a longer break costs (probable).** Across 103 studies, stopping reduced submaximal strength (SMD -0.62, -0.80 to -0.45), maximal force (-0.46, -0.54 to -0.37) and power (-0.20, -0.28 to -0.13), more with longer breaks and in previously inactive or older people [@Bosquet2013_detrainingMeta]. After 20 weeks off, muscle size was back to baseline but about 60% of a ~20% 1RM gain remained [@Psilander2019_muscleMemory]. In RCT exercise arms (86 studies, n=5670), muscle and lean mass were no longer above baseline at any detraining follow-up, while [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] and waist circumference stayed improved beyond six months [@Zhang2026_detrainingBodyComp].

**7. Does muscle come back faster? (uncertain).** For: rapid regain after 3-week breaks [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous]; lean leg mass +6.5%, back to baseline, then 12.4% above baseline after retraining, in 7-8 people without a control group [@Seaborne2018_epigeneticMemory]; retained myonuclei [@Cumming2024_myonuclearPermanence]. Against: previously trained limbs did not regrow faster than naive limbs in two within-person studies [@Psilander2019_muscleMemory; @Cumming2024_myonuclearPermanence], and human myonuclei are lost with atrophy [@Rahmati2022_myonuclearMeta].

**8. Minimal maintenance dose (probable).** After 16 weeks of training three days a week, young adults kept their hypertrophy for 32 weeks on one-third or one-ninth of the dose (one-third even added fibre size); older adults needed more (n=70) [@Bickel2011_maintenanceDose]. A narrative review concluded that strength and size were kept for up to 32 weeks with one weekly session of one set per exercise if relative load was kept, and endurance for up to 15 weeks with two sessions a week if exercise heart rate was kept [@Spiering2021_minimalDose].

**Who was studied.** Most trials lasted 8-24 weeks with fewer than 50 participants; periodisation and autoregulation data come largely from trained lifters, the detraining meta-analysis pooled mainly uncontrolled pre-post data, and maintenance doses come from people with at least 16 weeks of training. For you, the direction of these findings is more reliable than their exact size.
articles.practice:
- **Phase 1: double progression, no periodisation.** Each exercise has a rep range: main [[term:compound-exercise|compound lifts]] 8-12, accessories 8-12 or 10-15, small [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation lifts]] 12-20, with 2-4 working sets. When every working set reaches the top of the range at the target effort, add the smallest available increment next session (about 1-2.5 kg, i.e. the next dumbbell pair, machine pin or +2.5 kg on a barbell, for upper-body and isolation lifts; 2.5-5 kg for barbell squat and hinge; 5-10 kg for leg press; practical convention within the ACSM 2-10% range) and restart at the bottom ([[rule:double-progression]], [[tool:progression]], [[dec:D09]]). Bodyweight lifts progress by leverage and assistance: hands-elevated then floor [[ex:push-up]], assisted then strict [[ex:pull-up]].
- **Effort.** About 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2, then 2-3 RIR on free-weight compounds (never to failure alone), 1-2 on machines and 0-2 on isolation lifts ([[dec:D07]]); occasional sets to failure on safe machines teach you your personal RIR error ([[rule:rir-calibration]]).
- **Stalls.** No progress for three exposures on a lift: check sleep, food and technique first, then change that lift's stimulus for one block ([[rule:stall]]). A deload is not the default fix.
- **Later phases.** Planned variation such as weekly undulation (a heavier, a moderate and a lighter exposure per pattern) and blocks that end in a reduced-volume week come once you are past the novice stage ([[dec:D16]], [[rule:deload]]). Phase 3's 8-week blocks shift the *emphasis* (hypertrophy, then strength and power, then physique and conditioning) while every session still trains strength, size and conditioning together; that is the 'mixed' approach that did better than classical block periodisation (one quality trained at a time) in the trial above, so classical block periodisation itself is not used.
- **Breaks.** Up to 7 days off: simply resume. 8-21 days: about 90% of previous loads for a week. 22-56 days: about 80%, going back 2-3 weeks in the programme. More than 8 weeks: restart at Phase 1 week 3 at about 70% (practical convention; [[rule:breaks]], [[tool:breaks]]). Illness follows [[rule:illness]].
- **Busy months.** One or two sessions a week with 1-2 hard sets per main movement pattern at your usual relative load probably keeps most of what you have; the same logic sets the long-term maintenance dose ([[phase:pm]], [[dec:D18]]).
- **Logging.** Record load, reps and RPE (10 minus RIR) for every set in Hevy ([[plan:logging]]); [[tool:e1rm]] turns them into a trend so progress stays visible across rep ranges.
articles.uncertainties:
- No trial has compared progression schemes (double progression, single linear load progression, RIR autoregulation) in true novices over six months or more, and none measured adherence or enjoyment, which matter if boredom is your main risk of quitting.
- Whether periodisation adds strength for untrained people is unresolved: three meta-analyses point in different directions.
- Deload trials last 8-9 weeks; the best frequency and structure, and effects on injury and adherence, are unknown. The deload triggers in the rules are judgement, not validated.
- Whether retained myonuclei or methylation marks speed human regrowth is unresolved; every relevant study had 19 or fewer participants.
- Maintenance doses come from people who had trained for at least 16 weeks; someone with only a few months of training may need more.
- RIR accuracy in the first weeks of training, and whether personal calibration improves it, are poorly characterised.

What would change the advice: a long novice trial favouring one progression scheme; your logs showing repeated failed load jumps (use smaller increments or wider rep ranges), missed sessions from boredom (add variation earlier), or stalls before month 4 (introduce undulation earlier).

articles.title: Realistic expectations and natural limits
articles.tagline: How fast muscle comes, how much people differ, where the natural ceiling sits, and why a screen physique is not a timeline.
articles.summary:
In training studies averaging two to three months, young men gained on average about 1.5 kg of muscle. Strength rises much faster, because early gains are probably mostly your nervous system learning the movements, and some of the early increase in muscle size is fluid rather than new tissue.

Individual results vary widely: on the same programme some people barely change while others gain several times the average. Much of what looks like non-response in short studies may be measurement noise, so judge your own progress over at least 12 weeks using several measures together.

Gains slow as you become trained. A plausible first year is 2-5 kg of lean mass (inference), with smaller gains each year after.

[[term:ffmi|Fat-free mass index (FFMI)]] puts this in context. Yours is about 18.8 kg/m² (plausible 17.9-19.5), close to the median for young men. A lean, clearly athletic build at FFMI 21-22 would mean roughly 7-10 kg more [[term:ffm|fat-free mass]] (5-14 kg across the plausible range), a multi-year project. The approximate drug-free extreme of about 25 is about 20 kg away (18-23 kg), so becoming bulky by accident is not a realistic risk (inference from these numbers), and you can stop growing any region at the size you like.

Attractiveness research (photograph ratings, mostly Western raters, none South Asian) links upper-body muscularity, a V-shaped torso and leanness to higher ratings, and finds that men overestimate how muscular women want them to be. A film physique is not a fair benchmark: it reflects years of professionally supported training, often a taller frame, and lighting, timing and preparation for the camera. Use it for direction, not for a timeline.
articles.mechanisms:
**Early change is mostly skill and fluid (human mechanistic).** In the first weeks, strength rises through [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptation]]: after four weeks the same [[term:motor-unit|motor units]] were recruited at lower force thresholds and discharged faster [@DelVecchio2019_motorUnits], and [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] contributed increasingly only after about 3-5 weeks [@MoritaniDeVries1979_neuralVsHypertrophy]. Meanwhile muscle swells. Thigh cross-sectional area rose 3.5% after two sessions, too fast to be new contractile protein [@DeFreitas2011_timeCourse], and vastus lateralis area was 2.7% larger at week 3 while echo intensity and damage markers were still raised, indicating that part of the rise was oedema [@Damas2016_EJAP_oedema]. Integrated myofibrillar [[term:mps|protein synthesis]] peaks in week 1 but is probably spent largely on repairing Z-band damage; it tracks real fibre growth (r ≈ 0.9) only from week 3 [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS]. High synthesis is therefore not the same as growth: acute signalling and synthesis do not automatically translate into long-term accretion.

**Why gains slow (outcome pattern; cellular reasons theoretical).** On the same 21-week programme, untrained men gained 5.6% quadriceps area and strength athletes none [@Ahtiainen2003_trainedVsUntrained]. Three non-exclusive hypotheses explain the deceleration. (1) Habituation: the [[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]] reduces damage and possibly the anabolic signal per session, so a fixed programme becomes a smaller perturbation. (2) Translational capacity: higher training volume raised S6K1 and ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation (readouts of [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]] activity), total RNA and c-Myc expression alongside more growth [@Hammarstrom2020_volume_ribosomes]; because most muscle RNA is ribosomal (background), this points to ribosome biogenesis as a rate-limiting step, and larger fibres may need disproportionately more ribosomal and myonuclear support. (3) Structural ceilings: frame size, fibre number and endocrine milieu set whole-body limits. Early neural gains also saturate.

**Why people differ (human outcome plus statistics).** The observed spread of change in a trained group combines true individual response with measurement error and day-to-day biological variation. True variance can be estimated as SD²(trained) minus SD²(control). With a time-matched control, true variability beyond error was detectable for [[term:1rm|1RM]] (SD 1.80 kg) but not for six-week muscle-thickness change [@Dankel2019_trueVariability], so many 'non-responders' in short trials may be artefacts. Biology contributes as well: in a within-person trial, people whose total RNA rose more early in training were more likely to benefit from extra volume (odds of benefit +7.0% per 1% greater rise) [@Hammarstrom2020_volume_ribosomes]. Those markers need muscle biopsies, and no validated predictor of an individual's response is available.

**What FFMI measures (measurement and theory).** FFMI divides fat-free mass by height squared, as BMI does for total mass. Fat-free mass includes bone, organs, skin and body water as well as skeletal muscle (background), so FFMI is a proxy for muscularity, and its precision depends on the body-fat estimate: for you, the difference between 17% and 24% body fat (your plausible range) moves FFMI by about 1.6 kg/m² (arithmetic). The 1995 FFMI study added 6.3 × (1.80 − height in m) to normalise values to a height of 1.80 m [@Kouri1995_FFMI]; at 1.81 m this changes yours by only -0.06. In very large athletes, FFMI rose with body mass to about 90 kg and then levelled off, and an ultrasound-estimated skeletal-muscle index plateaued at about 17 kg/m², proposed as a possible human upper limit [@Abe2018_upperLimit].

**Why perceived muscularity might matter (theoretical; cross-sectional data).** Evolutionary accounts propose that visible upper-body strength signals physical formidability and that muscularity acts as a 'fitness indicator'. One test of this found muscular men rated sexier but also more dominant and volatile and less committed, a trade-off that could produce a preference peak at moderate muscularity [@Frederick2007_muscularity]. Preferences shifted with socio-economic setting [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural], suggesting they are partly cultural rather than fixed. These are hypotheses about average ratings, not causal tests.

**Why screen physiques look different (inference from background physiology).** Visible definition depends on subcutaneous fat thickness as much as on muscle size. Shortly after training, muscle volume rises transiently as blood flow increases and osmolytes such as inorganic phosphate and lactate draw water into active fibres. Light from above deepens the shadows at muscle borders, and camera angle, lens and posture change apparent proportions. A filmed physique is often a peak state prepared for particular days, which says little about year-round appearance or about how long it took to build.
articles.evidence:
**1. How much muscle in the first months? (probable).** A [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 111 studies (158 groups, n=1927 healthy men aged 18-40; interventions averaging about 9-10 weeks) found that whole-body muscle mass rose 1.53 kg ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 1.30 to 1.76; [[term:i2|I²]] 0%), fat-free mass 1.56 kg (1.23 to 1.89) and lean mass 1.65 kg (1.28 to 2.01) [@Benito2020_wholeBodyHypertrophy]. Duration did not explain the variation (0.01 kg per week, -0.04 to 0.06), so 10-week rates cannot be extrapolated linearly, and the data are uncontrolled pre-post changes, partly measured by [[term:bia|BIA]] and anthropometry. Regional area typically rises 4-10% over 8-12 weeks: thigh +9.6% at 8 weeks [@DeFreitas2011_timeCourse]; quadriceps +5.2% with 3 sets vs +3.7% with 1 set per exercise at 12 weeks [@Hammarstrom2020_volume_ribosomes]; fibre area about 17% and thickness about 10% after 10 weeks, with 1RM up about 20% [@Psilander2019_muscleMemory]. Strength rises proportionally more than size: over 20-24 weeks, leg size rose 4.8% and leg-press 1RM 21.1% on average [@Ahtiainen2016_heterogeneity].

**2. When is change real? (probable).** Thigh area rose 3.5% after two sessions and was next significantly increased at week 3 [@DeFreitas2011_timeCourse]; early increases coincided with oedema markers [@Damas2016_EJAP_oedema]. Girth changes in weeks 1-3 overstate growth.

**3. How much do people differ? (large observed spread: probable; true spread in hypertrophy: uncertain).** In 585 young adults on the same 12-week arm programme, biceps area changed by -2% to +59% and 1RM by 0% to +250% [@Hubal2005_variability]. In 287 adults (72 of them non-training controls) over 20-24 weeks, leg size ranged from -11% to +30% and leg-press 1RM from -8% to +60%; using thresholds set by the controls, 29% were low responders for size and 7% for strength [@Ahtiainen2016_heterogeneity]. But with a time-matched control in 151 people over 6 weeks, true between-person variability beyond error was detectable for 1RM and not for muscle thickness [@Dankel2019_trueVariability]. Extra volume helped on average, yet only 13 of 34 people showed a clear individual hypertrophy benefit [@Hammarstrom2020_volume_ribosomes].

**4. Does it slow down? (probable).** Untrained men gained 5.6% quadriceps area and 20.9% force on a 21-week programme on which strength athletes changed by -1.8% and 3.9% (n=16) [@Ahtiainen2003_trainedVsUntrained]. Continuously trained novices slowed after the first 6 weeks [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous]. Competitive powerlifters gained about 7.5-12.5% strength in their first year and only about 20% over 10 years, with survivorship bias and unrecorded drug-testing status [@Latella2024_longTermStrength].

**5. Natural limits and where you stand (uncertain).** Self-reported non-users of anabolic steroids had height-normalised FFMI values up to about 25.0 kg/m² (74 non-users vs 83 users), pre-steroid-era champions averaged an estimated 25.4, and many users exceeded 25; the authors called the findings preliminary [@Kouri1995_FFMI]. The median FFMI of young Swiss men (18-34 y, BIA-based) was 18.9 kg/m² [@Schutz2002_FFMIpercentiles], a Caucasian reference that may not transfer to other populations. Very large athletes of unknown drug status plateaued at a skeletal-muscle index of about 17 kg/m² [@Abe2018_upperLimit]. Your numbers (arithmetic, inference; body fat is method-dependent):

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Height and body mass | 1.81 m, 77 kg |
| Body fat (estimate) | about 20% (plausible 17-24%) |
| Fat-free mass | about 61.6 kg (58.5-63.9) |
| FFMI now | about 18.8 kg/m² (17.9-19.5; young-male median 18.9) |
| Illustration: FFMI 21-22 at 12-15% fat | FFM about 69-72 kg, body mass about 78-85 kg: about 7-10 kg more FFM (5-14 across the range) |
| Drug-free extreme, FFMI 25 | FFM about 82 kg: about 20 kg more (18-23) |

The illustration is not a target; it shows what a lean, clearly athletic build means in kilograms.

**6. What do raters find attractive? (uncertain; cross-sectional).** In mainly young Western samples, rated physical strength, cued mostly by upper-body muscularity, explained over 70% of the variance in rated bodily attractiveness, and about 80% with height and leanness added; no ceiling appeared within the stimuli used [@Sell2017_strengthAttractiveness]. Another series found moderately muscular men rated most attractive (an inverted U) [@Frederick2007_muscularity]. A V-shaped torso (low waist-to-chest ratio) was the main cue among urban British and Malaysian raters, whereas rural Malaysian raters preferred heavier, less triangular bodies [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural]. Volume-height index explained about 73% of variance in another sample, with a slim optimum of about 17.6-18.0 L/m² [@Fan2005_VHIperception]. Men overestimated the heaviness and muscularity women prefer in a partner [@Lei2021_muscularityMisperception]. All are ratings of photographs or models, not real-world outcomes, and no study with South Asian raters was located.

**Who was studied.** Growth data come from short trials in mostly young Western adults; the FFMI ceiling from a small 1995 sample; perception data from British, Malaysian, Chinese and other mainly Western raters. None included South Asian men or raters.
articles.practice:
- **What the app shows.** Population ranges, labelled as averages, and your own trends only after 8-12 weeks of data. Weeks 1-4: loads and reps climb fast from skill, and girths may rise partly from fluid. Weeks 8-12: about 1.5 kg of muscle on average, with individual results plausibly from about zero to over 3 kg (inference). Year 1: a plausible 2-5 kg of lean mass with good adherence and nutrition (inference). While you eat in a deficit to lose fat, expect the lower end ([[dec:D04]], [[sci:sci-energy]]).
- **Judging response.** Use at least 12 weeks with 85-90% session adherence and several signals together: [[tool:e1rm]] trends on 4-6 tracked lifts, [[ex:test-girths]] every 4 weeks under standard conditions, and photos with fixed lighting and pose ([[plan:monitoring]], [[tool:checkin]]). Do not judge muscle gain from the BIA scale's muscle-mass output ([[dec:D23]], [[sci:sci-bodycomp]]).
- **If everything is flat for 6 weeks.** Check sleep, energy and protein first, then add 2-4 weekly sets for priority muscles for one 5-6-week block ([[rule:lagging-muscle]]). Never label yourself a low responder from one short block.
- **Shape metrics.** Shoulder to natural waist is now 1.46 (118/81 cm) and waist to chest 0.84 (81/96 cm); the first should rise and the second fall as upper-body muscle grows and waist fat falls (inference).
- **Setting a ceiling.** Choose your own stop-growing point from photos, girths or FFMI ([[tool:bodycomp]]). When a region reaches it, [[rule:size-control]] moves it to maintenance volume; in young adults one-ninth of the original dose, or one weekly set per exercise at the usual relative load, preserved muscle for months [@Bickel2011_maintenanceDose; @Spiering2021_minimalDose] ([[dec:D26]]).
- **Using a reference physique.** Take proportions and leanness from it, never the timeline or the absolute size.
articles.uncertainties:
- No measured 12-month or multi-year lean-mass trajectories ([[term:dxa|DXA]] or MRI) in drug-free novice men were located, and none in South Asian men; the year-1 range and the timeline to FFMI 21-22 are inference.
- How much a deliberate energy deficit lowers these gains is outside this evidence base ([[sci:sci-energy]]).
- The size of true individual variation in hypertrophy is contested, and no validated predictor of your personal response exists.
- The drug-free FFMI extreme rests on a small, self-reported 1995 sample; no contemporary drug-tested distribution was found, and the median comes from Swiss Caucasian adults measured by BIA. Your FFMI band (about 1.6 kg/m² wide) mostly reflects uncertainty in your body-fat estimate.
- Perception studies are cross-sectional photograph ratings from particular cultures; they describe averages, not what any individual prefers, and no South Asian raters were located. Your own preference should set the target.

What would change these expectations: long-term DXA or MRI cohorts of drug-free novices; a better body-fat measurement for you, which would narrow the FFMI band; and, most of all, your own 12-week trends.

articles.title: Aerobic fitness and VO₂max
articles.tagline: Why blood volume and stroke volume set your aerobic ceiling, how intervals and easy work raise it, and how much you need.
articles.summary:
Your [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]], the most oxygen your body can take up and use per minute, is the standard measure of aerobic fitness. It is limited mainly by how much blood your heart pumps per beat and, to a lesser degree, by how much oxygen your muscles extract. In untrained people it rises within about three weeks of regular training [@Murias2010_timeCourse], and in one small trial the gain after six weeks depended mainly on a larger blood volume that lets the heart fill and eject more per beat [@Montero2015_haematologicalVO2peak].

Any regular aerobic training works for a beginner. In controlled trials, [[term:hiit|high-intensity interval training (HIIT)]] raised VO₂max by about 6 mL/kg/min compared with no exercise, and by a small extra margin (about 1.4 mL/kg/min, low certainty) compared with [[term:mict|moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)]] [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Long intervals such as 4 x 4 minutes have the most direct support. Apparent 'non-response' largely disappears when the weekly dose is high enough [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse].

You do not need a heart-rate monitor. The [[term:talk-test|talk test]] (can you still speak in full sentences?) and your [[term:rpe|rating of perceived exertion (RPE)]] track the thresholds that matter, whereas age-based heart-rate formulas can be about 20 beats per minute off for an individual [@Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax].

Higher fitness and more daily steps are strongly associated with longer life, but these are observational data and part of the link may be genetic. Aerobic exercise alone produces modest weight loss, about 0.5 kg per extra 30 minutes a week in trials of adults with overweight or obesity, partly because people eat a little more [@Jayedi2024_aerobicWeightLossDoseResponse; @Martin2019_EMECHANIC].

For you: mostly easy sessions plus, from Phase 1 week 7, one interval session a week, intensity judged by speech and effort, and a daily walking habit to offset a long desk shift.
articles.mechanisms:
**The Fick principle sets the arithmetic** (definitional identity, with human mechanistic data)

By mass balance, VO₂max equals maximal cardiac output (maximal heart rate x maximal [[term:stroke-volume|stroke volume]]) multiplied by the arterial-mixed venous O₂ content difference (a-vO₂diff): the [[term:fick-principle|Fick principle]]. Training can raise VO₂max only by delivering more blood per minute or by extracting more O₂ from each litre. [[term:hrmax|Maximum heart rate (HRmax)]] barely moves with training: age-predicted HRmax did not differ by habitual activity [@Tanaka2001_HRmax] and showed no interaction with activity level or VO₂max [@Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax], so central gains are carried by stroke volume (inference from these data). In young men cycling 3 x 45 min per week, VO₂max rose within 3 weeks, first mainly through a wider a-vO₂diff and later through higher cardiac output; at 12 weeks about 56% of the 18% gain was central and 44% peripheral [@Murias2010_timeCourse]. Pooled interval-training studies report maximal stroke volume +14.1% and maximal cardiac output +12.6% [@Rosenblat2022_centralPeripheralMA].

**Blood volume is the early limiter** (human mechanistic, including a causal manipulation)

In 16 untrained men, 6 weeks of moderate endurance training raised red-cell volume by 8%, plasma volume by 4% and haemoglobin mass by 6%, with VO₂peak +9% and peak cardiac output +7%. Removing blood to return red-cell volume to its pre-training value lowered VO₂peak by 7% and cardiac output by 10%, although the capillary-to-fibre ratio (+18%) and mitochondrial volume density (+43%) stayed elevated [@Montero2015_haematologicalVO2peak]. In this study, after six weeks of training, O₂ delivery rather than muscle oxidative capacity limited VO₂max. Lundby and colleagues argue that red-cell volume expansion, with the stroke-volume rise it supports, is the main driver of training-induced VO₂max gains, and that stroke volume also adapts independently of red-cell volume [@Lundby2017_biologyVO2max]. The textbook link (theoretical here, not separately sourced): a larger circulating volume raises end-diastolic filling and, through the Frank-Starling relationship, stroke volume, while more red cells raise the O₂ carried per litre of cardiac output.

**Capillaries and mitochondria: the peripheral side** (human outcome and mechanistic)

Capillaries per fibre rose by about 10-15% with continuous, interval and sprint training alike, mostly within the first 4 weeks and only in untrained or moderately trained muscle [@Molmen2024_mitoCapillaryMetaRegression]. More capillaries enlarge the exchange surface and lengthen red-cell transit time, favouring O₂ diffusion (inference, consistent with the early extraction-dominated phase). After adjustment for frequency, duration and baseline fitness, mitochondrial content rose similarly with continuous training (23 ± 5%), interval training (27 ± 5%) and [[term:sit|sprint interval training (SIT)]] (27 ± 7%); per hour of exercise, SIT was about 2.3 times as time-efficient as longer intervals and 3.9 times as continuous work [@Molmen2024_mitoCapillaryMetaRegression]. Content and function can change separately: training volume appears to be the main determinant of mitochondrial content, and relative intensity an important determinant of respiratory function [@Granata2018_mitoContentVsFunction]. In a work-matched single-leg design, the interval leg gained more citrate synthase activity (10.2 vs 8.4 mmol/kg protein/min) and mass-specific OXPHOS capacity (complex I+II 58.2 vs 42.2 pmol O₂/s/mg) than the continuous leg [@MacInnis2017_singleLegHIITvsMICT].

**Signalling to mitochondrial biogenesis** (human mechanistic for AMPK and PGC-1α; theoretical for CaMKII and p38 MAPK)

Sourced: acute exercise raises nuclear [[term:pgc1a|PGC-1α]] protein, PGC-1α mRNA and p53 Ser15 phosphorylation in an intensity-dependent way; with repeated training, PGC-1α protein plateaus within a few sessions and then tracks training volume, and TFAM protein follows mitochondrial content [@Granata2018_PGC1aPrescription]. High-intensity interval cycling raised muscle [[term:ampk|AMPK]] activity by about 90% [@Apro2015_AMPKmTORC1]. Theoretical (standard model, not verified against a source in this programme's evidence base): contraction lowers [[term:phosphocreatine|phosphocreatine]] and raises AMP and ADP relative to ATP, activating AMPK; repeated sarcoplasmic-reticulum Ca²⁺ release activates CaMKII; mechanical, oxidative and metabolic stress activate p38 MAPK. These inputs are proposed to converge on PGC-1α transcription and activation, and PGC-1α then co-activates transcription factors (such as NRF-1, NRF-2 and ERRα) that drive nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and TFAM-dependent mtDNA expression: [[term:mitochondrial-biogenesis|mitochondrial biogenesis]].

Acute signalling does not automatically translate into long-term adaptation. Acute exercise-induced signals do not necessarily predict training adaptations [@Granata2018_mitoContentVsFunction], and the early VO₂max gain depended on blood volume, not on the 43% rise in mitochondrial density [@Montero2015_haematologicalVO2peak]. Programme choices therefore rest on training outcomes, not on which session produces the largest signalling response.

**Why speech tracks intensity** (human mechanistic correspondences; theoretical explanation)

In a systematic review of cardiopulmonary patients, the last stage at which speech was comfortable coincided with the first [[term:ventilatory-threshold|ventilatory threshold (VT1)]] in workload, VO₂ and heart rate [@Vieira2022_talkTestSR], and the stage at which speech first becomes difficult lies close to the ventilatory threshold [@Persinger2004_talkTest]. Theoretical (standard physiology, not separately sourced): above VT1, rising glycolytic flux increases lactate and H⁺ production; bicarbonate buffering of H⁺ releases extra CO₂, so ventilation rises out of proportion to VO₂ and competes with the controlled expiration that continuous speech needs. VT1 also sits close to the intensity of maximal fat oxidation [@Meixner2025_zone2MarkerVariability], and expert consensus defines [[term:zone-2|zone 2]] as the intensity just below the first threshold [@Sitko2025_zone2Consensus].
articles.evidence:
**Does aerobic training raise VO₂max in an untrained adult?** (established)

Yes, typically by about 5-6 mL/kg/min in trials lasting from a few weeks to a few months. In a Cochrane [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of healthy sedentary adults, HIIT raised VO₂max by 5.98 mL/kg/min versus no exercise ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 4.66 to 7.30; 16 [[term:rct|RCTs]], 517 people; moderate [[term:grade|GRADE certainty]]) [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. An earlier meta-analysis found +4.9 (continuous) and +5.5 mL/kg/min (intervals) versus controls, with larger gains in less-fit people [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA]. In the trial closest to your profile (untrained men, 12 weeks, 3 x 60 min per week), relative VO₂max rose 21.5% with continuous running and 24.2% with recreational football versus -5.0% in controls, partly because body mass fell 5.7-5.9 kg [@Milanovic2015_untrainedMenRunningRCT].

**Intervals, continuous work or sprints?** (probable for HIIT vs MICT; uncertain for 4 x 4 vs sprints)

| Comparison | VO₂max difference | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| HIIT vs MICT | +1.39 mL/kg/min (0.44 to 2.34) | 37 RCTs; low certainty [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT] |
| Intervals vs continuous | +1.2 mL/kg/min (±0.9) | larger with longer repetitions [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA] |
| SIT vs continuous | d 0.04 (-0.17 to 0.24) | similar, in less time [@Gist2014_SITmeta] |
| SIT vs MICT | g -0.004 (-0.08 to 0.07) | all studies at unclear risk of bias [@Bonafiglia2021_SITvsMICTbias] |

Protocol features matter more than labels. Even low-volume HIIT beat no exercise, but only intervals of 2 min or longer, 15 min or more of hard work per session and programmes of 4-12 weeks or longer outperformed MICT ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.65-1.07) [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA]. Across HIIT studies the mean gain was 0.51 L/min ([[term:i2|I²]] 70%), and in the subset using longer intervals every participant responded [@Bacon2013_VO2maxTrainabilityMA].

The 4 x 4 format (4 min at 90-95% HRmax, 3 min active recovery) raised VO₂max 7.2% in moderately trained men, more than work-matched continuous running; 15 s/15 s intervals gave 5.5% [@Helgerud2007_4x4RCT]. In well-trained men 4 x 4 gave +6.5% versus +3.3% for 8 x 20 s supramaximal intervals and no significant change for 10 x 30 s all-out sprints [@Hov2022_HIITvsSIT_RCT]. In women only 4 x 4 raised VO₂max (7.3%), and all-out treadmill sprinting caused 8 injuries versus none with 4 x 4 [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT]. These are small trials in trained people from one group, so superiority for an untrained man is uncertain.

**Dose and 'non-response'** (probable)

After 6 weeks, the share of people whose change stayed within measurement error was 69%, 40%, 29%, 0% and 0% at 1-5 x 60 min per week; two extra weekly sessions for 6 more weeks removed non-response in every individual, and haemoglobin-mass change was the strongest determinant of VO₂max change [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse]. Responses do vary: in HERITAGE, gains ranged from about zero to over 1 L/min, with up to 47% heritability [@Bouchard1999_HERITAGE]. But most individual-response studies lacked a non-exercising control group, so true variation cannot be separated from measurement error and day-to-day biology [@Williamson2017_individualResponseCritique].

**Is zone 2 special?** (probable: no)

The case for zone 2 as the optimal intensity rests largely on observational data from elite athletes training at very high volumes; training studies do not show it is optimal for mitochondrial or fat-oxidative capacity, and higher intensities matter more when weekly time is limited [@Storoschuk2025_zone2Review]. Common zone-2 markers disagree between individuals (coefficients of variation 6-29%) [@Meixner2025_zone2MarkerVariability].

**Judging intensity without a heart-rate monitor** (probable)

The talk test tracks the ventilatory threshold across walking, jogging, cycling, elliptical and stair exercise, but is impractical for hard intervals [@ReedPipe2014_talkTestReview; @Persinger2004_talkTest]. On Borg's 6-20 scale the [[term:lactate-threshold|lactate threshold]] fell at RPE 10.8 ± 1.8 and the individual anaerobic threshold at 13.6 ± 1.8, regardless of sex, age, activity status or mode [@Scherr2013_RPE]; across studies RPE's validity coefficients were only about 0.6 [@Chen2002_RPEvalidityMA]. Age equations give an HRmax of about 186-191 bpm at 31 [@Tanaka2001_HRmax; @Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax], but about 95% of individuals lie within ±21 bpm of the estimate [@Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax].

**Fitness, steps, sitting and health** (established association; causality uncertain)

Across 199 cohorts, high versus low cardiorespiratory fitness carried an all-cause mortality hazard ratio of 0.47 (0.39-0.56), and each 1-[[term:met|MET]] increment 11-17% lower risk (GRADE very low to moderate) [@Lang2024_CRFoverview; @Kodama2009_CRFmortalityMA]; treadmill-test data showed no upper limit [@Mandsager2018_CRFmortalityCohort]. In twins discordant for activity the more active twin did not live longer, suggesting shared genes explain part of the gradient [@Karvinen2015_twinsGenesMortality]. Compared with 2000 steps/day, 7000 was associated with mortality HR 0.53 (0.46-0.60) [@Ding2025_stepsHealthDoseResponse]; under 60, risk plateaued at about 8000-10,000 [@Paluch2022_stepsMortalityMA], though one analysis found no clear upper limit [@Banach2023_stepsMortalityMA] and another placed the largest estimated benefit near 8800 steps/day [@Stens2023_stepsDoseResponseMA], and the step-cardiovascular association was not significant under 60 over about 6 years [@Paluch2023_stepsCVDharmonisedMA]. People sitting over 8 h/day but in the most active quartile (about 60-75 min/day of moderate activity) had no excess mortality (HR 1.04, 0.99-1.10) [@Ekelund2016_sittingActivityMortality]. WHO recommends 150-300 min/week of moderate or 75-150 min/week of vigorous aerobic activity, plus muscle strengthening on 2 or more days [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines].

**Fat loss** (established: modest)

Each 30 min/week of aerobic exercise reduced weight by 0.52 kg (0.44-0.61), waist by 0.56 cm and body fat by 0.37 percentage points, roughly linearly to 300 min/week, in trials mostly of overweight or obese adults [@Jayedi2024_aerobicWeightLossDoseResponse]. HIIT and MICT reduced fat mass and waist similarly [@Wewege2017_HIITvsMICTbodyComp; @Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Loss falls short of prediction mainly because intake rises, by 91-124 kcal/day in one RCT [@Martin2019_EMECHANIC].
articles.practice:
- **Mostly easy, some hard.** Most aerobic minutes are conversational ([[ex:cardio-steady]], [[ex:cardio-long]]): you can still speak in full sentences. This volume builds blood volume and capillaries at little recovery cost and, on average, does not measurably reduce strength or muscle gains ([[sci:sci-concurrent]]). Modality, dose and intensity for [[phase:p1]] are set in [[dec:D11]].
- **Intervals for VO₂max.** Introductory intervals ([[ex:cardio-int-intro]]) teach pacing before 4 x 4 min ([[ex:cardio-int-4x4]]), the long-interval format with the most direct support; the protocol and its place in the week are in [[dec:D13]]. Sprint work, if used, is done on a bike ([[ex:cardio-sprint]]), not all-out on a treadmill [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT].
- **Intensity by speech and effort.** Use the talk test for easy work and RPE for intervals ([[tool:intensity]]). If you buy a wearable, treat formula-based heart-rate zones as approximate and follow RPE and speech when they disagree ([[dec:D25]]).
- **Progression.** Sessions progress under [[rule:cardio-progression]]; running enters as run-walk under [[rule:running]] ([[dec:D14]], [[sci:sci-athletic]]).
- **Steps and sitting.** Even 150-200 min/week of structured cardio averages only 20-30 min/day, well short of the 60-75 min/day associated with offsetting long sitting (inference from [@Ekelund2016_sittingActivityMortality]). Daily walking and breaks during the 16:00-01:00 shift are covered in [[plan:activity]] and [[dec:D24]].
- **Testing and non-response.** Your aerobic tests ([[ex:test-rockport]] in Phases 0-1, [[ex:test-run-2400]] from Phase 2 once you can run 20+ minutes, and [[ex:test-rhr]]; [[dec:D03]]) are repeated under the same conditions. Treat small changes as noise; if two re-tests show nothing, the evidence-based response is more weekly training, not a verdict on your genes [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse].
- **Fat loss.** Cardio helps modestly; the energy balance itself is set through diet ([[sci:sci-energy]]).
articles.uncertainties:
- Whether 4 x 4 beats sprint intervals or continuous training for an untrained man is unsettled: the head-to-head RCTs are small, in trained adults and from one group, and mitochondrial gains were similar across modes [@Molmen2024_mitoCapillaryMetaRegression].
- All HIIT in the Cochrane review was supervised [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]; how well unsupervised intervals work for someone training alone is unknown.
- How much of the fitness-mortality and steps-mortality gradients is causal is unclear, so raising your own fitness may not cut your risk proportionally [@Karvinen2015_twinsGenesMortality].
- Fat-loss dose-response data come from overweight, mostly older adults; the effect in a lean young man who tracks intake is unknown.
- Your individual response cannot be predicted in advance, and the typical error of your own field tests is unknown, so a single re-test can mislead.
- No source addresses whether training one hour after waking on a 04:00-12:00 sleep schedule alters aerobic adaptation, or how accurate wrist heart-rate devices are during intervals.

What would change the recommendations: a laboratory test giving your measured HRmax and thresholds; RCTs comparing interval formats in untrained men; flat re-tests despite good adherence (add volume first).

articles.title: Lifting and aerobic training together
articles.tagline: Why aerobic work barely dents a beginner's strength and muscle gains, where the real costs lie, and how your week is arranged around them.
articles.summary:
[[term:concurrent-training|Concurrent training]] means doing resistance and aerobic training in the same programme. A long-standing worry, the [[term:interference-effect|interference effect]], is that aerobic work blunts gains in muscle size and strength. For a beginner the evidence is reassuring.

In an updated [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]], adding aerobic training to lifting made essentially no difference to maximal strength or whole-muscle growth ([[term:smd|standardised mean differences]] of -0.06 and -0.01) [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA], and an umbrella review of meta-analyses agreed, while finding that aerobic capacity improved more with combined training [@Held2026_CTumbrella]. Strength interference shows up mainly in already trained lifters [@Petre2021_trainingStatusMA].

Smaller penalties are real. Explosive strength is blunted when both are done in the same session, but not when they are at least three hours apart [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA]. Men may gain a little less lower-body strength [@Huiberts2023_sexStatusMA], and running may slow the growth of slow-twitch fibres [@Lundberg2022_fiberMA]. Lifting first and doing cardio second gives slightly larger lower-body strength gains without costing muscle growth or aerobic fitness [@Eddens2018_sequenceMA; @Murlasits2017_sequenceMA].

The molecular explanation, in which the energy sensor [[term:ampk|AMPK]] switches off the growth regulator [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]], has not held up well in human muscle [@Apro2015_AMPKmTORC1].

For you: lift first when the two share a session, keep hard intervals away from your heaviest leg training, and watch whether your lower-body lifts keep progressing. Cutting cardio pre-emptively would cost fitness and health benefits for no demonstrated gain in muscle.
articles.mechanisms:
**The hypothesis** (theoretical model)

Endurance-type signalling, notably activation of AMPK, can in principle inhibit mTORC1-dependent [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] and promote [[term:mpb|muscle protein breakdown (MPB)]], so aerobic work might blunt [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] [@Fyfe2014_interferenceReview]. The molecular routes in the standard model are theoretical here (not verified against a source in this programme's evidence base): AMPK phosphorylates TSC2, enhancing its GTPase-activating activity toward Rheb, so less GTP-bound Rheb is available to activate mTORC1 at the lysosome; AMPK also phosphorylates raptor, inhibiting mTORC1 directly. Less mTORC1 activity would mean less phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1, and so less translation initiation. On the breakdown side, endurance stress is proposed to raise expression of muscle-specific ubiquitin ligases such as MuRF1. Resistance exercise, meanwhile, activates mTORC1 through [[term:mechanotransduction|mechanotransduction]] ([[sci:sci-hypertrophy]]).

**The direct human test** (human mechanistic, randomised crossover in trained men)

Interval cycling before resistance exercise raised muscle AMPK activity by about 90%, yet S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation, S6K1 kinase activity (+55% at 90 min, +110% at 180 min) and eEF2 dephosphorylation rose equally with or without the prior cycling: mTORC1 signalling was not inhibited. Only the combined session raised MuRF1 mRNA and protein, pointing to a possible effect on proteolysis rather than on synthesis signalling [@Apro2015_AMPKmTORC1]. A review of acute human concurrent-exercise studies likewise found no molecular interference able to explain compromised hypertrophy [@Fyfe2014_interferenceReview].

Acute signalling does not automatically translate into long-term adaptation, in either direction. An intact S6K1 response after one session does not prove that months of combined training are free of cost, and a transient MuRF1 rise does not prove net muscle loss. Training outcomes settle the question.

**Why the effect is weak in vivo** (sourced observations plus labelled inference)

1. Outcome data show little or no whole-muscle hypertrophy deficit at the modest endurance doses studied [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA; @Held2026_CTumbrella; @MonserdaVilaro2022_CTtypeMA].
2. Strength interference appears mainly in trained people [@Petre2021_trainingStatusMA], consistent with untrained muscle responding to almost any novel stimulus (inference).
3. The decrement that does appear is in explosive strength in same-session designs, and it disappears with 3 h or more between modes [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA]. That pattern points to acute neuromuscular fatigue lowering the quality of the second session, rather than chronic molecular antagonism (inference).
4. Fibre-level effects are fibre-type- and mode-specific: running blunted type I fibre growth (SMD -0.81) while cycling did not [@Lundberg2022_fiberMA]. Whole-muscle AMPK-mTORC1 antagonism does not predict that; the greater eccentric loading and impact of running is one possible explanation (theoretical).
5. AMPK activation is transient, whereas the protein-synthesis response to resistance exercise lasts hours, so the two overlap only partly (theoretical, not tested in these sources).

**A fatigue-and-recovery model** (inference)

For a beginner the more useful mechanism is practical. Hard aerobic work shortly before lifting lowers the force, velocity or repetitions you can produce, and a chronic shortfall in session quality would slowly reduce the training stimulus. Leg-heavy intervals also add to the recovery demand on the same muscles. This model fits the order and separation findings in the evidence section, and it is what the scheduling rules guard against.
articles.evidence:
**Does aerobic training blunt strength and muscle growth?** (probable: not measurably, at modest doses, in untrained people)

| Analysis | Comparison | Main result | Certainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schumann 2021 [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA] | concurrent vs strength-only | maximal strength SMD -0.06 (-0.20 to 0.09); hypertrophy -0.01 (-0.16 to 0.18); explosive strength -0.28 (-0.48 to -0.08) | moderate |
| Held 2026, umbrella review [@Held2026_CTumbrella] | concurrent vs resistance-only | strength, power and hypertrophy comparable; aerobic capacity better (SMD 0.77) | moderate |
| Petré 2021 [@Petre2021_trainingStatusMA] | lower-body [[term:1rm|1RM]] by training status | untrained ES 0.03; moderately trained -0.20; trained -0.35 | moderate |
| Huiberts 2023 [@Huiberts2023_sexStatusMA] | by sex | lower-body strength blunted in men (SMD -0.43, -0.64 to -0.22), not women | low |
| Lundberg 2022 [@Lundberg2022_fiberMA] | fibre size | overall SMD -0.23 (-0.46 to -0.00); type I fibres with running -0.81 | low |
| Wilson 2012 [@Wilson2012_concurrentMA] | within-group pre-post | hypertrophy ES 1.23 strength-only vs 0.85 concurrent; power 0.91 vs 0.55 | low |

The two moderate-certainty syntheses agree that, for maximal strength and whole-muscle size, the average penalty is close to zero; Schumann found no moderation by running versus cycling, by more or fewer than 5 weekly concurrent sessions, or by untrained versus active status. Petré located the strength decrement in trained people. The older Wilson analysis (within-group effect sizes, not between-group comparisons) reported smaller gains with concurrent training, worse with running, and negative correlations of gains with endurance frequency (r -0.26 to -0.35) and session duration (r -0.29 to -0.75). Two signals matter for you: the male lower-body strength penalty (Huiberts, whose hypertrophy data were insufficient for conclusions) and the type I fibre penalty with running (Lundberg). In the other direction, untrained participants gained slightly less VO₂max with concurrent than with endurance-only training (p = 0.04) [@Huiberts2023_sexStatusMA], whereas the umbrella review found similar aerobic gains [@Held2026_CTumbrella].

**Does the type of aerobic training matter?** (uncertain)

Adding [[term:hiit|HIIT]] left hypertrophy and upper-body strength gains unchanged but slightly reduced lower-body strength gains (ES -0.248, p = 0.049), with longer rest between modes appearing protective [@Sabag2018_HIITconcurrentMA]. Squat 1RM was unaffected by added HIIT (SMD -0.06), but short- and long-interval formats impaired jump gains (SMD -0.53) whereas sprint formats did not (SMD 0.14) [@Kikuchi2026_HIITconcurrentMA]. At whole-muscle level no concurrent format differed from resistance-only (SMD below 0.03); at fibre level, programmes containing HIIT produced smaller fibre growth than resistance-only (SMD above 0.27), whereas continuous-only programmes did not [@MonserdaVilaro2022_CTtypeMA]. Running versus cycling: analyses disagree in direction (running worse in Wilson and Lundberg; a trend for cycling HIIT to impair lower-body strength, ES -0.377, p = 0.074, in Sabag; no moderation in Schumann).

**Same session or separate, and in which order?** (probable)

Explosive-strength attenuation was significant in same-session designs but not with 3 h or more between modes [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA]. In trained people the 1RM decrement appeared only with same-session training (ES -0.66, versus -0.10 for separate sessions) [@Petre2021_trainingStatusMA]. Within a session, resistance-then-endurance gave larger lower-body dynamic strength gains (+6.91 percentage points, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 1.96 to 11.87) with no difference in hypertrophy, VO₂max or body fat [@Eddens2018_sequenceMA]; a second meta-analysis found +3.96 kg (0.81 to 7.10) in lower-body 1RM with strength first and no effect on VO₂max (0.39 mL/kg/min, -1.03 to 1.81) [@Murlasits2017_sequenceMA]. The umbrella review found no significant sequence effect overall, with non-significant trends favouring resistance first [@Held2026_CTumbrella].

**Population caveats**

Trials used modest endurance doses, typically 2-3 sessions a week for weeks to a few months; compatibility at 4 or more weekly sessions, or 200-300 min a week over longer periods, is untested. The pooled data include women, older adults and trained lifters; none of the trials matches a 31-year-old untrained man training alone at 13:00 on a late sleep schedule, so applying the averages to you is an inference.
articles.practice:
Your week follows from four findings: the average penalty for a beginner is near zero, lifting first protects lower-body strength, hard intervals blunt explosive and jump gains when done in the same session, and a second session three or more hours later is impractical with a 16:00-01:00 shift (inference).

| Session | Where it goes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Easy cardio ([[ex:cardio-steady]], [[ex:cd-easy]]) | after any lifting session, or on its own | no measurable cost to strength or growth |
| Intervals ([[ex:cardio-int-4x4]]) | after upper-body lifting or on a non-lifting day, at least a day from the heaviest leg session | same-session HIIT blunts explosive strength and jump gains |
| Jumps ([[ex:plyo-pogo]], [[ex:plyo-box-jump]]) | early in a session while fresh, not after intervals | power work is the most fatigue-sensitive quality (practical convention) |
| Long easy session or class ([[ex:cardio-long]]) | a non-lifting day | adds volume without competing with lifting |

- **Lift first** when lifting and cardio share a session. A 5-10 min easy warm-up ([[ex:wu-cardio-easy]]) is not what the order trials tested and is fine (practical convention).
- **Do not cut cardio pre-emptively.** Each week, compare your main lower-body lift with your main upper-body lift in Hevy. If lower-body performance stalls for about 3 weeks while upper-body lifts progress and sleep, food and body weight are stable, first move intervals further from leg training, then reduce interval volume (drop any extra interval session added under the non-response check, or do 3 instead of 4 intervals). These thresholds are inferences; the general stall procedure is in [[rule:stall]].
- The split is set in [[dec:D05]] and [[dec:D12]], aerobic dose in [[dec:D11]] and interval scheduling in [[dec:D13]]; the aerobic side is explained in [[sci:sci-aerobic]].
articles.uncertainties:
- Trial endurance doses were modest. Whether interference appears in untrained men above about 4 sessions or 200-300 min of aerobic work a week, sustained beyond 16 weeks, is unknown; an older analysis linked higher endurance frequency and duration with smaller gains (low certainty) [@Wilson2012_concurrentMA].
- Whether running or cycling is the better partner for lifting is unresolved; analyses disagree in direction.
- Averages hide individual spread; the male lower-body signal [@Huiberts2023_sexStatusMA] may or may not apply to you.
- Interference grows with training status [@Petre2021_trainingStatusMA], but no source defines when a lifter becomes 'trained', so the balance may shift in later phases.
- No study has tested how an interval session affects lifting the next day; the one-day buffer is a hedge.
- Most trials measure whole-muscle size over weeks to months; whether small fibre-level costs (type I fibres with running) add up over years is unknown.

What would change the plan: lower-body lifts stalling while upper-body lifts progress; work hours that allow two sessions a day; a shift toward endurance or combat-sport goals.

articles.title: Running, jumping, balance, agility and coordination
articles.tagline: Why tendons and bones set the pace for a new runner and jumper, what plyometrics and balance training actually change, and how to progress without spikes.
articles.summary:
Running, jumping, balance and agility are all trainable, but the tissues involved adapt at different speeds. Muscles and the nervous system respond within weeks; tendons and bones take months. Many beginner injuries are thought to come from load rising faster than the slow tissues can follow (a framework, not a proven mechanism).

Novice runners are injured about twice as often per hour of running as established runners [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence]. The classic '10% per week' rule did not reduce injuries in a trial [@Buist2008_GRONORUN]; in a large cohort of mostly experienced runners, the clearest warning sign was a single run much longer than anything done in the previous month [@Frandsen2025_spikes]. Choose running shoes by comfort rather than by foot type [@Relph2022_shoesCochrane; @Malisoux2025_comfortperception].

[[term:plyometrics|Plyometric]] (jump) training improves jump height, [[term:rsi|reactive strength]], balance and, a little, muscle size [@Markovic2007_vertjump; @RamirezCampillo2023_RSI; @Ramachandran2021_plyobalance; @Arntz2022_hypertrophy]. Balance training works, but mostly for the exact task practised [@Kummel2016_specificity], and agility behaves like a skill too [@NygaardFalch2019_COD]. Dance, martial arts and group walks are enjoyable alternatives with modest evidence.

In trials in sport and military settings, strength training was the most protective exercise type against sports injuries, and stretching did not prevent them [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention; @Lauersen2018_strength]. Lifting and jumping also load bone, which responds slowly and modestly in adult men [@Mages2021_menBMD].

For you: start running as run-walk and cap each run against your recent longest; add low-volume jump blocks; train balance with tasks that resemble what you want to improve, starting with your weaker left leg; and treat your lifting programme as the main injury protection.
articles.mechanisms:
**Tissues adapt at different speeds** (theoretical framework)

A common model treats a running or jumping injury as a mismatch between the load placed on a tissue and its current capacity. Capacity grows with loading, but at tissue-specific rates: the nervous system and muscle quickly, tendon and bone slowly. The model fits the epidemiology in the evidence section, but no study in this programme's evidence base measured tissue capacity directly, so it remains a framework rather than a tested mechanism.

**Tendon: slow matrix renewal, faster material change** (human mechanistic and human outcome)

Bomb-pulse ¹⁴C dating shows that the collagen of the adult Achilles tendon core carries the atmospheric ¹⁴C signature of roughly the first 17 years of life: the load-bearing scaffold is laid down during growth and essentially not renewed in adulthood, whereas skeletal muscle turns over continuously [@Heinemeier2013_tendon14C]. Yet exercise clearly stimulates tendon collagen synthesis: after one-legged kicking, patellar-tendon collagen fractional synthesis rose within 6 h, peaked at about 24 h (0.077%/h, versus 0.121%/h for myofibrillar protein) and was still raised at 72 h [@Miller2005_tendoncollagen]. One reconciliation (theoretical; degradation was not measured) is that new collagen enters a small, more labile pool at the tendon periphery or in less cross-linked fibrils without renewing the core. Over weeks to months of loading, tendon stiffness rises mainly because the material stiffens (modulus SMD 0.82) rather than because the tendon thickens (cross-sectional area SMD 0.22), and high-strain (heavy) resistance protocols raise modulus and stiffness more than low-strain ones [@Lazarczuk2022_tendon]. How modulus rises without core renewal (cross-link profile, fibril packing, non-collagenous matrix, hydration) was not measured (theoretical). Practical consequence (inference): in a novice, muscle strength and power can outpace tendon adaptation, a plausible but untested reason for tendon pain when jumping and running volumes rise quickly.

**The stretch-shortening cycle** (human mechanistic)

Running and jumping use the [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]]: muscles are activated before ground contact, stretched under load (the [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] phase) and immediately shorten (the [[term:concentric|concentric]] phase), with a strong short-latency stretch-reflex contribution [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Elastic recoil of tendon and aponeurosis and potentiation of the contractile machinery are the usual additional explanations (background, not detailed in the sources). Plyometric training improves the reactive strength index (jump height relative to ground-contact time) [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI] and leg stiffness [@Moran2023_stiffness]: the leg spring returns load within a shorter contact, consistent with stiffer tendons plus altered pre-activation and reflex timing (the neural part is inferred, not measured). The spring is tuned to conditions: on softer surfaces runners stiffen the leg, so peak vertical force and loading rate stay unchanged while tibial acceleration falls [@Mitchell2023_surface]. Exhaustive stretch-shortening exercise produces two-phase fatigue: an immediate loss, partial recovery within 1-2 h, then a secondary decline usually deepest on day 2, coinciding with soreness ([[term:doms|DOMS]]) [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Hard jump sessions therefore leave a multi-day footprint.

**Sensorimotor adaptation: balance is learned task by task** (human mechanistic; interpretation theoretical)

Balance training induces plasticity at spinal (H-reflex) and supraspinal levels, shown with electrophysiology, transcranial magnetic stimulation and imaging [@Taube2008_balancemech]. Behavioural gains are strongly task-specific: large on the practised task and negligible on unpractised tasks, even with a similar posture [@Kummel2016_specificity]. What is learned therefore looks like a task-specific control strategy (in motor-learning terms, an internal model) rather than a general balance capacity (theoretical). Plyometric training improves balance about as much as balance training does [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance], pointing to shared components such as faster, better-timed ankle and knee muscle activation (theoretical). These neural changes are measurable within weeks, far faster than tendon or bone remodelling (inference).

**Bone: osteocyte mechanotransduction** (pathway mainly from animal and cell studies; human biomarker corroboration)

Osteocytes, embedded in mineralised matrix, sense mechanical stimulation and coordinate formation and resorption through the RANKL/OPG and sclerostin (Sost)/Dkk1/Wnt axes [@Robling2020_osteocyte]. Background biochemistry (textbook, theoretical here): sclerostin and Dkk1 bind the LRP5/6 co-receptor and block canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling in osteoblast-lineage cells, so loading-induced suppression of Sost releases a brake on bone formation; OPG is a decoy receptor that neutralises RANKL and limits osteoclastogenesis; the sensed stimulus is thought to be load-driven fluid flow through the lacunar-canalicular network, with dynamic, high-rate, unaccustomed loads more osteogenic than many repetitions of habitual loading. In men with low bone mass, 12 months of resistance or jump training lowered serum sclerostin and raised IGF-I while PTH was unchanged, consistent with mechanically driven Wnt disinhibition [@Hinton2017_sclerostin]. Serum sclerostin is an imperfect proxy for its expression in bone, and those men were older and osteopenic.
articles.evidence:
**Novice running injuries and progression** (probable for incidence; uncertain for progression rules)

Novices were injured at 17.8 per 1000 h of running ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 16.7-19.1) versus 7.7 for recreational runners [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence]. Knee, foot/ankle and lower leg account for about three-quarters of running injuries [@Fredette2022_trainingparams]; no previous running experience and male sex were moderate-quality risk factors [@vanPoppel2021_riskfactors].

| Study | Design | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Buist 2008 [@Buist2008_GRONORUN] | [[term:rct|RCT]], novices | '10% rule' 13-week plan vs 8-week plan: injuries 20.8% vs 20.3% |
| Frandsen 2025 [@Frandsen2025_spikes] | cohort, about 5200 runners | one run 10-30% longer than the 30-day longest: hazard rate ratio 1.64 (1.31-2.05); over 100% longer: 2.28; weekly workload ratios not associated |
| Nielsen 2014 [@Nielsen2014_progression] | cohort, novices | over 30% vs under 10% two-week progression: no overall difference; distance-related injuries HR 1.59 (0.96-2.66) |
| Bertelsen 2018 [@Bertelsen2018_starttorun] | RCT, obese novices | 3 vs 6 km/week start: risk difference -16.3% (-43.8 to 11.3); very low certainty |
| Ramskov 2018 [@Ramskov2018_RunClever] | RCT, recreational | progressing intensity vs volume: risk difference -14.0% (-36.9 to 8.9) |

Full compliance with prescribed schedules in these trials was very low (0 of 839 to 12 of 56; 8 of 532 in the 10%-rule trial), so null results test being handed a schedule, not following it [@Nielsen2020_compliance]. Links between weekly distance, frequency or intensity and injury are conflicting overall [@Fredette2022_trainingparams]. The session spike is the clearest signal, but it comes from mostly experienced runners.

**Cadence, shoes and surface** (uncertain; probable for not choosing shoes by foot type)

A higher step rate reduces knee flexion ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.66), knee-extensor moment, hip adduction and patellofemoral stress [@Anderson2022_steprate], and +5-10% at the same speed reduced energy absorbed at the knee [@Heiderscheit2011_steprate], yet step rate did not predict injury prospectively [@Malisoux2022_biomechrisk]. Shoes prescribed by foot posture did not reduce injury (rate ratio 1.03, 0.94-1.13; moderate certainty) [@Relph2022_shoesCochrane], and pronated feet in neutral shoes were not at excess risk [@Nielsen2014_pronation]. Harder midsoles raised risk (SHR 1.52, 1.07-2.16), mainly in lighter runners [@Malisoux2020_cushioning], and runners who perceived more cushioning or liked their shoes most had fewer injuries (HR 0.24-0.47) [@Malisoux2025_comfortperception], early support for the 'comfort filter' idea [@Nigg2015_comfortfilter]. Softer surfaces lowered tibial acceleration but not peak force or loading rate [@Mitchell2023_surface].

**Plyometrics** (probable)

| Outcome | Effect |
|---|---|
| Countermovement jump | +8.7% (7.0-10.4) [@Markovic2007_vertjump] |
| Reactive strength index | ES 0.54 (0.46-0.62), moderate certainty [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI] |
| Leg stiffness | ES 0.33; untrained 0.46; no benefit above 500 jumps/week [@Moran2023_stiffness] |
| Balance | ES 0.46, similar to balance training [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance] |
| Muscle size | SMD 0.47 (0.23-0.71); non-athletes 0.55 [@Arntz2022_hypertrophy] |
| Running economy at 12 km/h or slower | ES -0.31, in runners [@LlanosLagos2024_RE] |

Programmes longer than 7 weeks with more than 14 sessions worked better, more than about 1080 total jumps added nothing for reactive strength, and most studies did not report soreness or injury [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI]; added weight gave no extra jump benefit [@deVillarreal2009_dose]. Plyometrics alone did not significantly improve running performance, whereas heavy and combined strength training did [@LlanosLagos2024_performance].

**Balance and agility** (probable for balance; uncertain for agility)

Balance training improved steady-state balance (ES 0.73; untrained 0.82), most with about 11-12 weeks, 3 sessions/week, 11-15 min per session, 4 exercises, 2 sets and 21-40 s bouts [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR], but transfer to untrained tasks was negligible (SMD -0.07 to 0.18) [@Kummel2016_specificity]. Men aged 18-39 tested barefoot with arms crossed (best of 3, 45 s cap) reached 44.4 s (SD 4.1) eyes open and 16.9 s (SD 13.9) eyes closed [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. Your eyes-closed times (10 and 15 s) fall within that spread; your eyes-open times (20 and 30 s) fall well below it, which may partly reflect a different protocol (inference). Dominant and non-dominant legs do not differ in healthy people (SMD about 0) [@Schorderet2021_dominance], so a persistent one-third gap would be unusual. Change-of-direction ability improved with plyometric, strength, sprint and specific drills, with no clear winner, and behaves as a task-specific skill [@NygaardFalch2019_COD].

**Dance, martial arts and walking** (uncertain)

Dance improved body composition and musculoskeletal function more than other structured exercise, with equivalent cardiovascular effects [@FongYan2018_danceMA]. Hard martial arts showed benefits in methodologically weak studies [@OriguaRios2018_martialarts]; combat sports in students improved standing long jump (ES 1.04) and sit-and-reach (ES 0.80) but not VO₂max [@HernandezMartinez2025_combatsports]. Walking groups raised VO₂max by 2.66 mL/kg/min and lowered systolic pressure by 3.72 mmHg [@Hanson2015_walkinggroups].

**Injury prevention and bone** (probable for strength training; uncertain for bone)

Strength training reduced sports injuries (RR 0.315 and 0.338, dose-dependent), [[term:proprioception|proprioception]] training less (RR 0.550, mostly in team sports) and stretching not at all (RR 0.963, 0.846-1.095) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention; @Lauersen2018_strength]. In adult novice runners, a supervised hip-and-core programme before runs reduced injuries versus [[term:static-stretching|static stretching]] (HR 0.66, 0.45-0.97) [@Leppanen2024_RunRCT], but pooled runner programmes were null, with a benefit only for supervised programmes in a post-hoc analysis [@Wu2024_runnerprevention]. Exercise raised bone mineral density in men modestly (spine SMD 0.38, femoral neck 0.25) [@Mages2021_menBMD]; in men with low bone mass, resistance and jump training both raised spine BMD over 12 months, but only resistance training raised hip BMD [@Hinton2015_jumpRT].
articles.practice:
- **Running starts as run-walk** ([[ex:cardio-runwalk]]; [[dec:D14]]). Progression follows a session-spike rule rather than the 10% weekly rule: each run is capped relative to your longest run of the previous 30 days, and targets are recalculated from what you actually logged ([[rule:running]], [[tool:running]]). Pain at the knee, shin, foot or hip that is still there the next morning means repeating, not progressing ([[rule:pain]]; practical convention, in the spirit of the [[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring model]]).
- **Shoes and surface:** choose neutral, cushioned running shoes by comfort; gait analysis to select stability shoes is not needed. Road or treadmill both work; in midday heat the treadmill is the sensible default (practical convention).
- **Cadence:** no target while you are pain-free. If front-of-knee pain appears, a 5-10% higher step rate at the same speed is a reasonable trial (inference from biomechanical data).
- **Plyometrics** ([[ex:plyo-pogo]], [[ex:plyo-box-jump]], [[ex:plyo-broad-jump]], [[ex:plyo-lateral-bound]], [[ex:plyo-mb-throw]]): the evidence favours blocks of 7-10 weeks or more, modest contact counts (well under 500 jumps a week) and sessions done fresh, at least 48 h apart (the spacing is practical convention); the structure is set in [[dec:D17]].
- **Balance** ([[ex:bal-sls]], [[ex:bal-sl-reach]]): practise tasks that resemble what you want to improve. [[term:unilateral|Unilateral]] work starts with the left leg, and the asymmetry is re-tested under the standard protocol ([[ex:test-sls]]) before it is treated as real ([[dec:D28]]).
- **Agility and coordination** ([[ex:agi-shuffle]], [[ex:agi-ladder]]): a short change-of-direction block is enough alongside strength and jump training; for coordination, learning a real skill such as a dance style or martial art is likely to transfer better than generic drills (inference from task specificity). Classes and hikes can fill a long easy slot ([[ex:cardio-long]]).
- **Injury prevention** is mainly your lifting programme; stretching serves flexibility, not prevention ([[sci:sci-flexibility]]).
- **Bone** needs no separate programme: heavy lifting, jumps and running supply the load (inference).
articles.uncertainties:
- The session-spike threshold comes from mostly experienced runners (mean age about 46); whether it applies to young novices doing run-walk, and whether capping sessions actually prevents injury, is untested.
- Whether run-walk reduces injuries compared with continuous running is unknown.
- Whether an unsupervised hip-and-core routine reproduces the supervised Run RCT effect is unknown, and that trial's ankle-and-foot arm was associated with more acute injuries [@Leppanen2024_RunRCT].
- Safe plyometric contact limits for untrained adults who also run are not established, and the best frequency differs by outcome (three sessions a week for reactive strength, two or fewer for stiffness).
- Whether your low eyes-open stance times are a true deficit or a protocol artefact, and whether the left-right gap is stable across days, needs a standardised re-test.
- Transfer of generic coordination drills to dance, martial arts or hiking is unstudied, and no injury data for beginner martial-arts classes were found.
- Bone data in healthy men aged 18-40 are sparse, and whether an energy deficit blunts the response is unknown.

What would change the plan: pain recurring at a particular run length, tendon pain after jump sessions, or re-test results.

articles.title: Warm-ups, stretching and flexibility
articles.tagline: How to warm up one hour after waking, when stretching helps or costs you, and what actually changes when flexibility improves.
articles.summary:
A warm-up makes the session that follows go slightly better, and it probably matters more for you than for most people: at 13:00 you are about one hour into your biological day, which behaves like early morning for a conventional sleeper. About 6 min of easy whole-body movement, a few dynamic drills, single-leg balance and two or three lighter [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] make up your warm-up; the best dose is uncertain.

Holding a [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for 60 s or more per muscle immediately before lifting costs a few per cent of strength; holds under about 30 s, or holds followed by more warm-up activity, cost very little. [[term:dynamic-stretching|Dynamic stretching]] carries no such cost. Stretching before a session also does not appear to prevent injury.

Flexibility itself is very trainable. Regular stretching increases [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] by about one standard deviation on average, and resistance training through a full range improves it by a similar amount. Over the first weeks most of the gain is greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]]: your nervous system accepts more stretch before it calls a halt. Longer and more intense programmes also make the muscle itself less stiff. Gains partly fade within weeks of stopping, so a smaller maintenance dose is needed once you reach your goal.

Stretching at normal doses does not build muscle, does not weaken it over time and does not meaningfully reduce soreness. Lifting does not make you less flexible. A cool-down does not speed recovery; yours is 2 min of easy movement followed by stretches for range of motion.

For you this means a fixed warm-up template before every session, hamstring stretches (2 × 30 s per leg at about 7/10) in every cool-down, about 5 min per leg a week, plus an optional 5-minute home routine, and the toe-touch and knee-to-wall tests repeated every 4-6 weeks under identical conditions.
articles.mechanisms:
**Why a warm-up helps: temperature plus neural readiness (human mechanistic; cellular detail theoretical).** Body temperature is the factor most often linked to time-of-day differences in performance [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation]. As background physiology (not measured in these studies), cross-bridge cycling, myosin ATPase activity, Ca^2+^ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and its re-uptake by SERCA, and nerve and muscle-fibre conduction velocity all accelerate with temperature, so warmer muscle develops and relaxes force faster. Warmer connective tissue and the viscous component of muscle also resist lengthening less, fitting the 2.4 cm flexibility gain after a 30-min rather than a 5-min morning warm-up [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility]. Temperature is not the whole story: passive heating was largely ineffective as a warm-up [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup], and a morning warm-up that raised rectal temperature to evening values did not restore evening lifting performance [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts]. Neural activation, serum biomarkers, oxygen-uptake kinetics and [[term:chronotype|chronotype]] also contribute [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation], consistent with central and muscle [[term:circadian-rhythm|circadian]] clocks imposing a daily rhythm on neuromuscular readiness (theoretical; see [[sci:sci-sleep]]). Because performance tracks internal time and habitual sleep timing [@FacerChilds2018_chronotype], a session one hour after waking sits in your biological morning (inference).

**Specific warm-up sets (theoretical).** Sets approaching the working load raise local muscle temperature, increase neural drive (more [[term:motor-unit|motor units]] recruited, faster firing) and rehearse the movement; a few light repetitions alone were judged insufficient [@Ribeiro2020_specific_warmup_RT]. Classic post-activation potentiation, in which myosin light-chain kinase phosphorylates the regulatory light chain and raises the Ca^2+^ sensitivity of force, decays within minutes, so any enhancement lasting through a session is usually attributed to temperature, intramuscular fluid shifts and neural factors. For a novice, rehearsing technique under progressively heavier loads is probably the largest benefit (inference).

**The acute stretch-induced force deficit (human mechanistic).** Force loss after static stretching follows a sigmoidal dose-response: trivial below about 30 s per muscle and consistent from about 60 s, whatever the task or contraction mode [@Kay2012_acute_static_stretch]. Performance at long muscle lengths improves slightly (+2.2%) while overall performance falls [@Behm2016_acute_stretching], and only long stretches reduce stiffness acutely [@Warneke2024_recalc_passive_properties]. Two mechanisms are proposed (theoretical). Mechanically, a more compliant muscle-tendon unit shifts the working range of the force-length relationship towards longer sarcomere lengths and slows force transmission to bone. Neurally, motor-unit activation falls transiently after a prolonged stretch. Their relative shares have not been apportioned. The higher muscle temperature of a full warm-up probably offsets part of the deficit [@Chaabene2019_static_stretching_review].

**Long-term ROM gains I: stretch tolerance (human mechanistic).** In a passive flexibility test the end point is where the sensation becomes intolerable, not a mechanical stop. After 3 weeks of hamstring stretching, the passive torque-angle curve (stiffness, energy absorbed and torque at a fixed knee angle) was unchanged and reflex EMG stayed small, yet participants accepted a larger angle at a higher peak torque [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance]. Reviews of 3-8-week programmes agree: a small rise in maximal tolerated torque with trivial change in muscle or tendon mechanics [@Freitas2018_chronic_stretch_mechanics; @Weppler2010_sensory_theory], and a recalculation confirmed that passive peak torque at end range rises (effect size 0.55) [@Warneke2024_recalc_passive_properties]. The joint simply travels further along an unchanged torque-angle curve. The neural substrate (sensitivity of thin-fibre muscle afferents, spinal or supraspinal processing, expectation and learning) has not been identified (theoretical). This probably explains why early gains come quickly and partly regress when stretching stops [@Konrad2025_detraining_ROM] (inference).

**Long-term ROM gains II: tissue remodelling (human mechanistic).** With longer, more intense or supervised stretching the muscle itself changes. Muscle stiffness falls (effect size -0.38 overall, -0.61 with long static stretching) while tendon stiffness does not [@Warneke2024_recalc_passive_properties]. Twelve weeks of calf stretching lowered shear-wave velocity, an elastography index of stiffness, by 0.8-2.3 m/s and lengthened gastrocnemius fascicles by 0.4 cm [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching]; across studies, fascicles lengthen only with high volumes and intensities [@Panidi2023_stretch_architecture_meta].
