The usual cellular explanations, sarcomeres added in series, remodelling of endomysial and perimysial collagen, and altered titin-based passive tension, were not measured (theoretical). Adaptation is tissue-specific: stretching that tensioned the sciatic nerve tract lowered nerve stiffness without changing muscle [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching]. A straight-knee toe touch loads the hamstrings, lumbopelvic structures and sciatic nerve together, so any of them could be your limiting tissue (inference).

**Why lifting improves ROM, and why stretching barely builds muscle (human outcome; mechanisms theoretical).** Resistance training through a full range repeatedly exposes muscle to controlled end-range tension, plausibly the same stimulus that drives tolerance and fascicle lengthening; body-mass-only training did not improve ROM significantly, hinting at a load threshold [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM]. [[term:hypertrophy|Hypertrophy]], by contrast, depends on active fibre tension sensed through [[term:mechanotransduction|mechanotransduction]] and converging on [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]] and its effector p70S6K. Passive stretch loads mainly titin and the extracellular matrix and generates little active tension, so a growth signal emerges only with very long exposure: in one 6-week trial, 1 h a day of calf stretching thickened the calf about as much as hypertrophy training [@Warneke2023_stretch_vs_RT_calf], whereas 30 min twice a week changed no architectural measure [@Yahata2021_high_volume_SS_null]. Any acute signalling a stretch produces would not automatically translate into long-term growth, and because short-term ROM gains are mainly sensory they do not track hypertrophy [@Arntz2024_SS_hypertrophy_meta].
articles.evidence:
| Question | Best estimate | Certainty |
|---|---|---|
| Does a warm-up help? | Better performance in 79% of criteria; little harm [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance] | Probable |
| Static stretch just before lifting | -1.1% with holds under 60 s, -4.6% with 60 s or more per muscle [@Behm2016_acute_stretching] | Probable |
| Regular stretching and ROM | Effect size about 1.0 (95% CI 0.84-1.17) [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM] | Established |
| Resistance training and ROM | Effect size 0.73, no different from stretching [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM] | Probable |
| Stretching and muscle size | SMD 0.118 (prediction interval -0.233 to 0.469) [@Arntz2024_SS_hypertrophy_meta] | Probable: negligible at practical doses |
| Stretching and injury | Relative risk (RR) 0.963 (95% CI 0.846-1.095) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention] | Probable |
| Cool-down and 48-h soreness | 0 mm (95% CI -11 to 11) on a 100-mm scale [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS] | Probable |

**Does warming up help, and what should it contain?** A [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 32 controlled studies found that warming up improved performance in 79% of the criteria examined, though as a vote count with no pooled effect size [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance]. In a review of 31 [[term:rct|RCTs]], high-load dynamic warm-ups improved upper-body strength and power, while passive heating or cooling was largely ineffective [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup]. In a crossover trial in 13 trained people, adding 20 min of cycling at 60% of maximal heart rate to the same specific warm-up raised leg-press [[term:1rm|1RM]] by 8.4% [@Abad2011_general_specific_warmup]. Warm-up sets reaching about 80% of the training load improved later bar velocity more than a few light repetitions (effect sizes 0.4-0.8, about 0.02 m/s) [@Ribeiro2020_specific_warmup_RT]. The three-layer model (general, specific, conditioning) is expert consensus, not outcome data [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi]. Certainty: probable that warming up helps; uncertain for the best dose. Outcomes were acute 1RM or bar speed in trained people, never repetitions in hypertrophy sets or long-term growth.

**Training one hour after waking.** In 10 trained men, evening average force was 2.6-3.3% and peak velocity 11.5-13.6% higher than in the morning, and a morning warm-up that raised rectal temperature to evening values did not close the gap [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts]. In 16 adults with clear morning or evening chronotypes, a 30-min rather than 5-min morning warm-up added about 2.4 cm of flexibility [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility]. Across 11 studies, long-term strength and size gains did not differ between morning and evening training, and strength adapted to the habitual training time [@Grgic2019_time_of_day_RT]. Certainty: probable for long-term equivalence; applying any of this to a 04:00-12:00 sleeper is inference, because no shifted sleepers were studied.

**Acute stretching.** Across 83 studies (2,012 participants), static stretching reduced maximal strength slightly versus passive controls (effect size -0.21), substantially with bouts of 60 s or more (-0.84) and slightly versus active controls (-0.17 to -0.28), while general athletic performance was not impaired [@Warneke2024_stretch_force_deficit]. Holds under 30 s averaged -1.1% and 30-45 s -1.9% [@Kay2012_acute_static_stretch]. Dynamic stretching gave +1.3% and [[term:pnf|PNF stretching]] -4.4%, and when dynamic activity followed the stretch there was no clear effect [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. Most trials tested 3-5 min after an isolated stretch, probably overstating the cost within a full warm-up. Stretching or foam rolling changed acute ROM no more than other warm-up activities (effect size 0.01) [@Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM]. Certainty: probable.

**Long-term stretching.** Across 77 studies the ROM gain versus control was about 1.0 ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 0.84-1.17) with high heterogeneity ([[term:i2|I²]] 75%); static and PNF beat dynamic or ballistic stretching, women gained more, and volume, intensity and frequency were not significant moderators [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]. A multilevel meta-analysis found a similar effect ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.96, 95% CI 0.70-1.22), larger with passive than active static stretching (0.97 vs 0.59), plus small strength gains (SMD 0.21) [@Arntz2023_chronic_SS_strength]. A smaller review linked at least 5 min a week and at least 5 days a week to gains [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM], and in an RCT calf stretching at 6-7/10 discomfort raised ROM by 40% in 4 weeks versus 15% at 0-1/10 [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. After 2-6 weeks off, ROM fell (effect size -0.41) but stayed above baseline (0.55), and only physically active people kept their gains [@Konrad2025_detraining_ROM]. Certainty: established that stretching works; uncertain for the dose.

**Lifting versus stretching, and stretching for muscle.** In 55 studies, resistance training improved ROM (effect size 0.73), did not differ from stretching (0.08), and combining it with stretching was no better than stretching alone (-0.001); untrained people gained most (1.04 vs 0.43), and body-mass-only training was not significant [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM]. Stretching produced small hypertrophy in one meta-analysis (d 0.20, significant only with long durations and high frequencies) [@Warneke2024_SS_strength_hypertrophy_meta] and a trivial, unclear effect in another [@Arntz2024_SS_hypertrophy_meta]; positive human studies used an apparatus or external load [@Nunes2020_stretch_hypertrophy_review]. No source reports ROM loss from hypertrophy training.

**Injury and cool-down.** Across 25 RCTs (26,610 participants in sports injury-prevention trials), stretching programmes did not prevent injury, whereas strength training (RR 0.315, 95% CI 0.207-0.480) and balance training (RR 0.550) did [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention]. A 10-min cool-down did not change 48-h soreness [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS], post-exercise stretching did not aid recovery (very low certainty) [@Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery], and a narrative review found cool-downs largely ineffective for performance, injury and soreness [@VanHooren2018_cooldown]; see [[sci:sci-recovery]].

**Testing.** Fingertip-to-floor distance is highly reliable (intraclass correlation, ICC, 0.99) and tracks radiographic trunk flexion (r -0.96) in back-pain patients, but it measures the whole posterior chain [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test]. Sit-and-reach is only moderately valid for the hamstrings (r 0.46-0.67), less so in inflexible people [@Mayorga2014_sit_and_reach_validity]. Straight-leg raise and active knee extension are reliable, but changes under 6-8° are within error [@Neto2015_AKE_SLR_reliability]; for knee-to-wall, changes under about 1.6-1.9 cm are noise [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability]. All were examiner-measured; self-measurement has not been validated.
articles.practice:
**Before every session** ([[dec:D10]], [[tool:warmup]]):

1. General warm-up: about 6 min of continuous easy-to-moderate movement ([[ex:wu-cardio-easy]]; [[term:rpe|RPE]] 2-3 rising to 4-5 of 10), a few minutes longer when you feel stiff (practical convention). Rotate the machine, or use skipping or footwork, for variety.
2. Dynamic drills, 3-5 min, matched to the session: for example [[ex:wu-leg-swing-fb]], [[ex:wu-wgs]], [[ex:wu-bw-squat]] and [[ex:wu-ankle-rock]].
3. Balance in every lifting warm-up: [[ex:bal-sls]], 2 × 30 s per leg, left leg first ([[dec:D28]]).
4. [[term:ramp-up-sets|Ramp-up sets]] before the first exercise of each movement pattern, as set out in [[rule:ramp-up]]: two or three sets of falling repetitions that climb towards the working load (practical convention built on the trials above).

Avoid static holds of 60 s or more before lifting. If a short pre-lift stretch helps you feel ready, keep it to 15-30 s and follow it with the ramp-up sets.

**Flexibility block** ([[dec:D27]]): [[ex:st-ham-supine]] or [[ex:st-ham-bench]], 2 holds of 30 s per leg at a strong but tolerable 7 out of 10 in every cool-down (about 5 min per leg a week), plus an optional 5-min home routine on other days or during a work break. Some cool-downs add [[ex:st-calf-wall]] for the knee-to-wall test. Loaded full-range hinges and squats ([[ex:db-rdl]], [[ex:goblet-squat]], [[ex:split-squat]]) contribute as well. Once you can touch your toes comfortably, keep the cool-down stretches and cut any home routine to 2-3 days a week rather than stopping.

!> Stop and change position if a stretch causes tingling, numbness or pain running down the leg: nerve tissue may be the limiting structure.

**Testing**: [[ex:test-ftf]] and [[ex:test-knee-wall]] every 4-6 weeks, at the same time after waking and after the standard warm-up; best of 3 trials ([[plan:monitoring]]). **Cool-down**: 2 min of [[ex:cd-easy]] (3 min after cardio sessions), then the stretches above; it serves range of motion, not recovery.
articles.uncertainties:
- No study included late or shifted sleepers. That a 13:00 session behaves like an early-morning session is inference; your own logs over 4-6 weeks are the better test.
- The minimum effective warm-up for hypertrophy-oriented sets in untrained people is unknown: the trials measured acute 1RM or bar velocity in trained participants, not repetitions completed or long-term growth.
- The stretching dose-response is unresolved. The largest meta-analysis found no significant moderators, whereas smaller analyses and one RCT favour more time, frequency and intensity; head-to-head hamstring trials are lacking.
- Whether stretching adds anything to full-range resistance training in novices has not been tested directly.
- How much of your toe-touch limit reflects hamstring tolerance, muscle-tendon stiffness, sciatic-nerve mechanosensitivity or lumbopelvic mobility is unknown; tissue-specific adaptation has only been shown at the ankle.
- Retention data cover only 2-6 weeks without stretching, and the reliability of self-measured tests is unknown.
- Results vary widely between studies (I² 75%); untrained people and women gain more on average.

What would change the plan: no change beyond test error after 8 weeks of consistent stretching (raise intensity, lengthen holds or try self-PNF); nerve-type symptoms while stretching; or trials showing that stretching adds nothing to full-range lifting (drop to maintenance).

articles.title: Soreness and recovery
articles.tagline: Why muscles ache a day or two after training, what genuinely speeds recovery, and the one popular tool that costs you gains.
articles.summary:
Muscle soreness that peaks a day or two after training, [[term:doms|delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)]], is normal in your first weeks and whenever an exercise is new. It mostly follows unaccustomed [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] (lengthening) work, fades within about a week and is neither a sign of injury nor of a better workout: in animal studies soreness appears even when no muscle damage can be detected.

The most reliable protection is the [[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]]: one exposure to an exercise sharply reduces soreness from the next, for months after a maximal eccentric bout. Soreness therefore falls quickly if you keep your exercise list stable and build volume over the first two or three weeks. A proper warm-up may help a little.

Most recovery tools do less than their marketing suggests. Stretching does not reduce soreness. Massage and foam rolling ease perceived soreness slightly; compression garments do not appear to speed strength recovery; heat is cheap but poorly studied. Cold-water immersion after lifting is the one tool to avoid: it probably blunts muscle and strength gains a little.

In one trial, training to failure lengthened recovery by one to two days compared with stopping well short at the same volume. A planned lighter week, a [[term:deload|deload]], is a fatigue-management tool rather than a growth stimulus: in short trials it neither helped nor harmed muscle gain.

The recovery measures that matter most are unglamorous: enough sleep (see [[sci:sci-sleep]]), enough protein and energy (see [[sci:sci-protein]]), sensible effort and gradual progression. Sudden sharp pain during a set, a precise tender spot or bruising is not DOMS and needs assessment.
articles.mechanisms:
**What happens in the muscle (human mechanistic).** Unaccustomed loading, especially eccentric, disrupts sarcomeres: in untrained men starting resistance training, Z-band streaming was greatest in week 1 [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS]. The usual damage markers follow familiar cell biology (interpretation, theoretical): creatine kinase (CK) in blood reflects increased sarcolemmal permeability, IL-6 and CRP an acute-phase inflammatory response, and prolonged MRI T2 tissue oedema. Early increases in muscle cross-sectional area are partly this oedema, with echo intensity and damage markers still raised at week 3 [@Damas2016_EJAP_oedema]. Integrated myofibrillar [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]], measured with deuterium oxide, was highest in week 1 yet unrelated to later growth, and correlated strongly with hypertrophy (r about 0.9) only at weeks 3 and 10, once damage had subsided [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS]. Early synthesis is largely spent on repair rather than on adding contractile protein. Consensus classes DOMS as a functional disorder with oedematous swelling and stiffness but no macroscopic fibre tear [@MuellerWohlfahrt2013_Munich_consensus].

**Why soreness is delayed: neurotrophic sensitisation (animal).** In rats, the mechanical withdrawal threshold of muscle falls 1-3 days after lengthening contractions, even with contraction parameters that cause no detectable damage [@Mizumura2024_DOMS_neurochemistry]. Two interacting pathways are implicated: bradykinin acting on B2 receptors leads to upregulation of nerve growth factor (NGF), and cyclo-oxygenase-2 (COX-2) activity leads to upregulation of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF). These factors sensitise thin-fibre muscle nociceptors to mechanical stimuli, so pain appears on movement and pressure rather than at rest; the delay fits the time needed to induce and synthesise them (theoretical extension). Damage markers co-vary with soreness but probably do not generate it, which is why the two can dissociate (inference). Translation to human DOMS is not established, and the COX-2 step is only a mechanistic rationale for anti-inflammatory drugs, whose effects on soreness and adaptation lie outside this evidence base.

**The repeated-bout effect (human mechanistic).** One bout of eccentric exercise reduced strength loss, soreness, swelling, CK release and T2 change after a second bout 6 months later; partial protection remained at 9 months and none at 12 [@Nosaka2001_RBE_duration]. The proposed mediators act together: neural adaptation (altered [[term:motor-unit|motor-unit]] recruitment spreading load), changed muscle mechanical properties, extracellular-matrix remodelling that may distribute strain more evenly, and biochemical signalling [@Hyldahl2017_repeated_bout_effect]. In rats a repeated bout also blunted NGF upregulation [@Mizumura2024_DOMS_neurochemistry].

**Failure and metabolic stress (human mechanistic).** Sets to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] produced larger acute losses of jump height and bar velocity than sets stopping at half the possible repetitions with equal total volume, and slowed neuromuscular, metabolic and hormonal recovery (CK, ammonia and growth hormone) by roughly 24-48 h [@MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery]. As background biochemistry (theoretical), ammonia rises when ATP turnover outstrips resynthesis: adenylate kinase converts two ADP into ATP and AMP, and AMP deaminase converts AMP into IMP and ammonia, so plasma ammonia marks severe energetic stress in the working fibres.

**Cold-water immersion (human mechanistic, with long-term outcomes).** Immersion after strength sessions blunted the rise in Pax7+ [[term:satellite-cells|satellite cells]], NCAM+ (committed) cells and p70S6K phosphorylation over 2-48 h [@Roberts2015_CWI_RT_adaptation]. p70S6K lies downstream of [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]], so less phosphorylation means weaker translational signalling, and fewer activated satellite cells means less myonuclear accretion, consistent with the [[term:myonuclear-domain|myonuclear domain]] concept (theoretical). Acute signalling differences do not automatically translate into long-term adaptation, but here they did: over 12 weeks, type II fibre area and myonuclei per fibre rose only without immersion [@Roberts2015_CWI_RT_adaptation]. Lower muscle temperature and blood flow are the presumed upstream causes (theoretical, not measured).

**Massage, foam rolling, compression and heat (theoretical).** These change perceived soreness slightly while barely changing stiffness or performance [@Davis2020_massage_meta; @Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta; @Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM], which fits altered pain processing (afferent input modulating nociceptive transmission, warmth, relaxation and expectation) better than structural repair. Without blinding, expectation cannot be separated from physiology.

**Fatigue, deloads and sleep (theoretical and human mechanistic).** Deloads rest on a two-component fitness-fatigue model: training produces slowly decaying adaptation and faster-decaying fatigue, so briefly reducing training stress lets fatigue clear while fitness is kept; the consensus definition mirrors this logic [@Bell2023_deloadDelphi]. Sleep belongs to the same system: one night without sleep lowered next-day postprandial muscle protein synthesis by 18%, raised cortisol by 21% and lowered testosterone by 24% [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS].
articles.evidence:
| Method | Effect on soreness or recovery | Certainty |
|---|---|---|
| Warm-up before the session | 13 mm less soreness at 48 h on a 100-mm scale (95% CI 2 to 24) [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS] | Uncertain: one RCT |
| Stretching before or after | 0.5-1 point on a 100-point scale [@Herbert2011_Cochrane_stretch_DOMS] | Probable: no meaningful effect |
| Massage | Small soreness reductions, no performance benefit [@Davis2020_massage_meta] | Uncertain |
| Foam rolling afterwards | Perceived pain g 0.47 [@Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta] | Uncertain |
| Compression garments | No strength sparing at any time point [@Negyesi2022_compression_meta] | Uncertain |
| Active cool-down | 0 mm (95% CI -11 to 11) [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS; @VanHooren2018_cooldown] | Probable: no effect |
| Cold-water immersion | Small soreness relief [@Wiecha2025_DOMS_umbrella]; smaller gains (SMD -0.22) [@Pinero2024_CWI_hypertrophy_meta] | Probable: avoid after lifting |

**How long does protection last?** In 35 men, one bout of maximal eccentric elbow-flexor exercise protected against soreness, swelling, CK rise and T2 change from a repeat bout 6 months later; only faster strength recovery remained at 9 months and nothing at 12 [@Nosaka2001_RBE_duration]. Mechanistic syntheses support several co-acting mediators [@Hyldahl2017_repeated_bout_effect]. Certainty: probable. The protective dose of an ordinary first resistance session, and how far protection transfers between exercises, were not tested.

**Is it DOMS or an injury?** The Munich consensus classes DOMS as a type 1B functional disorder: onset hours after unaccustomed eccentric exercise, diffuse involvement of a whole muscle or group, swelling and stiffness, usually settling within a week. Partial tears present with sudden sharp or stabbing pain at a precise moment, well-localised tenderness and sometimes a palpable defect or haematoma [@MuellerWohlfahrt2013_Munich_consensus]. This is expert opinion, not a validated decision rule.

**Does stretching reduce DOMS?** Not meaningfully. In a Cochrane review, pre-exercise stretching reduced next-day soreness by 0.52 points on a 100-point scale ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] -11.30 to 10.26; 3 studies) and post-exercise stretching by 1.04 points (-6.88 to 4.79; 4 studies); a field trial in 2,377 people found 3.8 points less peak weekly soreness (-5.17 to -2.43), statistically significant but clinically trivial [@Herbert2011_Cochrane_stretch_DOMS]. An RCT-only [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] found no effect at 24-72 h (effect sizes -0.09 to -0.24, CIs spanning zero, [[term:i2|I²]] 0%) [@Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery]. Certainty: probable.

**What does reduce it?** In an [[term:rct|RCT]] of 52 people, a 10-min uphill-walking warm-up before backward downhill walking reduced soreness at 48 h by 13 mm, while a cool-down had no effect [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS]. Across 99 studies, active recovery, massage, compression, water immersion, contrast therapy and cryotherapy reduced DOMS (Hedges g -0.40 to -2.26), massage most, and recovery techniques lowered CK ([[term:smd|SMD]] -0.37), IL-6 (-0.36) and CRP (-0.38) [@Dupuy2018_recovery_techniques_meta]. An umbrella review, however, rated 17 of 29 underlying reviews critically low in quality: the best-supported option was contrast therapy immediately after exercise (class II), with massage at 24 h and compression or cryostimulation at 48 h class III, and heat (g 1.82) and cooling (g 0.36) only class IV [@Wiecha2025_DOMS_umbrella]. Massage did not improve strength, sprint, jump or endurance [@Davis2020_massage_meta]. Foam rolling after exercise reduced perceived pain (g 0.47) and slightly limited strength loss (g 0.21) [@Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta]. Compression did not spare strength at any point from 0 to 96 h or more (SMD -0.03 to 0.26, all CIs spanning zero) [@Negyesi2022_compression_meta]; a later analysis reporting small benefits gave no confidence intervals and conflicts with it [@Li2025_compression_strength_meta]. Certainty: uncertain. These interventions cannot be blinded and soreness is subjective, so expectation effects are likely; a large effect paired with the lowest evidence class signals small, biased trials.

**Does cold-water immersion cost gains?** In a 12-week RCT (21 participants), 10 min of immersion after each twice-weekly session gave smaller strength and muscle-mass gains than active recovery [@Roberts2015_CWI_RT_adaptation]. A Bayesian meta-analysis of 8 studies estimated hypertrophy of SMD 0.36 (95% credible interval 0.10-0.61) with training alone versus 0.14 (-0.08 to 0.36) with immersion; the difference, -0.22 (-0.47 to 0.04), had a 95.7% probability of being negative [@Pinero2024_CWI_hypertrophy_meta]. Across 10 studies (170 participants, 92% male), immersion reduced strength gains (effect size -0.23, 95% CI -0.45 to -0.01), significantly for limb-only (-0.31) but not whole-body immersion (-0.08, -0.53 to 0.38) [@Grgic2023_CWI_strength_meta]. Certainty: probable, for small effects. All trials immersed soon after training.

**Does training to failure slow recovery?** In a crossover trial, bench-press and squat sessions of 3 x 10 to failure slowed recovery by roughly 24-48 h compared with 6 x 5 at the same volume [@MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery]. Certainty: uncertain (one small trial).

**Do deloads help?** The definition, a planned period of reduced training stress to relieve fatigue and prepare for further training, is consensus rather than outcome data [@Bell2023_deloadDelphi]. In 19 untrained men, limbs given low-volume deload weeks at weeks 4 and 8 gained similar muscle thickness and 10RM to continuously trained limbs (all CIs including zero) [@Pancar2026_deloadUntrained]. In 39 trained lifters, a full week off after week 4 did not change muscle-thickness gains (vastus lateralis -0.27 mm, 95% credible interval -1.9 to 1.4) while strength gains modestly favoured continuous training (squat [[term:1rm|1RM]] -3.6 kg, -10.4 to 3.2; probability 0.85) [@Coleman2024_deloadRCT]. In untrained men, 3-week breaks between 6-week blocks gave similar 24-week gains to continuous training [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous]. Certainty: uncertain; over 8-24 weeks deloads appeared neither to boost nor to impair growth, and their proposed benefits for fatigue and joints are untested.

**Sleep.** One night without sleep cut next-day postprandial muscle protein synthesis by 18% in a randomised crossover trial [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS]; the wider evidence is in [[sci:sci-sleep]].
articles.practice:
**Soreness**

- Soreness 1-3 days after your first sessions and after any new exercise is expected; it says little about how productive the session was.
- Keep it manageable: always do the general warm-up ([[dec:D10]]); give each new exercise fewer working sets in its first week and build to full volume over 2-3 weeks (inference from the repeated-bout evidence); keep the core exercise list stable within a block and take variety from warm-ups and cardio instead.
- Train through mild DOMS. If a muscle is very sore, reduce its load or sets that day rather than skipping the session (inference).
- Keep most sets short of failure as set out in [[dec:D07]]; this also shortens recovery.
- After a long break, restart at reduced volume as set out in [[rule:breaks]].
- Note soreness (0-10) per muscle group in Hevy to spot patterns, not as a target ([[plan:logging]]).

**Recovery tools** ([[dec:D29]])

- No cold-water immersion or ice baths after lifting while muscle and strength are the priority. If you want cold exposure for comfort, keep it to rest days (inference; timing has not been tested).
- Foam rolling (about 30-60 s per muscle, a practical choice) and a warm shower are optional comfort measures. Compression garments and paid sports massage are not worth the money for you.
- Do not stretch to treat soreness; stretching is for range of motion ([[sci:sci-flexibility]]).

**Deloads**: follow [[rule:deload]]; a deload is a reduced-volume week, not a week off (practical convention).

**The real recovery levers**: sleep ([[plan:sleep]]) and protein and energy ([[plan:nutrition]]).

!> Stop the exercise and get it assessed for sudden sharp pain at a precise moment during a set, a well-localised tender spot, bruising or a palpable gap, or pain that has not settled after about a week ([[rule:pain]]).

!!> Very severe muscle pain or swelling, or dark (cola-coloured) urine after an unusually hard session, can signal [[term:rhabdomyolysis|exertional rhabdomyolysis]]: seek medical care the same day (standard clinical advice; see [[sci:sci-safety]]).
articles.uncertainties:
- The neurochemistry of DOMS comes from rats; whether the NGF and GDNF pathways operate the same way in human muscle is not established.
- The protective dose of an ordinary first resistance session, how long its protection lasts and how far it transfers to similar exercises have not been measured; the 6-9-month figure comes from maximal eccentric elbow-flexor work.
- No source here tested whether training through moderate DOMS impairs adaptation, or how anti-inflammatory drugs affect soreness and growth.
- Recovery-tool trials are unblinded with subjective outcomes, and most reviews are of critically low quality; real effects may be smaller than reported.
- Cold-water immersion was always applied soon after training. Whether immersion hours later, or cold showers, blunt adaptation is unknown, as is why limb-only immersion looked worse than whole-body immersion.
- Deload trials lasted 24 weeks at most and measured neither injuries nor adherence; scheduled and symptom-triggered deloads have not been compared.
- The failure-recovery estimate rests on one small crossover trial.

What would change the advice: sham-controlled trials showing meaningful effects of a recovery tool on performance or adaptation; evidence that delayed cold exposure is harmless; long novice deload trials with injury and adherence outcomes.

articles.title: Energy balance, fat loss and recomposition
articles.tagline: How intake and expenditure shape fat loss and muscle gain, and why your own weight trend is the best calculator
articles.summary:
Your weight changes when the energy you eat and the energy you spend stay out of balance for weeks, not days. [[term:energy-balance|Energy balance]] is simple in principle but hard to measure: equations for [[term:tdee|total daily energy expenditure (TDEE)]] miss individuals by roughly 340 kcal a day, and many people under-record what they eat. Your weight has been stable for six months, so what you habitually eat is your maintenance intake; two to three weeks of careful logging plus daily weighing will pin it down better than any formula.

In [[phase:p1]] the programme aims for [[term:recomposition|body recomposition]]: eating at maintenance or up to about 300 kcal a day below it, with high protein and progressive lifting. People new to resistance training who carry ordinary amounts of fat are probably the group most likely to lose fat and gain muscle at the same time (inference). Larger deficits remove fat faster but shrink muscle gain, which on average disappears near a 500 kcal/day deficit. A beginner does not need a surplus to build muscle, and in trained lifters faster weight gain mostly added fat.

Expect the scale to mislead you in the short term. Water stored with glycogen, salt and weekend eating move weight by a kilogram or more, so the programme reads a smoothed trend alongside waist and strength. Your [[term:whtr|waist-to-height ratio]] (0.45-0.48) is already below the 0.5 risk boundary, so there is no health reason to rush fat loss. Abdominal exercises do not burn belly fat selectively; visible abdominal definition comes from whole-body fat loss. If you diet later, lose about 0.5-0.7% of body weight a week and never let intake fall so low that training, mood or hormones suffer.
articles.mechanisms:
Each mechanism is labelled by evidence type. Short-term hormonal and metabolic responses do not by themselves predict long-term body composition; the targets in this programme rest on the outcome evidence in the next section.

**1. What sets expenditure** (human outcome and human mechanistic). TDEE is the sum of [[term:ree|resting energy expenditure (REE)]], the [[term:tef|thermic effect of food (TEF)]], exercise and [[term:neat|non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT)]]. [[term:ffm|Fat-free mass (FFM)]] explains about two-thirds or more of between-person variation in REE [@Mifflin1990_REE; @Cunningham1991_FFMequation], but small high-metabolic-rate organs (liver, kidney, heart, brain) dominate it, not resting muscle (textbook physiology). Asian-Indian men had lower REE than Chinese men of the same weight, and the gap vanished only when trunk FFM, which contains those organs, replaced total FFM [@Song2016_AsianIndianREE]. Protein has the largest thermic cost: during 8 weeks of overfeeding, REE rose by about 160-227 kcal/d with 15-25% protein but not with 5%, consistent with the cost of protein turnover, peptide-bond synthesis and urea production [@Bray2012_overfeedingProtein].

**2. Lipolysis, and why local exercise is not local fat loss** (human mechanistic). Adipocyte triacylglycerol is hydrolysed in sequence by adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) and monoacylglycerol lipase, with perilipin on the lipid droplet gating lipase access [@Lafontan2009_lipolysis]. Catecholamines stimulate lipolysis through β-adrenergic receptors, cAMP and PKA phosphorylation of HSL and perilipin; insulin suppresses it, canonically via PI3K-Akt activation of phosphodiesterase 3B, which lowers cAMP; natriuretic peptides add a cGMP-dependent stimulus [@Lafontan2009_lipolysis]. The balance of adrenergic receptor subtypes differs by depot, sex and genotype, plausibly one reason fat depots shrink in an individual order (inference). In a deficit, lower insulin raises whole-body fatty-acid release (inference; sympathetic activity actually fell in the deficit described in point 4). In one study of 10 men, contracting muscle did acutely raise blood flow and lipolysis in adjacent subcutaneous fat, measured by xenon washout and microdialysis [@Stallknecht2007_spotLipolysis], but those fatty acids enter the circulation and are oxidised wherever demand exists, and the local increment is small against whole-body flux. Acute local lipolysis therefore does not translate into preferential long-term loss from that depot.

**3. Partitioning: the Forbes curve and the P-ratio** (human outcome and modelling). The P-ratio is the share of an energy imbalance stored or mobilised as protein rather than fat. Forbes's relation, extended by Hall, predicts that the fat-free share of a weight change falls as initial body fat rises: a leaner person loses proportionally more lean tissue in a deficit and gains proportionally more in a surplus [@Hall2007_ForbesPratio]. Body fat (fat mass) stores about 39.5 MJ (about 9,440 kcal) per kg and lean tissue, mostly water, about 7.6 MJ (about 1,820 kcal) [@Hall2011_energyImbalance], so a deficit drawn from lean tissue removes about five times more mass and looks deceptively fast on the scale. Two inputs shift partitioning beyond body fat: dietary protein (8 weeks of overfeeding with 15-25% protein added about 3 kg of lean mass, 5% protein added none, at similar fat gain) [@Bray2012_overfeedingProtein] and mechanical loading (with 2.4 g/kg protein and intense training, lean mass rose even in a 40% deficit) [@Longland2016_highProteinDeficit]. Across training studies, average lean gain disappeared near a 500 kcal/d deficit, a between-study estimate rather than an individual limit [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass]. The loading side is covered in [[sci:sci-hypertrophy]].

**4. Adaptive thermogenesis: leptin, thyroid and NEAT** (human mechanistic). [[term:adaptive-thermogenesis|Adaptive thermogenesis]] is the fall in expenditure beyond what tissue loss predicts. Lean men fed half their energy needs for 3 weeks lowered REE by 266 kcal/d; part reflected organ loss (liver -13%, kidney -8%) and the adaptive remainder was about 72-108 kcal/d [@Muller2015_MinnesotaRevisited]. It appeared within 3 days and tracked falling insulin and negative fluid balance; leptin (-44%), T3 (-39%) and sympathetic activity (-38%) fell sharply but did not track it over that short window. Over longer maintenance of a reduced weight, falling leptin, which signals depleted fat stores to the hypothalamus, is proposed to lower sympathetic tone and thyroid-hormone activity, raise the efficiency of muscle work and increase appetite [@Rosenbaum2010_adaptiveThermogenesis]. Because T3, acting through nuclear thyroid-hormone receptors, sustains expression of ATP-consuming pumps such as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and SERCA (textbook endocrinology), lower T3 plausibly lowers resting ATP turnover. NEAT is the most variable component: in 16 non-obese adults it explained a roughly tenfold range in fat gain during overfeeding (r = 0.77) [@Levine1999_NEAT].

**5. Glycogen-water and scale noise** (human mechanistic). Glycogen is stored with about 3-4 g of water and 0.45 mmol of potassium per gram [@Kreitzman1992_glycogenWater], so a few hundred grams of glycogen carry roughly a kilogram of water (arithmetic). This explains fast early losses on low-carbohydrate or very-low-energy diets, fast regain after refeeds, and apparent lean-mass loss on DXA or BIA during ketogenic diets.

**6. Low energy availability** (human mechanistic). [[term:energy-availability|Energy availability]] is intake minus exercise energy expenditure, per kg of FFM. When it falls below basal needs, costly systems are turned down: in the same 3-week deficit, testosterone fell 11% and T3 39% [@Muller2015_MinnesotaRevisited]. The IOC describes a continuum from short, adaptable low availability to problematic [[term:reds|relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs)]], which affects men as well as women [@Mountjoy2023_REDs].
articles.evidence:
Certainty labels: established, probable, uncertain, inference. Most trials studied trained athletes, people with obesity or mixed samples; almost none studied untrained, normal-weight South Asian men, so magnitudes transfer to you with caution.

**Can expenditure be predicted?** Probable at group level, not for individuals. Mifflin-St Jeor most often predicts REE within 10% in non-athletes [@Frankenfield2005_RMRequationsSR] and gives about 1,751 kcal/d for you [@Mifflin1990_REE]. In recreational athletes, weight-based equations including Mifflin placed fewer than half of people within 10%, while FFM-based equations did better [@tenHaaf2014_athleteREE]. South Asian data conflict: Asian-Indian men had about 54-67 kcal/d lower REE than Chinese men after adjustment [@Song2016_AsianIndianREE], yet all eight equations tested underestimated measured REE by 375-636 kcal/d in a small study of Indian weightlifters [@Joseph2017_IndianWeightlifterREE]. Doubly-labelled-water equations predict your TEE at about 2,680 (inactive), 2,900 (low active) or 3,075 kcal/d (active), with an individual error of about 339 kcal/d, a 95% range near ±660 kcal/d [@NASEM2023_EER].

**Can logged intake and static rules be trusted?** Probable that they cannot without calibration. Adults with obesity who believed they were diet-resistant (n = 10) had expenditure within 5% of prediction but under-reported intake by 47 ± 16% and over-reported activity by 51 ± 75% [@Lichtman1992_underreporting]. The 7,700 kcal/kg rule overestimated weight loss in controlled studies because expenditure falls as weight falls [@Thomas2013_3500kcalRule]; each sustained 100 kJ/d (about 24 kcal/d) change in intake eventually moves weight by about 1 kg, half of it within about a year [@Hall2011_energyImbalance]. Weight also cycles weekly, peaking after weekends [@Orsama2014_weightRhythms].

**How do deficit size and rate affect lean mass?** Probable.

| Source | Who | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Meta-analysis [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass] | Adults doing resistance training | Lean gain smaller with a deficit (ES -0.57, p = 0.02); strength not different (ES -0.31, p = 0.28); average lean gain lost near 500 kcal/d |
| RCT [@Garthe2011_weightLossRate] | Elite athletes | 0.7 vs 1.0% a week achieved: lean mass +2.1% vs -0.2% |
| Meta-analysis [@AshtaryLarky2020_rateMA] | Mostly people with obesity | At equal weight loss, gradual loss: fat mass -1.0 kg more (95% CI -1.70 to -0.29) and RMR about 97 kcal/d higher; FFM not different |
| RCT [@Longland2016_highProteinDeficit] | Young men, 40% deficit, training 6 days a week | 2.4 vs 1.2 g/kg protein: lean mass +1.2 ± 1.0 vs +0.1 ± 1.0 kg; fat -4.8 vs -3.5 kg in 4 weeks |

Individual spread is as large as the means. Expert consensus for lean trained people is 0.5-1% of body weight per week [@Helms2014_contestPrep].

**Does recomposition happen?** Probable. Resistance training, usually without a prescribed diet, lowered body fat by 1.46 percentage points (95% CI 1.14 to 1.78), fat mass by 0.55 kg and visceral fat (SMD -0.49) versus control [@Wewege2022_RTbodyFat]. Simultaneous fat loss and lean gain is documented in novices and in trained people, with measurement error comparable to the changes studied [@Barakat2020_recomp].

**Is a surplus needed?** Uncertain. In the only direct RCT (17 trained lifters, 8 weeks), a 15% surplus added no more muscle thickness or squat strength than 5% or maintenance but added more skinfold fat, with a bench-press advantage; across people, the rate of weight gain predicted fat gain (R² 0.49) far better than muscle gain [@Helms2023_surplus]. Overfeeding by about 954 kcal/d for 8 weeks stored 50% to over 90% of the excess as fat, and lean mass rose only with 15-25% protein [@Bray2012_overfeedingProtein]. No surplus prescription has been validated [@Slater2019_surplus]; the usual 10-20% advice is expert opinion [@Iraki2019_offseason].

**Do diet breaks or macronutrient ratios matter?** Probable that they matter little. Alternating 2-week restriction and maintenance blocks gave men with obesity more fat loss per protocol (12.3 vs 8.0 kg) [@Byrne2018_MATADOR], but in resistance-trained adults 1-week breaks changed neither fat, FFM, REE nor hormones, while reducing hunger [@Peos2021_ICECAP]. At equal energy and protein, lower-fat diets gave only 16 g/d more fat loss than lower-carbohydrate diets [@HallGuo2017_dietComposition], and a 12-month RCT in adults with overweight found a 0.7 kg difference in weight loss (95% CI -0.2 to 1.6) [@Gardner2018_DIETFITS]. Ketogenic diets with training lowered FFM by 1.26 kg (95% CI -1.82 to -0.70) [@AshtaryLarky2022_ketoRT]; time-restricted eating did not significantly change FFM and reduced fat mass slightly (-1.25 kg), probably by reducing intake [@Ali2026_TRE_RT].

**Can you spot-reduce?** Probable that you cannot meaningfully. Six weeks of abdominal exercise changed neither abdominal fat nor waist [@Vispute2011_absSpot]; 12 weeks of single-leg training reduced fat in the arms and trunk but not in the trained leg [@RamirezCampillo2013_localRT]. One small energy-matched RCT in overweight men found about 0.7 kg more trunk-fat loss with abdominal endurance work [@Brobakken2023_spotReduction]; it is unreplicated.

**What about maintenance and very low intakes?** Uncertain. In weight-control registries, physical activity was the most consistent correlate of keeping weight off [@Paixao2020_registries]; physiology defends a reduced weight, and over 80% of people treated for obesity regain [@Rosenbaum2010_adaptiveThermogenesis]. Male case data link energy availability below about 25 kcal/kg FFM/d with muscle loss and mood and hormonal disturbance near 4-5% body fat [@Fagerberg2018_LEAmale]; the thresholds are extrapolated.

**Is your waist a health concern?** Probable that it is not. Waist-to-height ratio discriminates cardiometabolic risk better than BMI [@Ashwell2012_WHtR], with 0.5 as a pragmatic boundary across populations (mean AUROC 0.704 vs 0.671 for BMI) [@Browning2010_WHtRboundary]. Asian Indians carry more abdominal fat at a given BMI [@Misra2009_AsianIndianConsensus], and the high-risk waist for normal-BMI men is 90 cm or more [@Ross2020_waistConsensus]. Your ratios (0.45 at the natural waist, 0.48 at the navel) and waists (81 and 86 cm) are below both, though above the 78 cm first action level that one Indian study proposed for men [@Misra2006_IndianWaist].
articles.practice:
- **Starting estimate.** The [[tool:energy]] tool gives a provisional maintenance of about 2,700 kcal/d (plausible range 2,450-2,900); replace it by calibrating through [[phase:p0]] and weeks 1-2 of [[phase:p1]] while eating as usual: weigh food, weigh yourself daily on waking, and if the 14-day smoothed trend is flat, your mean logged intake is maintenance. If it is not flat, correct by about 110 kcal/d per 0.1 kg a week of trend (short-term approximation; practical convention).
- **[[phase:p1]] strategy** ([[dec:D04]]). From week 3, eat at maintenance to 300 kcal/d below it, aiming for a trend of 0 to -0.25 kg a week, with about 1.8 g/kg/d of protein (floor about 125 g/d) ([[sci:sci-protein]]) and progressive training. Phase 1 is working if waist is stable or falling while strength and limb girths rise, even when weight is flat.
- **Monitoring** ([[dec:D23]], [[tool:checkin]]). Read the 7-day average and the 14-28-day slope, never single days. Measure waist weekly at both sites under the same conditions ([[ex:test-girths]]), take photos every 4 weeks, and never base decisions on BIA outputs, whose individual body-fat error is about ±5-6 points ([[sci:sci-bodycomp]]).
- **Adjusting** ([[rule:energy-adjustment]]). Review every 2-4 weeks; if the trend sits outside the target band by more than 0.1 kg a week at two consecutive reviews, change intake by 100-200 kcal/d. Maintenance falls by about 24 kcal/d per kg lost, plus some adaptation (inference), so slowing loss is expected, not failure.
- **Later phases** ([[rule:phase-nutrition]]). A fat-loss block targets 0.5-0.7% of body weight a week (never above 1%), with optional 1-week maintenance breaks every 3-6 weeks for hunger. A muscle-gain block uses a surplus of about 150-300 kcal/d, aiming for 0.1-0.25 kg a week; cut it by 100-150 kcal/d if navel waist rises more than about 1 cm a month (judgement).
- **Guardrail** ([[rule:energy-availability]]). In any deficit, intake minus exercise energy should stay at or above 30 kcal/kg FFM/d (about 1,830 kcal/d at an FFM of 61 kg) and never fall below 25.
- **Core work** such as [[ex:pallof-press]] and [[ex:cable-crunch]] is for trunk strength, not belly fat. Daily steps support NEAT ([[dec:D24]]).
articles.uncertainties:
- Whether equations over- or underestimate expenditure in young South Asian men is unresolved: organ-size data point one way, the weightlifter study the other. Calibrating from your own intake and weight makes this largely irrelevant for you.
- No trial has compared surplus sizes in true novices, so the muscle-gain prescription is judgement.
- Male thresholds for low energy availability are extrapolated from studies of women and from case reports.
- Diet breaks have not been tested in lean beginners.
- Free-living recomposition on self-cooked Indian food is probably smaller than in metabolic-ward trials (inference), and short-term changes can sit within BIA and DXA error.
- The effect of your 04:00-12:00 sleep and night work on appetite and partitioning was not reviewed here ([[sci:sci-sleep]]).
- Individual variation is large throughout: fat gain during overfeeding varied about tenfold, largely through NEAT, and lean-mass responses in deficits vary as much as their means.

What would change the plan: a reference scan (for example DXA) showing body fat clearly above about 22% would favour a fat-loss phase first, and clearly below about 15% a small surplus (judgement thresholds); a 12-week plateau in both waist and strength would trigger a phase change; a persistent mismatch between logged intake and weight trend points to logging error before unusual metabolism.

articles.title: Protein and nutrition for muscle
articles.tagline: How much protein you need, how to spread it across a late day, which Indian foods deliver it, and what carbohydrate, fat and diet quality add
articles.summary:
Protein supplies the amino acids that muscle uses to build new protein after training, and it is the nutrient whose dose most clearly matters for your goals. In trials that added protein to resistance training, lean-mass gains rose steeply up to about 1.3 g per kg of body weight a day and levelled off around 1.6 g/kg; intakes up to about 2.2 g/kg cover the uncertainty around that bend. The programme sets your target at about 1.8 g/kg (about 140 g a day at 77 kg), with 125 g as the floor, and raises it to about 2.2 g/kg if you later diet.

The daily total matters more than timing. Four meals of 30-45 g each fit your day and put every meal in the range that strongly stimulated [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] for several hours in acute studies. Eating soon after waking, before your 13:00 session, and again after training avoids stretching the overnight fast; your post-work meal at about 02:00 doubles as pre-sleep protein.

Source matters mainly through digestibility. In Indian adults, egg and chicken protein was 86-92% digestible against 63-75% for common legumes, so meals built on dal probably need about 20-25% more protein, or an egg, curd or paneer addition (inference). Soy and animal protein supplements gave similar training results in small trials when the total was adequate.

At these intakes, protein did not harm kidney function in short trials in healthy adults. Carbohydrate rarely limits lifting when you are fed, fat should stay above about 20% of energy, and fibre, fruit, vegetables and fewer ultra-processed foods matter for health and appetite control.
articles.mechanisms:
Evidence types are labelled. Most mechanistic data here are acute, hours of tracer-measured synthesis or a single biopsy's signalling; they explain why targets are set as they are, but acute MPS and phosphorylation do not by themselves predict months of muscle growth.

**1. Net protein balance** (human mechanistic). Muscle mass changes with the integral, over days, of MPS minus [[term:mpb|muscle protein breakdown (MPB)]]. Fasted, net balance is negative; each protein-containing meal turns it positive for some hours, mainly by raising MPS through amino-acid supply, with a smaller insulin-mediated suppression of MPB. Resistance exercise raises both MPS and MPB and sensitises muscle to amino acids for at least 24 h [@Jager2017_ISSNprotein], so a session's gain is harvested over several meals rather than in a narrow post-exercise window. Your distinctive feature is the overnight fast: from about 02:00 to 12:00 balance is negative, and training at 13:00 without food prolongs it.

**2. Leucine sensing and mTORC1 at the lysosome** (in vitro; standard cell biology, not measured in the catalogued human studies). [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]] couples amino-acid supply to translation on the lysosomal surface. Cytosolic [[term:leucine|leucine]] binds Sestrin2 and releases its inhibition of GATOR2; GATOR2 restrains GATOR1, the GTPase-activating protein for RagA/B, so the Rag heterodimer adopts the RagA/B-GTP, RagC/D-GDP state, binds raptor and docks mTORC1 on the Ragulator scaffold, where Rheb-GTP activates it. Arginine acts in parallel through cytosolic CASTOR1, which likewise restrains GATOR2 until arginine binds, and through the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9. Downstream, mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1, freeing eIF4E for cap-dependent initiation, and S6K1, which acts on rpS6, eIF4B, PDCD4 and eEF2 kinase. Mechanical loading activates mTORC1 partly independently of PI3K-Akt ([[term:mechanotransduction|mechanotransduction]]; see [[sci:sci-hypertrophy]]). This is why consensus statements specify about 0.7-3 g of leucine per meal [@Jager2017_ISSNprotein]: leucine is a signal as well as a substrate. In humans, however, phosphorylation of S6K1 Thr389, rpS6 Ser240/244 and eIF2Bε Ser539 did not differ between protein doses that did change MPS [@Moore2009_doseMPS], so treat the leucine threshold as a heuristic for meal quality, not a switch demonstrated in vivo.

**3. Insulin's permissive role** (cell biology and human mechanistic). Insulin acts through Akt, which phosphorylates TSC2, relieving its GAP activity towards Rheb, and PRAS40, converging on the same mTORC1 pool. In vivo, at ordinary fed concentrations, insulin looks permissive rather than driving: amino-acid availability sets MPS, and insulin mainly restrains MPB. A protein meal therefore does not need a large carbohydrate load to be anabolic (inference).

**4. Saturation and amino-acid oxidation** (human mechanistic). After leg exercise, muscle protein synthesis rose with dose up to about 20 g of high-quality protein and then plateaued, while leucine oxidation rose at 20 and 40 g [@Moore2009_doseMPS]; 40 g of whey also raised phenylalanine oxidation and urea production [@Witard2014_wheyDose]. Biochemically, surplus leucine is transaminated in muscle by mitochondrial BCAT2 to α-ketoisocaproate, which inhibits BCKDH kinase and so activates the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, its own disposal route; amino nitrogen travels as alanine and glutamine to the liver, where carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1, activated by N-acetylglutamate, feeds the urea cycle (textbook steps). The plateau is not fixed. After whole-body training, 40 g beat 20 g by about 20% regardless of lean mass [@Macnaughton2016_20v40], and 100 g of mostly casein, which clots in the stomach and empties slowly, raised synthesis for more than 12 h with negligible extra oxidation [@Trommelen2023_100g]. The data fit a model in which the hourly amplitude of MPS saturates while its duration scales with the amount and absorption rate of the protein.

**5. Digestibility and DIAAS** (human mechanistic). What a meal offers muscle is the indispensable amino acids (IAA) reaching the portal blood, not label protein. In Indian adults, true ileal IAA digestibility was measured with a dual-isotope method: a test protein intrinsically labelled with ²H is fed with a U-¹³C spirulina reference, and the plasma ²H:¹³C enrichment ratio relative to the meal ratio, scaled by the reference digestibility, gives digestibility without intubation. Legumes scored 63-75% and egg or hen meat 86-92% [@Kashyap2019_legumeTID; @Kashyap2018_eggMeatTID]. Plausible causes are protease inhibitors, compact 7S and 11S storage globulins, tannins, phytate and protein trapped in intact cotyledon cell walls (food-chemistry and animal work, not tested here); dehulling raised mung bean from 63% to 71%. [[term:diaas|DIAAS]] adds composition: 100 × the lowest ratio of digestible IAA to the reference pattern. Cereals are lysine-poor and legumes low in methionine plus cysteine, so dal with rice or roti complements the patterns, though not the digestibility gap.

**6. Energy deficit** (theoretical). Lower insulin and transient falls in energy charge activate [[term:ampk|AMPK]], which phosphorylates TSC2 and raptor and restrains mTORC1, while gluconeogenesis draws on amino-acid carbon, so more ingested protein is oxidised. This is the rationale for higher targets when dieting ([[sci:sci-energy]]).
articles.evidence:
Certainty labels: established, probable, uncertain, inference. Dose-response meta-analyses pool mostly young and middle-aged adults of mixed training status; MPS studies are small tracer studies in young men; the digestibility data come from Indian adults. Several trials enrolled young untrained men much like you.

**How much protein a day?** Probable.

| Source | Studies | Main result |
|---|---|---|
| [@Morton2018_proteinRT] | 49 RCTs, 1,863 people | Added protein with training: [[term:ffm|fat-free mass (FFM)]] +0.30 kg (95% CI 0.09 to 0.52), [[term:1rm|1RM]] +2.49 kg; no further FFM gain above about 1.62 g/kg/d; larger effect in trained people (0.75 kg) |
| [@Nunes2022_proteinLBM] | 62 RCTs | Lean mass [[term:smd|SMD]] 0.22 (0.14 to 0.30), moderate certainty; under 65 years, significant only at 1.6 g/kg/d or more |
| [@Tagawa2021_doseLBM] | 105 articles | +0.39 kg lean mass per +0.1 g/kg/d below 1.3 g/kg/d, +0.12 kg above it |
| [@Tagawa2022_doseStrength] | RCTs | Strength gain plateaus near 1.5 g/kg/d; extra protein helped only with training (+2.01% vs +0.13%) |
| [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA] | 22 comparisons | Above vs at the RDA: +0.77 kg lean mass with training (3 comparisons); no effect without training or dieting |

The direction is close to established; the breakpoint is probable but rests on between-trial comparisons, and DXA or BIA lean mass includes water. Tagawa and Nunes carry potential industry conflicts. For a beginner, training dominates; protein ensures intake is not limiting.

**During a deficit?** Probable direction, uncertain dose. Protein above the RDA reduced lean-mass loss by 0.36 kg (95% CI 0.06 to 0.67; 14 comparisons) [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA]. In lean trained athletes, FFM fell in 9 of 13 groups; the one lean group in a large deficit that kept FFM ate 2.5-2.6 g/kg, and the authors suggest 2.3-3.1 g/kg of FFM [@Helms2014_deficit; @Jager2017_ISSNprotein].

**How much per meal?** Probable. Myofibrillar MPS over 4 h rose 49% with 20 g and 56% with 40 g of whey, with no detectable rise at 10 g [@Witard2014_wheyDose]; mixed MPS plateaued at 20 g in a 6-person study [@Moore2009_doseMPS]. After whole-body training, 40 g gave about 20% more than 20 g (0.059 vs 0.049 %/h) [@Macnaughton2016_20v40], and 100 g prolonged the response beyond 12 h [@Trommelen2023_100g]. The practical target is about 0.4 g/kg per meal over at least 4 meals, up to 0.55 g/kg [@SchoenfeldAragon2018_perMeal]. These are acute surrogates, not hypertrophy outcomes.

**Distribution, timing and fasting?** With energy and protein matched, an apparent benefit of more frequent meals depended on one study [@Schoenfeld2015_mealFreq] (probable: little effect). Feeds every 3-4 h are consensus [@Kerksick2017_ISSNtiming]. Across 23 hypertrophy studies (525 participants), a peri-workout benefit vanished after adjustment, total protein being the strongest predictor [@Schoenfeld2013_timing] (probable). Fasted versus fed training is uncertain: four small trials showed no significant differences, with wide intervals (FFM SMD 0.53, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] -0.80 to 1.86) [@Vieira2025_fastedRT]. Acute carbohydrate helped lifting mainly against fasted controls or beyond about 10 sets per muscle [@Henselmans2022_carbRT], and without meal 1 your session would follow a 10-hour fast.

**Pre-sleep protein?** Uncertain. In 44 young men starting training, 27.5 g of protein nightly for 12 weeks increased summed 1RM (+164 vs +130 kg) and quadriceps area (+8.4 vs +4.8 cm²) versus a non-caloric placebo [@Snijders2015_presleep], but total protein differed, so timing is not isolated.

**Does source matter?** Probable that it matters little at adequate totals: soy and animal proteins gave similar lean-mass and strength gains (soy vs whey p = 0.96; 9 studies) [@Messina2018_soy]. Digestibility differs [@Kashyap2019_legumeTID; @Kashyap2018_eggMeatTID]:

| Food (Indian adults) | True ileal IAA digestibility |
|---|---|
| Hen meat | 92% |
| Whole egg | 89% |
| Egg white | 86% |
| Chickpea | 75% |
| Yellow pea | 72% |
| Mung bean, dehulled | 71% |
| Mung bean, hulled | 63% |

**Is it safe?** Probable for healthy kidneys: across 28 RCTs (1,358 people), the change in GFR did not differ between higher- and lower-protein diets (SMD 0.11, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.27) [@Devries2018_kidney]; trials were short and excluded kidney disease. No bone-outcome source is catalogued; harm is unlikely with adequate calcium (inference).

**Carbohydrate and fat?** In 15 of 17 long-term diet-plus-training studies, carbohydrate intake did not change strength or hypertrophy [@Henselmans2022_carbRT] (probable). Low-fat diets lowered total testosterone modestly (SMD -0.38, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.01; 6 studies, 206 men), with no link shown to muscle outcomes [@Whittaker2021_lowfatT] (uncertain).

**Diet quality and Indian guidance?** Probable. The highest fibre intakes were associated with 15-30% lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, with the greatest reduction at 25-29 g/d [@Reynolds2019_carbQuality]; each extra 200 g/d of fruit and vegetables with 10% lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.87 to 0.93) [@Aune2017_fruitveg]. On an ultra-processed diet matched for presented nutrients, people ate 508 kcal/d more and gained 0.9 kg in 2 weeks [@Hall2019_UPF]. The Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024 organise eating around 10 food groups and Indian dietary diversity [@ManojShah2025_DGIcomparison]; they set population adequacy, not training targets.
articles.practice:
- **Daily target** ([[dec:D19]]): about 1.8 g/kg, or 140 g/d at 77 kg (band 1.6-2.2 g/kg, 125-170 g). Treat 125 g as the floor, judge adherence on the 7-day mean, and recompute when your 7-day average weight moves by 2 kg or more. In a fat-loss block, raise it to about 2.2 g/kg within a 2.0-2.4 band ([[rule:phase-nutrition]]).
- **Meal 1** ([[dec:D20]]), about 12:00-12:15, 45-60 min before training: 30-40 g protein and 40-70 g carbohydrate with little fat or fibre, plus 400-500 mL water (for example milk, whey, banana and oats).
- **Meal 2**, within 1-1.5 h after training (about 14:30-15:00): 40-45 g protein and 70-100 g carbohydrate, your largest carbohydrate meal.
- **Meal 3**, about 19:30-20:30 at work: 30-40 g protein.
- **Meal 4**, about 01:15-02:00: 35-45 g protein including a casein-rich dairy food (curd, hung curd, milk or paneer); this is your pre-sleep protein.
- If eating on waking causes nausea, train fasted with water and eat meal 2 within an hour; prefer the fed option on [[ex:cardio-int-4x4]] days.
- **Sources**: about 60% of protein from eggs, chicken, fish, dairy, soy chunks or whey (practical convention). When a meal relies on dal, chana or rajma, add 20-25% more protein or add curd, egg or paneer (inference from the digestibility data); prefer dehulled dals and pair a cereal with a legume. Whey is optional ([[sci:sci-supplements]]).
- **Carbohydrate** fills the remaining energy (about 300-350 g/d during recomposition; not below about 2.5 g/kg while training most days, a judgement). **Fat** defaults to about 1.0 g/kg (about 75 g, 25-30% of energy), never below 20% or 0.8 g/kg (about 60 g); measure cooking oil.
- **Diet quality**: at least 30 g fibre a day, at least 400 g vegetables plus 200-300 g fruit, half or more of cereals as whole grains or millets, and ultra-processed foods at most about one serving a day (judgement).
- Energy targets are in [[sci:sci-energy]]; meal templates and budget are in [[plan:nutrition]].
articles.uncertainties:
- Whether intakes above about 1.6 g/kg add lean mass in untrained men during their first months is unresolved; the protein effect was larger in trained people, and the breakpoint rests on between-trial comparisons.
- Pre-sleep protein has not been separated from extra total protein in a trial, and no meta-analysis of it was found.
- Digestibility values exist for single legumes, egg and hen meat, not for cooked Indian mixed meals such as dal-rice or rajma-chawal; the 20-25% correction is inference.
- Fasted versus fed training rests on four small trials; your own logs (reps at a given load and [[term:rpe|RPE]] on fed versus fasted days) will be more informative.
- Multi-year kidney data above 2 g/kg are lacking, and the evidence does not cover kidney disease, diabetes with albuminuria or a single kidney.
- Bone safety at high protein intakes is inference, and the minimum-fat recommendation is a safety margin, not a measured threshold.
- The wording of the Indian dietary guidelines on protein supplements and the ICMR-NIN protein requirement were not verified for this programme.

What would change the plan: a trial showing extra lean gain above about 2 g/kg in novices, a kidney diagnosis, body fat above about 25% (switch to target-weight scaling), or persistent appetite or digestive problems at 140 g a day.

articles.title: Supplements
articles.tagline: Which parts of your stack have evidence behind them, what to drop, what not to add, and how to buy safely in India
articles.summary:
Most supplements do little for muscle, and the few that help add far less than consistent training, enough protein and good sleep. Of your current stack, only creatine has strong evidence for your goals. Added to resistance training, it gives about 1 kg more lean mass, part of it water, and moderately larger strength gains, mainly by topping up the [[term:phosphocreatine|phosphocreatine]] that powers hard sets. Five grams a day with a meal is enough and loading is unnecessary. In trials it has not harmed healthy kidneys, but it raises blood creatinine slightly, which can make a routine kidney test look worse than it is.

Caffeine improves performance from about 2-3 mg per kg of body weight (150-230 mg for you). It works by blocking [[term:adenosine|adenosine]], the signal that builds sleep pressure, so with a 04:00 bedtime its timing matters: take it at 12:00 before training, finish any second, smaller dose by 17:00-18:00 and take none after 19:00.

Vitamin D3 and B12 stay as cheap insurance, because both deficiencies are common in India; neither is expected to build muscle in people who are not deficient. L-theanine, magnesium and omega-3 have no convincing training benefit, so keep them only for a specific, limited purpose. Stop vitamin K2, which has no indication at 31, and folic acid, which can hide B12 deficiency, unless a doctor prescribed them.

Do not add HMB, beta-alanine, citrulline, beetroot nitrate, pre-workouts or fat burners, do not use melatonin routinely, and avoid ashwagandha, which can injure the liver. Independent testing of protein supplements sold in India found mislabelling, contaminants and potentially liver-toxic herbal additives, so buy single-ingredient products and, if you want protein powder, a mainstream sports whey.
articles.mechanisms:
Evidence types are labelled. The verdicts rest on the outcome evidence in the next section; acute biochemical or signalling effects do not by themselves predict training benefits over months.

**1. Creatine and the phosphocreatine shuttle** (human mechanistic; textbook biochemistry). Creatine kinase (CK) catalyses PCr + MgADP + H⁺ ⇌ Cr + MgATP, a near-equilibrium reaction that buffers ATP during maximal efforts, when demand far outstrips oxidative supply. Mitochondrial CK, coupled to the adenine nucleotide translocase, converts exported ATP to PCr; cytosolic MM-CK at the M-band and beside SERCA and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase regenerates ATP where it is used, keeping local ADP low and the free energy of ATP hydrolysis high. Supplementation raises intramuscular creatine [@Kreider2017_ISSNcreatine], so PCr recovers further between sets and a load can be lifted for a few more repetitions. That extra work, rather than a direct anabolic signal, is the main proposed route to [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] ([[sci:sci-hypertrophy]]); reported satellite-cell and cell-swelling effects have not been shown to add growth independently of it.

**2. Saturation, water and creatinine** (human mechanistic). Muscle takes up creatine through SLC6A8 (2 Na⁺ and 1 Cl⁻ per molecule), which is down-regulated as stores fill; intake beyond saturation is excreted, so outcomes depend on reaching saturation rather than on dose, consistent with loading and dose not moderating trial results [@Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA]; 3-5 g/d saturates muscle in about 3-4 weeks (textbook value). Creatine is osmotically active, and [[term:dxa|DXA]] and [[term:bia|bioelectrical impedance (BIA)]] count the extra muscle water as lean tissue. Creatine and PCr cyclise non-enzymatically to creatinine at about 1.7% of the pool a day, so a larger pool raises serum creatinine without any change in filtration; cystatin C, an alternative filtration marker, is unaffected.

**3. Caffeine and adenosine receptors** (in vitro pharmacology and human mechanistic). Caffeine antagonises A1 and A2A adenosine receptors (Ki roughly 10-50 µM). A 3 mg/kg dose for you (231 mg in about 50 L of body water) peaks near 24 µM: enough to occupy many receptors, but far below the 0.1-1 mM needed for phosphodiesterase inhibition or ryanodine-receptor Ca²⁺ release (calculation). The ergogenic effect is therefore mainly central: lower perceived effort and pain, greater motor drive. Hepatic CYP1A2 converts caffeine mainly to paraxanthine, also an adenosine antagonist; the half-life averages about 5 h (range 2-10 h). Adenosine is an endogenous sleep-regulatory signal that accumulates with time awake [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine]; A1 receptors inhibit wake-promoting neurons and A2A receptors promote sleep (textbook), so antagonism delays sleep onset and reduces slow-wave sleep. With first-order elimination, 200 mg at 12:00 leaves 22-50 mg at 04:00 (half-life 5-8 h), and a further 100 mg at 18:00, the latest second dose, adds 25-42 mg (calculation). Adenosine also appears to signal to the [[term:circadian-rhythm|circadian clock]] [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine], so late caffeine may delay an already late clock (inference).

**4. L-theanine** (animal and in vitro; limited human data). This glutamine analogue from tea crosses the blood-brain barrier on LAT1, binds glutamate receptors only weakly in vitro, raises brain GABA, dopamine and serotonin in rodents and increases alpha-band EEG activity in humans. No pathway links it to [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] or training adaptation.

**5. Magnesium** (human mechanistic; sleep effects animal and theoretical). Intracellular Mg²⁺ exists mainly as Mg-ATP, the true substrate of myosin ATPase, SERCA, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and CK, but the free pool is tightly regulated. Absorption through saturable TRPM6/TRPM7 channels and paracellular flux is incomplete, a healthy kidney excretes the excess, and unabsorbed Mg²⁺ holds water in the colon, so diarrhoea limits the dose. Mg²⁺ blocks NMDA channels and modulates GABA-A receptors in rodents, but cerebrospinal-fluid magnesium changes little with supplements in replete people, so sleep effects are plausible mainly in deficiency.

**6. Vitamin D and the VDR** (human mechanistic; muscle data animal and in vitro). Hepatic CYP2R1 makes 25(OH)D, the status marker, whose 2-3-week half-life means about 3 months to a new steady state; renal CYP27B1 makes calcitriol, which acts through VDR-RXR heterodimers on vitamin D response elements, for example inducing intestinal Ca²⁺ transport. VDR-null mice have small muscle fibres but also low calcium and phosphate, so correcting deficiency may help muscle mainly by restoring mineral handling and lowering PTH, predicting benefit only in deficient people.

**7. Vitamin K and γ-carboxylation** (human mechanistic; calcification data animal). γ-Glutamyl carboxylase uses vitamin K hydroquinone to convert specific glutamates to γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla), yielding vitamin K epoxide, which VKORC1, the warfarin target, recycles. Gla residues give Ca²⁺-binding function to clotting factors, osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein (MGP), whose loss calcifies arteries in knockout mice. MK-7 (half-life about 3 days) lowered uncarboxylated markers dose-dependently in haemodialysis patients [@Westenfeld2011_MK7DoseCarboxylation]. Calcitriol induces osteocalcin and MGP, the theoretical case for pairing K2 with D3; at 1,000 IU/d the extra demand is small (inference).

**8. Omega-3 fatty acids** (human mechanistic; mediator biology in vitro and animal). EPA and DHA enter membrane phospholipids over weeks (blood EPA+DHA rose 110% in 10 weeks [@Heileson2023_fishOilRTyoungRCT]), altering membrane order and raft composition, and are precursors of resolvins, protectins and maresins via cyclo-oxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways, the basis of recovery claims. None of this has been shown to add muscle in young, well-fed lifters.

**9. B12, folate and the methyl-folate trap** (human mechanistic; textbook). Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to transfer the methyl group of 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate (5-methyl-THF) to homocysteine. Because MTHFR is effectively irreversible, B12 deficiency traps folate as 5-methyl-THF, starving thymidylate synthesis and causing megaloblastic anaemia. Folic acid enters through dihydrofolate reductase, bypasses the trap and corrects the anaemia but not the neuropathy, which reflects lost methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity and impaired S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation: this masking underlies the folic-acid upper limit. Intrinsic-factor uptake saturates at about 1.5-2 µg per meal, but about 1% of an oral dose diffuses passively, so 500 µg supplies about 5 µg.
articles.evidence:
Certainty labels: established, probable, uncertain, inference. Effect sizes are [[term:smd|standardised mean differences (SMD)]] or Hedges g, a bias-corrected SMD. Creatine and caffeine trials include young untrained adults like you; most vitamin, mineral and omega-3 evidence comes from older adults, women, patients or prevalence surveys.

**Does creatine add muscle and strength?** Established for strength and lean mass, probable for muscle tissue itself. [[term:meta-analysis|Meta-analyses]] of [[term:rct|randomised controlled trials (RCTs)]] comparing training plus creatine with training plus placebo:

| Source | Studies | Result |
|---|---|---|
| [@Desai2024_creatineBodyComp] | 12 RCTs, adults under 50 | Lean mass +1.14 kg ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 0.69 to 1.59); body fat -0.88 percentage points (-1.66 to -0.11) |
| [@Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA] | 63 studies, 1,489 people | Strength g 0.54 (upper body) and 0.55 (lower body); lean mass g 0.30 |
| [@Burke2023_creatineRegionalHypertrophy] | 10 RCTs, direct muscle measures | Pooled effect 0.11 (95% credible interval -0.02 to 0.25); muscle thickness +1.0 to 1.6 mm |

Training status and volume did not moderate the lean-mass effect [@Desai2024_creatineBodyComp], nor did loading or daily dose moderate outcomes [@Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA].

**Is creatine safe?** Probable for healthy kidneys and hair. Across 19 trials, serum creatinine rose by 0.13 mg/dL (0.07 to 0.18) while urea and eGFR did not change (eGFR -5.20 mL/min/1.73 m², -15.00 to 4.60; 8 trials) [@Tsiaras2026_creatineKidneyMA]: more creatinine production, not less filtration. For you, that rise would lower calculated eGFR by roughly 7-15%, depending on your baseline creatinine (CKD-EPI 2021; calculation). The ISSN describes up to 30 g/d for 5 years as safe in healthy people [@Kreider2017_ISSNcreatine]. In a 12-week RCT in trained men (38 completers), 5 g/d changed neither DHT, the DHT:testosterone ratio nor hair density, follicle counts or thickness [@Lak2025_creatineHairRCT]; it was small and short.

**Does caffeine help, and what does it cost?** Established for acute performance: taken about 60 min before exercise, 3-6 mg/kg gives small to moderate gains in strength, muscular endurance, movement velocity, sprinting and jumping, with the most consistent gains in aerobic endurance; about 2 mg/kg may be the minimum effective dose, and about 9 mg/kg adds side effects without benefit [@Guest2021_ISSNcaffeine]. Your current 100 mg is about 1.3 mg/kg; 2-3 mg/kg is 154-231 mg. Effects on muscle growth are untested. Sleep costs are probable and dose- and time-dependent: across 24 studies, caffeine cut total sleep by 45 min and deep N3/N4 sleep by 11.4 min and delayed sleep onset by 9 min; avoiding lost sleep required about 107 mg at least 8.8 h, or about 217 mg at least 13.2 h, before bed [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA]. For a 04:00 bedtime, the latest 200 mg dose falls near 14:45 and the latest 100 mg near 19:10, if the cut-offs carry over to a shifted schedule (inference).

**Do theanine and magnesium add anything?** Uncertain at best. Against placebo, theanine plus caffeine improved attention-switching accuracy at 2 h (SMD 0.33, 0.13 to 0.54), while reaction time and mood were inconclusive [@Payne2025_theanineMA], and effect size tracked the caffeine dose more than the theanine dose [@Camfield2014_theanineCaffeineMA]; the pooled comparisons were against placebo, not caffeine alone, and no catalogued trial measures training or shows it offsets caffeine's sleep costs. In 3 small trials of older adults with insomnia, magnesium shortened sleep onset by 17.4 min (95% CI 7.4 to 27.3) without significantly changing total sleep, at low to very low [[term:grade|GRADE]] certainty [@Mah2021_magnesiumInsomniaMA]. A Cochrane review found no effect on idiopathic cramps (probable) and possibly more minor gastrointestinal adverse events (RR 1.51, 0.98 to 2.33) [@Garrison2020_magnesiumCrampsCochrane]. No catalogued trial shows a performance benefit of either in people who are not deficient.

**Vitamin D: correction or performance aid?** Established that deficiency is common: 67% of Indian adults (61 to 73%), with a South Asian mean 25(OH)D of 19 ng/mL [@Siddiqee2021_SouthAsiaVitDPrevalence]. In healthy 18-40-year-olds, mostly women, supplementation increased upper- and lower-limb strength (both SMD 0.32; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.54 and 0.01 to 0.63; 7 trials) [@Tomlinson2014_vitDStrengthMA], probably only in those starting low (uncertain). The Endocrine Society suggests against empiric doses above the dietary reference intake for disease prevention in healthy adults under 75, and against routine 25(OH)D testing, including in people with darker skin [@Demay2024_EndoSocVitDGuideline]; it does not address probable deficiency in South Asia.

**Vitamin K2?** Uncertain, with no indication at 31: insufficiency markers cluster in children and adults over about 40 [@Theuwissen2014_vitKStatusHealthy], MK-7 trials report only surrogate markers, in postmenopausal women (dp-ucMGP halved) [@Knapen2015_MK7ArterialStiffness] and haemodialysis patients [@Westenfeld2011_MK7DoseCarboxylation], and none has tested D3 with versus without K2 in young men.

**Omega-3?** Probable no effect on muscle mass; strength uncertain. A 4-trial meta-analysis found improved strength but no change in muscle mass [@Uchida2024_omega3RT_MA]. In young adults training for 10 weeks, lean mass rose similarly (+3.4% vs +2.4%, p = 0.457) and bench-press [[term:1rm|1RM]] rose more (+17.7% vs +9.7%, p = 0.047), but absolute squat did not differ [@Heileson2023_fishOilRTyoungRCT]: borderline results among several outcomes.

**B12 and folic acid?** Probable that deficiency is common: pooled Indian data give 53% for B12 (41 to 64%) and 37% for folate (27 to 46%), across mixed ages and diets, with no estimate for omnivorous men [@Venkatesh2021_IndiaMicronutrientDeficiency]. No catalogued trial tests either supplement in non-deficient men; the verdicts rest on prevalence, physiology and the masking mechanism (inference).

**What about candidate additions?** HMB: probable no benefit; in young adults it did not change fat-free mass, fat mass or strength (11 studies) [@Jakubowski2020_HMByoungMA], although a position stand by commercially affiliated authors claims benefits in untrained people [@Rathmacher2024_ISSNHMB]. Ashwagandha: uncertain benefit (overall g 0.47, 0.25 to 0.69; prediction interval -0.40 to 1.33) [@Li2026_ashwagandhaPerformanceMA; @Bonilla2021_ashwagandhaBayesianMA] against an established harm of unknown frequency, idiosyncratic and mainly cholestatic liver injury 2-12 weeks after starting [@Bjornsson2020_ashwagandhaDILI]. In an Indian series, 5 of 8 people injured by single-ingredient products had chronic liver disease, and 3 of them died of acute-on-chronic liver failure [@Philips2023_ashwagandhaHILI_India]. Beta-alanine, citrulline, nitrate and melatonin lack catalogued evidence here and by mechanism target 0.5-10 min efforts, endurance or circadian timing, not hypertrophy (inference).

**Are products sold in India what the label says?** Probable that quality varies widely.
