Most popular protein supplements tested missed their labelled protein, some exceeded it (suggesting amino-acid spiking), major brands had aflatoxins and pesticide residues, many contained lead and arsenic, and some contained potentially hepatotoxic herbal extracts [@Philips2024_CitizensProteinProject]. A follow-up found mainstream sports wheys averaged 75.6 g protein/100 g and 12.5% were taurine-spiked, whereas pharmacy 'medical' powders averaged 29.1 g/100 g, 83% were mislabelled and 89% taurine-spiked [@Philips2025_CitizensProteinProject2]. Spiking pays because protein is usually estimated from nitrogen (× 6.38), so 1 g of taurine reads as about 0.7 g of protein (calculation).
articles.practice:
Verdicts follow [[dec:D21]]; the daily schedule is on [[plan:supplements]], with meals numbered as in [[dec:D20]].

| Item | Verdict | Dose and timing |
|---|---|---|
| Creatine monohydrate | Keep | 5 g/d with meal 2 (first meal on rest days); no loading; same dose in every phase to avoid water shifts ([[sci:sci-bodycomp]]) |
| Vitamin D3 | Keep | 1,000 IU (25 µg)/d with a meal containing some fat |
| Vitamin B12 | Keep | 250-500 µg/d with a meal |
| Caffeine | Optional | 150-200 mg at 12:00 on training days; at most 100 mg more, finished by 17:00-18:00; none after 19:00 |
| L-theanine | Optional | 100-200 mg with the 12:00 caffeine, if you value it |
| Magnesium glycinate | 4-week trial | 100-200 mg elemental with meal 4; stop without clear benefit or with loose stools |
| Omega-3 | Optional | Only with fewer than 2 oily-fish meals a week: 250-500 mg/d EPA+DHA |
| Vitamin K2, folic acid | Remove | Unless prescribed for a documented reason |
| Protein powder | Optional | Only if cheaper or easier per gram of protein than food ([[sci:sci-protein]]) |
| HMB, beta-alanine, citrulline, nitrate, pre-workouts, fat burners | Do not add | No benefit for your goals |
| Melatonin | Not routinely | Light and caffeine timing first |
| Ashwagandha | Avoid | Also in blends and protein powders |

- **Upper limits** (regulatory values): caffeine under 400 mg/d; supplemental magnesium 350 mg/d elemental (bisglycinate is about 14% magnesium); vitamin D 4,000 IU/d (60,000 IU weekly averages about 8,600 IU/d, a time-limited treatment); folic acid 1,000 µg/d (a 5 mg tablet is five times this). Keep EPA+DHA at or below 1 g/d (practical convention): higher doses were linked with atrial fibrillation in older adults in trials outside the catalogued evidence.
- **Sleep first** ([[dec:D22]], [[sci:sci-sleep]]): if falling asleep at 04:00 takes over 30 min, drop the second caffeine dose, then halve the first.
- **Blood tests**: mention creatine and ask for cystatin C if kidney function is questioned; for B12, ask for methylmalonic acid or holotranscobalamin.
- **Buying**: single-ingredient products with an FSSAI licence and a stated dose; no proprietary blends; check labels for *Withania somnifera*, green tea extract, Garcinia and turmeric extracts. For powder, a mainstream sports whey with an amino-acid profile ([[term:leucine|leucine]] about 10% of protein), no added taurine, glycine or creatine, ideally with an independent batch certificate.
articles.uncertainties:
- Your exact products and doses are not yet known, so the upper-limit checks (elemental magnesium per tablet, weekly versus monthly 60,000 IU vitamin D, 400 µg versus 5 mg folic acid, EPA+DHA per capsule) are pending, as is whether any item was prescribed.
- Some supporting figures come from sources outside the catalogued evidence: the 400 mg/d caffeine limit and nutrient upper limits, the atrial-fibrillation signal with high-dose fish oil, and a reported caffeine-creatine antagonism during loading that is unlikely to matter at your doses (inference). Treat them as provisional.
- Creatine lean-mass gains are partly water, and kidney and hair data beyond a year are sparse.
- The caffeine cut-offs assume that hours before bed carry over to a shifted schedule, which is untested. Your caffeine half-life (about 2-10 h between people) and daytime sleeping conditions matter more than averages, so your own sleep log decides.
- No pooled Indian B12 figure for omnivorous men was found, and your status is unknown.
- Product surveys are snapshots; brands and batches change.

What would change the plan: a prescription or diagnosed deficiency; kidney, liver, heart-rhythm or blood-pressure problems, or medicines such as proton-pump inhibitors, metformin, anticoagulants or CYP1A2 inhibitors; two oily-fish meals a week (drop omega-3); a normal B12 with methylmalonic acid on a daily animal-food diet (drop B12); a later training time (re-anchor caffeine to at least 13 h before bed); independent trials showing benefit for an item marked do not add.

articles.title: Sleep and your circadian schedule
articles.tagline: Why keeping your late schedule fixed matters more than moving it, how light, caffeine and meals hold it steady, and what short sleep costs your training.
articles.summary:
You already sleep about 7-8 hours, which meets the expert recommendation of at least 7 hours a night. The task now is to protect that sleep: keep the window fixed every day, make the bedroom dark and cool, and time light, caffeine, food and training so they support it.

Sleep matters for your goals. One night without sleep lowered [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] the next day by 18%, and sleeping 6 hours or less cut exercise performance by about 7.6% on average. During a calorie deficit, two small trials found that shorter sleep shifted weight loss away from fat and towards lean tissue.

Sleeping late is probably less important than sleeping irregularly. In a large cohort, people with the least regular sleep timing had the highest mortality, and a late but consistent schedule avoids [[term:social-jetlag|social jetlag]]. Because your work ends at 01:00, moving sleep much earlier would probably shorten it, so the default is 04:00-12:00 every day, days off included.

Your internal clock, the [[term:circadian-rhythm|circadian rhythm]], is set mainly by light reaching specialised cells in the eye. Daylight soon after waking and dim light in the three hours before bed help hold it steady; daylight leaking into the bedroom after sunrise works against it. Caffeine blocks [[term:adenosine|adenosine]], which builds sleep pressure while you are awake, so caffeine belongs early in your day. Your 13:00 sessions end long before bedtime and should not disturb sleep, and regular training probably improves sleep quality modestly. One hour after waking some grogginess, [[term:sleep-inertia|sleep inertia]], lingers; its effect on lifting is unknown.

If poor sleep persists despite these measures, the first-line treatment is [[term:cbt-i|CBT for insomnia (CBT-I)]], not pills or supplements.
articles.mechanisms:
**Two regulators (theoretical framework).** A homeostatic sleep pressure that builds with time awake interacts with a circadian signal that promotes wakefulness across the biological day (the two-process model; background physiology, not tested in the sources here). Sleep consolidates best when both line up at the same clock time every day.

**The clock: SCN and the transcription-translation loop (cellular and animal mechanistic).** The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus is the master pacemaker; it synchronises clocks in peripheral tissues, skeletal muscle included, through neural, endocrine and temperature signals, while feeding and activity reset peripheral clocks directly (background physiology). In each cell the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer drives transcription of target genes, including its own repressors; a PER1/2-CRY1/2 complex with casein kinase 1δ/ε then represses CLOCK-BMAL1, giving an oscillation of roughly 24 h [@Laothamatas2023_clockMechanism]. Phosphorylation by CK1δ/ε also marks PER for proteasomal degradation, which helps set the period (background). Clock outputs time much of metabolism, and metabolic signals feed back on the clock [@Laothamatas2023_clockMechanism]. In humans, five nights at 4 h in bed blunted the amplitude of the skin-temperature rhythm and interval exercise preserved it [@Saner2020_sleepRestrictionHIIE]; clock genes were not measured, so a molecular explanation remains theoretical.

**Light input: melanopsin and ipRGCs (human laboratory dose-response, synthesised by expert consensus).** Non-visual effects of light, such as clock resetting and neuroendocrine and alerting responses, are mediated mainly by [[term:melanopsin|melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)]], so they track melanopic irradiance better than ordinary lux; melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) quantifies this input [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations]. As background, melanopsin is a Gq-coupled opsin most sensitive near 480 nm that depolarises the cell through phospholipase C and TRPC channels, and ipRGCs reach the SCN through the retinohypothalamic tract (glutamate and PACAP). Light in the biological morning advances the clock and light in the biological evening and early night delays it (background chronobiology). On your schedule the advancing window probably begins around your 12:00 wake, while the delaying window spans the hours before bed and much of your sleep period, when sunrise light can leak in (inference).

**Melatonin (phase-marker data from a small RCT; synthesis pathway background).** The SCN drives pineal melatonin synthesis through a sympathetic relay: noradrenaline acting on β1-adrenergic receptors raises cAMP and activates arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase, the rate-limiting enzyme in converting serotonin to melatonin, and light at night shuts the pathway down (background physiology). Dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) therefore marks internal time. In night owls, practical changes to sleep, light, meal, caffeine and exercise timing moved DLMO and the cortisol awakening peak about 2 h earlier [@FacerChilds2019_nightOwlPhaseAdvance].

**Adenosine and caffeine (mechanistic review, animal and human).** [[term:adenosine|Adenosine]] is accepted as an endogenous sleep-regulatory substance, and caffeine reduces sleepiness by antagonising adenosine receptors [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine]. As background, extracellular adenosine rises during waking, partly from ATP that astrocytes release and ectonucleotidases hydrolyse; A1 receptors (Gi-coupled) inhibit wake-promoting neurons and A2A receptors (Gs-coupled) support sleep-promoting circuits. Caffeine is cleared over several hours at rates that vary with hepatic CYP1A2 activity (background pharmacology), so a dose taken many hours before bed still lengthens sleep onset and cuts deep N3 sleep [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA]. Adenosine may also act on the circadian clock, linking the two regulators [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine].

**Slow-wave sleep and growth hormone (pooled observational physiology).** In 149 healthy men, growth hormone (GH) secretion tracked slow-wave sleep (SWS) independently of age; SWS fell from 18.9% of sleep at 16-25 years to 3.4% at 36-50, and GH secretion by 372 µg per decade [@VanCauter2000_SWS_GH]. In men the largest GH pulse usually follows sleep onset, and GHRH promotes both SWS and GH release (background endocrinology). No source here links sleep-related GH to training-induced [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]], and a hormonal rise does not automatically translate into growth (inference).

**Sleep loss and muscle (human mechanistic).** One night without sleep lowered next-day postprandial [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis]] by 18%, raised cortisol by 21% and lowered testosterone by 24%, without changing gene markers of protein breakdown [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS]. Five nights at 4 h in bed lowered sarcoplasmic protein synthesis, mitochondrial respiration and glucose tolerance, and three interval sessions prevented these changes [@Saner2020_sleepRestrictionHIIE]. Glucocorticoid induction of REDD1, which inhibits [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]], is one plausible link (theoretical; not measured). These are acute markers after severe sleep loss, and acute changes in synthesis do not automatically translate into less long-term growth.

**Heat, light during sleep and sleep inertia (human laboratory; narrative reviews).** With normal bedding, heat increases wakefulness and reduces slow-wave and REM sleep, and humidity adds to the thermal load, reflecting the coupling of sleep and thermoregulation [@OkamotoMizuno2012_thermalEnvironment]. Sleeping under 100 lux raised heart rate, shifted sympathovagal balance towards sympathetic activity and increased next-morning insulin resistance, suggesting an autonomic route from light to glucose metabolism [@Mason2022_lightDuringSleep]. On waking, [[term:sleep-inertia|sleep inertia]] impairs alertness and cognition and fades exponentially; it is worse after sleep loss or when waking at an adverse circadian time [@Jewett1999_sleepInertiaTimeCourse; @Hilditch2019_sleepInertiaReview]. Residual adenosine and slow reactivation of prefrontal cortex are proposed contributors (background).
articles.evidence:
| Question | Best estimate | Certainty |
|---|---|---|
| How much sleep? | At least 7 h a night [@Watson2015_sleepDurationConsensus] | Probable (consensus) |
| 6 h or less before exercise | Performance -7.6% (95% CI -11.9 to -3.1) [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA] | Probable |
| One night without sleep | Next-day MPS -18% [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS] | Uncertain (one small trial; acute marker) |
| Short sleep in a deficit | Less fat and more lean mass lost [@Nedeltcheva2010_sleepCaloricRestriction] | Probable (small trials) |
| Regular sleep timing | 20-48% lower mortality [@Windred2024_sleepRegularityMortality] | Probable (association only) |
| Chronic insomnia | CBT-I first-line [@Qaseem2016_ACPinsomniaGuideline] | Established (guideline) |

**How much sleep, and would more help?** A sleep-medicine consensus recommends at least 7 h a night for adults, noting that individual need varies [@Watson2015_sleepDurationConsensus]. Across 25 athlete studies, sleep extension and naps worked best and sleep-hygiene education alone had no effect [@Cunha2023_sleepInterventionsAthletes]; in one uncontrolled trial, 11 basketball players who slept 111 min more a night sprinted and shot better [@Mah2011_sleepExtensionBasketball]. Certainty: probable for the 7-h floor; extending beyond 7-8 h in non-athletes is untested.

**Sleep loss, performance and muscle.** Across 69 publications, 6 h of sleep or less reduced performance by 7.6% ([[term:i2|I²]] 98%), strength included [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA]. Total deprivation and waking early consistently impaired performance, a later bedtime did not consistently do so, and morning tasks were largely spared; 89% of participants were men. In 13 young adults, one night without sleep lowered muscle protein synthesis from 0.072 to 0.059 %/h [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS]. [[term:hiit|High-intensity interval]] exercise during five nights of 4-h sleep preserved sarcoplasmic protein synthesis and glucose tolerance in young men [@Saner2020_sleepRestrictionHIIE] but not mood, reaction time or fatigue [@Saner2023_sleepRestrictionMoodAlertness]. Certainty: probable for acute effects; these exposures were far harsher than your 7-8 h, and no study measured muscle growth under restriction.

**Sleep during a deficit.** In a 14-day crossover (n = 10), 5.5 h rather than 8.5 h of sleep opportunity cut fat loss from 1.4 to 0.6 kg and raised [[term:ffm|fat-free mass]] loss from 1.5 to 2.4 kg [@Nedeltcheva2010_sleepCaloricRestriction]. In an 8-week [[term:rct|RCT]] (n = 36), about 1 h less sleep on 5 nights a week left absolute losses unchanged but made a smaller share of the loss fat, and catch-up sleep on the other 2 nights did not correct this [@Wang2018_sleepRestrictionWeightLoss]. Neither included resistance training or high protein; participants were overweight and mostly middle-aged. Certainty: probable for direction, uncertain for size.

**Regularity, chronotype and social jetlag.** In 60,977 UK Biobank adults (mean age 63), the four more regular quintiles had 20-48% lower all-cause mortality than the least regular, and regularity predicted mortality better than duration [@Windred2024_sleepRegularityMortality]. Definite evening types had 10% higher mortality than definite morning types (95% CI 2-18%) [@Knutson2018_chronotypeMortality]. Social jetlag correlated weakly with BMI (r 0.12) [@Arab2023_socialJetlagObesityMA]; another [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] found small associations with BMI, waist and HbA1c but none with obesity, metabolic syndrome or type 2 diabetes, and rated its evidence low [@Bouman2022_socialJetlagMetabolicMA]. Certainty: probable for associations, uncertain for causation.

**Should your schedule move earlier?** In night owls, an RCT of earlier fixed sleep and wake times, morning light, fixed meals and timed caffeine and exercise advanced sleep timing and DLMO by about 2 h without shortening sleep, and improved self-reported depression and stress, morning reaction time and grip strength [@FacerChilds2019_nightOwlPhaseAdvance]. Certainty: inference for you; no trial has studied late workers, and a large advance would collide with your 01:00 finish.

**Light and the bedroom.** Consensus thresholds at the eye are at least 250 lux melanopic EDI by day, at most 10 lux from 3 h before bed and at most 1 lux during sleep; they were not designed for non-standard schedules [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations]. In over 88,000 light-sensor wearers, the brightest days predicted lower mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.66-0.83) and the brightest nights higher mortality (1.21-1.34) [@Windred2024_lightExposureMortality]. Certainty: probable for darkness and avoiding heat [@OkamotoMizuno2012_thermalEnvironment; @Mason2022_lightDuringSleep]; uncertain for eye masks and earplugs, which improved subjective but not consistently objective sleep in 19 mostly intensive-care studies [@Locihova2017_earplugsEyeMask].

**Caffeine.** Across 24 studies, caffeine cut total sleep by 45 min and deep sleep by 11.4 min and lengthened sleep onset by 9 min; to protect total sleep, about 107 mg should come at least 8.8 h and 217.5 mg at least 13.2 h before bed [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA]. Certainty: probable; the cut-offs are model estimates for average responders.

**Training time and sleep inertia.** Across 23 studies, evening exercise did not impair sleep, although vigorous exercise ending within 1 h of bed might [@Stutz2019_eveningExerciseMA]; across 66 studies, regular exercise improved sleep modestly, most clearly subjective quality [@Kredlow2015_exerciseSleepMA]. Evening performance exceeds morning in conventionally timed people (handgrip effect size 0.39) [@Knaier2022_diurnalVariation], and late chronotypes perform worse than early ones in the morning [@FacerChilds2018_chronotype], yet long-term strength and hypertrophy did not differ between morning and evening training [@Grgic2019_time_of_day_RT; @Bruggisser2023_timeOfDayMeta]. After 8 h of sleep, inertia persisted despite showering, breakfast and room light, decaying with time constants of 0.67 h (alertness) and 1.17 h (cognition) and nearing baseline at 2-4 h [@Jewett1999_sleepInertiaTimeCourse]; by our calculation about 77% and 57% of those deficits clear within 1 h. No study related lifting to time since waking. Certainty: probable for sleep effects; inference for your sessions.

**Late eating.** Eating within 3 h of bed was associated with night waking in 793 students (odds ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.15-2.27) [@Chung2020_mealProximitySleep], and eating within 1 h with prolonged waking in US time-use data [@Iao2021_bedtimeEatingATUS]. Pre-sleep casein (20-40 g) raises overnight protein synthesis [@Reis2020_presleepProteinSR], and 27.5 g nightly enlarged 12-week strength and quadriceps gains versus a non-caloric placebo, but total protein was not matched [@Snijders2015_presleep]. Certainty: uncertain.

**Measurement and insomnia.** A Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score above 5 identifies poor sleepers (sensitivity 89.6%, specificity 86.5%) [@Buysse1989_PSQI]; the Consensus Sleep Diary standardises daily logging but was not validated at publication [@Carney2012_consensusSleepDiary]. Consumer trackers detect sleep well but wake poorly (specificity 0.18-0.54), especially on disrupted nights [@Chinoy2021_consumerSleepTrackers]; heart-rate-based Fitbits did not differ significantly from polysomnography in total sleep time [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep]. The American College of Physicians recommends [[term:cbt-i|CBT-I]] first for chronic insomnia (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), with medication only if it fails [@Qaseem2016_ACPinsomniaGuideline].
articles.practice:
**Sleep window** ([[dec:D22]], [[plan:sleep]])

- Keep an 8-h sleep opportunity, 04:00-12:00, every day including days off, and aim for at least 7 h asleep.
- Keep day-to-day variation within about 30 min, and do not shift the window earlier: with a 01:00 finish that would probably shorten sleep (inference).
- If a night must be short, go to bed later rather than waking earlier, and keep the 12:00 wake and 13:00 session. Train as planned after one short night; after several, trim sets or load and prioritise sleep.

**Bedroom**: blackout curtains or an eye mask, standby lights covered, earplugs or steady background noise if needed, and a cool room (air conditioning or a fan).

**Light**: outdoor daylight within 1-2 h of waking, such as walking part of the way to the gym or [[ex:cardio-steady]] outdoors on rest days (10-20 min; practical convention). Keep your workspace bright until about 01:00, then use dim, warm light and low screen brightness.

**Caffeine** ([[dec:D21]], [[sci:sci-supplements]]): take the pre-workout 150-200 mg at about 12:00-12:30, any second dose of about 100 mg by 17:00-18:00 and nothing after about 19:00, keeping the daily total under 400 mg; these cut-offs sit inside the model estimates above.

**Training** ([[dec:D10]]): keep 13:00 with the full warm-up and ramp-up sets ([[tool:warmup]]); if your first heavy sets feel sluggish, lengthen the general warm-up by a few minutes, or train nearer 14:00 if your day allows (inference). Avoid hard sessions such as [[ex:cardio-int-4x4]] after about 02:00. Test at your usual training time and log start times in Hevy ([[plan:logging]]).

**Food** ([[dec:D20]], [[plan:nutrition]]): finish meal 4, which is protein-rich with casein or dairy and doubles as your pre-sleep protein, by about 02:00, at least 2 h before bed ([[sci:sci-protein]]).

**Deficit phases** ([[dec:D04]]): if sleep drops below about 6.5 h on several nights a week, shrink or pause the deficit until it recovers (practical convention; [[rule:energy-adjustment]]).

**Monitoring** ([[plan:monitoring]]): PSQI at baseline and every 4-8 weeks, plus a 1-minute daily diary of bed, sleep-onset and wake times, awakenings, quality, caffeine and last-meal times. A wearable ([[dec:D25]]) is for timing and duration trends only.

!> See a clinician, and ask about CBT-I, if your PSQI stays above 5 or poor sleep with daytime impairment persists. Loud snoring or witnessed breathing pauses need assessment for sleep apnoea (standard clinical advice).
articles.uncertainties:
- No study included people who work until 01:00 and sleep 04:00-12:00; applying the light thresholds, the night-owl trial and time-of-day data to you is inference.
- Whether your late timing reflects a late [[term:chronotype|chronotype]] or only your work hours is unknown; no circadian phase marker has been measured.
- The muscle evidence is acute and comes from severe sleep loss. No trial has measured hypertrophy under mild chronic restriction, or whether extending sleep from 7-8 h to 8-9 h helps a non-athlete.
- The deficit trials excluded resistance training and high protein, both of which you will have, so the size of the effect for you is unknown.
- Regularity, chronotype and light findings are observational and probably confounded; the regularity cohort averaged 63 years.
- Eye-mask and earplug evidence comes from intensive care, and the sources here did not test trackers on current models or during daytime sleep.
- Sleep need and caffeine sensitivity vary between people; the caffeine cut-offs are averages.

What would change the plan: a diary showing under 7 h on many nights or a PSQI above 5 (escalate); a change in work hours (re-plan the window); trials of schedule advancement in late workers; hypertrophy trials under mild sleep restriction; your own logs showing clearly better sessions with a later start.

articles.title: Measuring body composition
articles.tagline: What your scale, tape and fitness tests actually measure, how large their errors are, and how to see a slow trend through day-to-day noise.
articles.summary:
Your bathroom scale measures two things: your weight, and how strongly your legs resist a tiny alternating current ([[term:bia|bioelectrical impedance analysis, BIA]]). Every other number it shows, from body-fat percentage and muscle mass to visceral fat and 'metabolic age', is calculated from that reading plus the height, age and sex you entered [@Nunez1997_legtolegBIA]. Consumer BIA devices repeat themselves closely, but for one person their body-fat estimate can be off by 3-7 percentage points, and even the better ones misjudge change over three to four months by about 2 points [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices]. That error is larger than the change you are likely to make in a few months, and eating, drinking or training before a reading adds more [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange].

The programme therefore relies on simpler signals whose errors are known. Body weight, taken each morning under the same conditions and averaged over 7 days, shows the trend that single readings hide, because weight swings by about 0.3% across an ordinary week [@Maher2023_weightfluctuation]. Your waist divided by your height ([[term:whtr|waist-to-height ratio]]) flags cardiometabolic risk better than BMI [@Ashwell2012_WHtR]; yours is about 0.475, below the 0.5 boundary. Tape-based body-fat equations disagree with each other by several points, so you see a range (currently a working estimate of about 20%, plausibly 17-24%), not a single figure.

Fitness is tracked with field tests (a timed walk, push-ups, pull-ups, a broad jump and single-leg balance) whose noise has been measured, so you can tell real improvement from day-to-day variation. A wearable is optional: it counts steps well and measures resting heart rate reasonably, but no brand estimates calorie expenditure accurately enough to set your food intake [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR; @Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy].
articles.mechanisms:
**What the scale measures** (physics from first principles; expert review and validation data)

A foot-to-foot scale contains load cells, which weigh you, and metal footpads that act as electrodes. It drives a weak alternating current (50 kHz in single-frequency designs) through your legs and measures the resulting voltage; their ratio is [[term:impedance|impedance]] (Z) [@Nunez1997_legtolegBIA]. Impedance has two components. Resistance (R) is the opposition of ionic body water to current. Reactance (Xc) is the phase lag introduced by cell membranes: a lipid bilayer separating two electrolyte solutions is a capacitor. At low frequency membranes block current, which then flows through extracellular water; as frequency rises their reactance falls and current increasingly crosses cells. At 50 kHz it travels mainly through extracellular water and partly through cells [@Kyle2004_BIAprinciples]. The [[term:phase-angle|phase angle]], arctan(Xc/R), rises with the amount of intact membrane and falls when cells are lost or water moves outside them. It is a prognostic marker in disease [@Norman2012_phaseAngle], with no established use for tracking a healthy trainee in the sources read.

**From resistance to fat: the two-compartment model** (physical model plus a physiological constant; the water-shift examples are partly inference)

For a uniform cylinder, R = ρL/A, so its volume is V = AL = ρL²/R. Treating the body as a conductor whose length scales with height gives the core BIA term, height²/R, which predicts total body water. Fat holds little water and conducts poorly, so it is never measured; it is what remains. The device converts body water to [[term:ffm|fat-free mass (FFM)]] by assuming that water is about 73% of FFM, a ratio that is stable across mammals [@Wang1999_hydrationConstant], then computes fat mass as weight minus FFM. The weak point follows directly: anything that changes body water or its distribution without changing tissue moves both estimates. Meals and drinks, sweating, skin temperature, glycogen (stored with about 3-4 parts water [@Kreitzman1992_glycogenWater]) and the extra intracellular water that creatine brings all qualify; the glycogen and creatine cases are mechanistic inference. As an illustration (arithmetic, not a study result): you hold roughly 45 L of water, so a 2% shift in measured resistance corresponds to about 0.9 L, which the 0.73 constant turns into 1.2 kg of 'FFM' and, at unchanged weight, about 1.6 percentage points of body fat. Real equations lean less heavily on impedance than this, but the direction holds, and it fits the findings that unstandardised readings blunt or exaggerate true change [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange] and that food and fluid shift impedance-based estimates substantially [@Kerr2017_foodfluid].

**Why a foot-to-foot device knows little about your trunk** (physics plus validation data; how each output is derived is inference, because the equations are unpublished)

Current enters one sole, rises through that leg, crosses the pelvis and descends the other leg. Your arms and most of your trunk, including all visceral fat, lie outside the path. Leg-to-leg height²/Z alone predicted body water and FFM less well than arm-to-leg BIA and caught up only when age, sex and waist-to-hip ratio were added as covariates; footpads also read about 15 Ω higher than gel electrodes (526 vs 511 Ω) while correlating at r = 0.99 [@Nunez1997_legtolegBIA]. Any BIA equation is valid only in the population where it was built and at normal hydration [@Kyle2004_BIAprinciples]. The proportional bias of foot-to-foot devices [@Nickerson2019_FFBIAmen] and the wide spread between brands [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices] are what heavy reliance on covariates and proprietary equations would produce.

| Scale output | How it is obtained |
|---|---|
| Weight | Measured (load cells) |
| Leg-to-leg impedance | Measured; the input to every estimate below |
| BMI | Arithmetic from weight and entered height |
| Body fat %, FFM, body water | Proprietary equation: impedance, weight, entered height, age and sex |
| Muscle, skeletal muscle, protein, bone mass, BMR, metabolic age | Further model outputs (equations unpublished) |
| Visceral and subcutaneous fat | Model outputs; the current path does not cross the abdomen |

**Optical versus electrical heart-rate sensing** (engineering principle plus validation studies)

A wrist device shines light into the skin and infers each pulse from rhythmic changes in the light absorbed by arterial blood (photoplethysmography). Movement alters the optical path and can make the algorithm lock onto your cadence instead of your pulse, so error grows during activity; skin tone was not a significant source of error [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy]. A chest strap detects the heart's electrical depolarisation directly and agreed almost perfectly with ECG [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors]. Gripping and wrist flexion, which describe most of a weights session, are probably the worst case for optical sensing (inference; with gripped elliptical arm levers every optical device agreed less well with ECG, rc < 0.80 [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors]).

**Signal versus noise** (measurement statistics)

A change is real only when it exceeds the method's error for change, often expressed as the minimal detectable change (MDC). Averaging n independent readings shrinks random error by about √n. A 7-day rolling mean of body weight has a further property: it always contains one reading from each weekday, so it cancels the systematic weekly cycle by construction (statistical reasoning applied to the cycle reported in [@Maher2023_weightfluctuation]).
articles.evidence:
**How accurate is a consumer BIA scale for one person?** Probable: poor to moderate.

Fifteen devices were compared with a four-compartment criterion. Repeatability was excellent (precision error 0-0.5 %BF), individual accuracy was not: standard error of estimate (SEE) 3.1-7.5 %BF, constant error -3.5 to +11.7 %BF, concordance 0.48-0.94 [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices]. In men, a foot-to-foot scale had a root-mean-square error of 5.6 %BF against [[term:dxa|DXA]] (concordance 0.66) [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA]; against a three-compartment model the 95% limits of agreement were ±5.7 %BF and ±5.2 kg FFM, with proportional bias [@Nickerson2019_FFBIAmen]. No peer-reviewed validation of any Renpho scale was found.

**Can it track change?** Probable: only large changes, under strict standardisation.

Over 12-16 weeks the devices still had an SEE of 1.7-2.6 %BF for change (concordance 0.37-0.78) [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices]. When either measurement was taken without controlling food, drink and activity, most methods, BIA included, blunted or exaggerated true change; DXA was more robust [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange]. Post-meal readings shifted impedance-based fat and FFM estimates substantially [@Kerr2017_foodfluid]. For scale, resistance training without a prescribed diet lowered body fat by about 1.5 percentage points on average (95% [[term:confidence-interval|CI]] 1.1-1.8) [@Wewege2022_RTbodyFat], which is inside the change error of the better devices.

**Tape-based equations** Probable: each carries about ±4-6 %BF individual error.

The [[term:navy-method|US Navy method]] uses navel waist minus neck, plus height; [[term:rfm|relative fat mass (RFM)]] uses height and waist; the Deurenberg equation uses BMI, age and sex.

| Equation | Against a criterion |
|---|---|
| Navy | Predicted DXA fat better than BMI or waist alone [@Friedl1997_circumferenceDXA]; circumference equations including it underestimated DXA by about 4.4-5.9 points in men (1,904 soldiers, 643 of them women) [@McClung2025_CBEvsDXA] |
| RFM | Beat BMI against DXA in large US samples [@Woolcott2018_RFM]; no systematic bias in 61 Mexican adults (intercept 1.12, 95% CI -2.44 to 4.68; R² 0.84) [@GuzmanLeon2019_RFMvalidation] |
| Deurenberg | SEE 4.1 %BF, R² 0.79; overestimates in obesity [@Deurenberg1991_BMIequation] |

For you they give 16.7% (Navy), 19.1% (Deurenberg) and 19.3-21.9% (RFM, depending on waist site), all within one another's error (arithmetic from the published equations). None was validated in South Asian men in the sources read, and because Deurenberg uses BMI it reads gained muscle as gained fat. Your [[term:ffmi|fat-free mass index (FFMI)]] at about 20% fat is about 18.8 kg/m² (17.9-19.5 across 17-24%), near the median of 18.9 for men aged 18-34 [@Schutz2002_FFMIpercentiles]; what that means for your goal is in [[sci:sci-expectations]].

**Waist, waist-to-height ratio and South Asian cut-offs** Probable.

Across 120 studies, the association of waist with mortality, cardiovascular disease and diabetes did not depend on the measurement site [@Ross2008_waistprotocol], but absolute values do (yours: 86 cm at the navel, 81 cm at the narrowest point), so one protocol must be used consistently [@Ross2020_waistConsensus]. In a [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 31 studies (over 300,000 adults), WHtR discriminated hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular disease better than BMI (area under the curve about 4-5% higher) and better than waist alone [@Ashwell2012_WHtR]. The mean boundary across outcomes and countries was 0.50 for both sexes [@Browning2010_WHtRboundary], and NICE uses 0.5 for increased and 0.6 for high central adiposity in all ethnic groups [@NICE2025_NG246]; an allometric analysis, tested only in young people, argues that a fixed ratio under-flags tall individuals [@Nevill2025_WHtRcritique]. Asian Indians carry more abdominal fat at a given BMI [@Misra2009_AsianIndianConsensus]. In 2,050 north Indians a waist of 78 cm detected at least one cardiovascular risk factor (sensitivity 74.3%, specificity 68.0%), giving proposed action levels of 78 and 90 cm for men [@Misra2006_IndianWaist]; WHO added Asian BMI action points at 23 and 27.5 [@WHO2004_AsianBMI]. Your waist lies between the two Indian levels at both sites, and your BMI of 23.5 sits just above 23 and will rise as you gain muscle.

**Weighing frequency and smoothing** Probable.

Adding self-weighing to structured weight-loss programmes gave an extra -1.7 kg (95% CI -2.6 to -0.8); weighing alone showed no clear effect in one trial, and daily and weekly weighing did not differ [@Madigan2015_selfweighingMA]. Self-weighing was not associated with worse mood, body attitudes or disordered eating, apart from a small negative association with psychological functioning [@Benn2016_selfweighingpsych]. Weight cycles by about 0.3% across the week, heaviest early in the week, with festive jumps of up to 0.65% [@Maher2023_weightfluctuation; @Orsama2014_weightRhythms]. At 77 kg the weekly swing (about 0.23 kg) equals one to two weeks at the planned lean-gain rate (0.1-0.25 kg/week). No trial compares smoothing methods.

**Progress photos** Uncertain. No study evaluated self-taken photos judged by eye. An industry-linked algorithm applied to standardised smartphone photos agreed with DXA better than a foot-to-foot scale in men (concordance 0.90 vs 0.66) [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA], but that is not human visual comparison.

**Field fitness tests** Probable for reliability; uncertain for prognosis.

- The Rockport 1-mile walk predicts [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] with a cross-validated SEE of 0.355 L/min, about 4.6 mL/kg/min at your weight [@Kline1987_Rockport]. The 1.5-mile (2.4 km) run had the highest validity of the distance-based tests (r 0.79, 95% CI 0.73-0.85) [@MayorgaVega2016_walkrunMA]. A non-exercise model had an SEE of 5.7 mL/kg/min in men [@Nes2011_nonexerciseVO2], and each 1-[[term:met|MET]] higher estimate was associated with 21% lower cardiovascular mortality in men under 60 [@Nes2014_nonexerciseMortality].
- A 15-s push-up test had ICC 0.989 and an MDC of 2 reps [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC]; a battery including maximal pull-ups had between-day ICC 0.87-0.98 in soldiers [@Lester2014_pullupReliability]. Firefighters managing more than 40 push-ups had far fewer cardiovascular events than those managing fewer than 10 (rate ratio 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.36; 37 events), an association rather than a target [@Yang2019_pushups].
- In the broad jump, learning alone added 12 cm on the first retest (MDC 29 cm); after familiarisation the MDC fell to 1 cm [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ].
- In single-leg stance, men aged 18-39 averaged 44.4 s eyes open (45 s cap) and 16.9 s (SD 13.9) eyes closed, best of three [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. If your test matched that protocol, both legs fall short eyes open, the left more so; eyes closed, both lie within the wide normal spread.
- Each 10 bpm higher resting heart rate was associated with all-cause mortality RR 1.17 (95% CI 1.14-1.19; [[term:i2|I²]] 94%) in observational data [@Aune2017_RHRmeta].

**Wearables** Probable.

In laboratory studies Fitbit, Apple and Samsung counted steps accurately, heart-rate accuracy varied by brand (Fitbit tended to underestimate), and no brand measured energy expenditure accurately [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR]. Against ECG a chest strap agreed almost perfectly (rc 0.996) and wrist devices ranged from 0.67 to 0.92 [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors]; optical error was about 30% larger during activity than at rest [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy]. Sleep-staging Fitbits matched polysomnography for total sleep time, but wake detection was limited (specificity 0.58-0.69) and stage times are rough [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep]. Tracker-based programmes raised daily steps modestly ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.24, 95% CI 0.16-0.33) [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA]; phone step counting showed wide error in one very small study [@Caputo2021_smartphoneSteps]. Google describes the Fitbit Air as a screenless band that tracks steps, sleep and heart rate, with advanced features behind a subscription [@GoogleHelp2026_FitbitAir]; no independent validation was found.
articles.practice:
- **Daily weight, judged weekly.** Weigh straight after waking (about 12:00) and using the toilet, before food, drink, caffeine, supplements or training, in the same minimal clothing, with the scale on a hard, level floor. Every reading is logged; decisions use the 7-day mean compared week on week, and food intake changes only on a 2-4-week trend ([[rule:energy-adjustment]], [[tool:energy]]).
- **Waist weekly**, in the same state, at the navel (primary, matching the Navy equation) and at the narrowest point, two readings each, averaged ([[ex:test-girths]]). During muscle gain, a sustained rise in navel waist is the earliest sign that fat gain is outpacing muscle gain.
- **Body fat as a range**, recalculated monthly from tape, height and weight ([[tool:bodycomp]]); the BMI-based estimate is dropped once you have gained muscle.
- **The Renpho is for weight.** Its body-fat, FFM, muscle and water figures appear only as a 4-week rolling mean of standardised readings with about ±5-6 %BF individual error and are never used for decisions; visceral fat, bone, protein, BMR, subcutaneous fat and metabolic age are ignored ([[dec:D23]]).
- **Fitness tests** at each reassessment ([[dec:D03]]): [[ex:test-pushup]] and [[ex:test-pullup]] with fixed form standards; [[ex:test-broad-jump]], best of three, after two familiarisation sessions; [[ex:test-sls]], best of three per leg, left first, barefoot ([[dec:D28]]); [[ex:test-rockport]], moving to [[ex:test-run-2400]] once you can run about 20 minutes continuously (inference); and [[ex:test-rhr]] averaged over 3 mornings. Changes of 2 reps or less are treated as noise (inference from the 2-rep MDC of a timed push-up test).
- **Freeze the protocol** before [[phase:p1]] and record changes in creatine, caffeine, sleep, illness, travel and festivals in the weekly check-in ([[tool:checkin]]); expect a step change in weight and BIA water when creatine starts or stops.
- **Photos** monthly, with the same place, light, distance, pose and fasted state, as a private record that is never scored (practical convention).
- **A wearable is optional** ([[dec:D25]]): use it for steps, resting heart rate and sleep timing, ignore its calorie figure, and pair a chest strap with your phone for heart-rate-guided intervals.
articles.uncertainties:
- No study has validated the Renpho Elis 1, so its frequency, equations and error for change are unknown; a validation against DXA or a four-compartment model showing small longitudinal error would earn its body-fat output more weight.
- None of the tape equations was validated in South Asian men, who carry more abdominal fat at a given BMI. A single DXA scan would anchor your estimates better than any equation (cost and access in India were not assessed).
- The reliability of self-measured waist, the size of creatine-related water shifts, and the within-person reliability of the Rockport walk and 2.4 km run in hot, humid conditions were not found in the sources read.
- Fixed WHtR thresholds may under-flag tall people [@Nevill2025_WHtRcritique]; at 181 cm you are tall for your population, so a value approaching 0.5 deserves attention. The NICE wording was checked only through a search summary.
- Visual judgement of progress photos has no validation at all.
- Device studies lag new releases: results for older Fitbits may not transfer to the Fitbit Air.
- The links between resting heart rate, push-up capacity and mortality are observational; improving the number may not lower your risk in proportion.

articles.title: Training safely alone
articles.tagline: Whether you need a medical check first, which warning signs mean stop, and how to judge effort, learn technique and read pain without a coach or spotter.
articles.summary:
For a healthy adult with no symptoms, current guidance does not require a doctor's clearance or an exercise test before starting. A short self-screening form, the PAR-Q+, does the job, and any 'yes' answer leads to follow-up questions and, if needed, a qualified professional [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening; @PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus].

The serious risks are real but rare. Vigorous effort briefly raises the risk of a heart attack or cardiac arrest in unfit people with hidden heart disease, while regular training lowers that risk overall [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk], and such events are often preceded by warning symptoms [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening]. [[term:rhabdomyolysis|Exertional rhabdomyolysis]], a breakdown of muscle that can injure the kidneys, follows unaccustomed, excessive sessions; about 15% of reported cases followed weightlifting [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo; @Backer2022_exertionalRhabdoSR]. Heat stroke is a further emergency in a hot climate [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness]. These risks are why your first weeks avoid sets to [[term:momentary-failure|failure]] and punishing volume, and why the app keeps a list of stop-and-get-help signs.

Everyday injury risk is low: bodybuilding-style training causes roughly 0.24-1 injury per 1,000 hours, mostly strains and sprains [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]. The hazard a spotter would normally guard against, a free weight dropping on you, caused two-thirds of the weight-training injuries seen in US emergency departments [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]; when you train alone, [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]] and machines remove most of it, and dumbbells can be dropped clear (inference).

Without a coach you also judge your own effort, technique and pain. Estimates of [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] are about one rep off on average and sharpen near failure [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], so you calibrate them. Cues aimed at the movement's effect improve learning [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA], and reviewing video of your own sets, with an expert choosing what to correct, helped in a small trial [@Shin2023_videoFeedbackSquat]. In one small trial in Achilles tendinopathy, carrying on within monitored pain limits did as well as rest [@Silbernagel2007_painMonitoringRCT], so mild discomfort that settles by the next day calls for adjusting the exercise, not stopping (inference).
articles.mechanisms:
**Why vigorous effort raises cardiac risk briefly while training lowers it** (expert statements built on epidemiology; the physiological detail is standard cardiovascular physiology, not verified in the sources read)

Hard effort raises heart rate, contractility, blood pressure and sympathetic drive, and with them myocardial oxygen demand. In a heart with occult coronary or structural disease, a mismatch between oxygen supply and demand, or catecholamine-driven electrical instability, can trigger ischaemia or arrhythmia; this is why risk concentrates in unfit, susceptible people during unaccustomed vigorous bouts [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk]. Training lowers the relative stress of any fixed workload, consistent with risk falling as fitness rises and with events often being preceded by symptoms that a screen or a stop rule can catch [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening].

**Exertional rhabdomyolysis** (clinical case series and narrative review; the cellular pathway is background physiology, not verified in the sources read)

Unaccustomed or excessive contractions, especially loaded lengthening ([[term:eccentric|eccentric]]) ones, damage the sarcolemma. Calcium floods the fibre, activating calpains and phospholipases and overloading mitochondria until ATP supply fails and the fibre necroses. Creatine kinase and myoglobin leak into the plasma, and the main clinical danger is kidney injury, signalled by dark urine [@Backer2022_exertionalRhabdoSR; @Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]. The usual explanation (background) is that myoglobin, at about 17 kDa, is filtered at the glomerulus, forms casts in acidic tubular fluid and promotes oxidative injury through its haem iron; the same haem makes a urine dipstick read positive for blood without red cells, through its pseudoperoxidase activity. Heat, drugs, infection and inherited disorders lower the threshold, whereas creatine monohydrate does not appear to be a trigger [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]. One bout of a new exercise reduces the damage caused by the next ([[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]]; see [[sci:sci-recovery]]), so the risk concentrates in the first sessions of any new exercise (inference).

**Heat strain** (consensus statements; physiological detail is background knowledge)

Most of the chemical energy used by working muscle appears as heat rather than work. The body sheds it by evaporating sweat and by sending blood to the skin; when hot, humid air limits evaporation, core temperature climbs. In exertional heat stroke, outcome probably relates to how long severe hyperthermia lasts, which is why survival hinges on early recognition, stopping and rapid whole-body cooling [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness]. Repeated exercise in the heat over 1-2 weeks reduces physiological strain [@Racinais2015_heatConsensus]; the adaptations behind this (plasma-volume expansion, earlier and greater sweating, lower heart rate and core temperature) are background physiology.

**Blood-pressure peaks in heavy lifting** (human physiological experiment with direct intra-arterial measurement, n = 5)

Three effects add up: contracting muscle compresses its own vessels, a reflex pressor response raises arterial pressure, and a [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]] (straining against a closed glottis) raises intrathoracic pressure, which is transmitted to the arteries. Pressure rose steeply in each [[term:concentric|concentric]] phase, fell in each eccentric phase and climbed further as failure approached; mouth pressures of 30-50 Torr indicated the Valsalva contribution [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting]. Two levers follow: stopping short of failure avoids the highest peaks, and a brief [[term:bracing|brace]] released within the rep limits breath-holding time (inference). Whether bracing protects the spine was not examined in the sources read.

**Why effort estimates sharpen near failure** ([[term:meta-analysis|meta-analytic]] moderator data plus a hypothesis)

Prediction error shrinks close to failure, in shorter sets and in later sets [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy; @Remmert2023_RIRtrainedUntrained]. A plausible explanation is that the signals of impending failure, slowing repetitions and steeply rising effort as higher-threshold [[term:motor-unit|motor units]] are recruited ([[term:size-principle|size principle]]), become distinct only in the last few reps, whereas in long sets they are blurred by general discomfort (hypothesis; not tested in the studies read). The authors of one study suggest that familiarity with very high effort matters more than training experience [@Droguett2025_RIRnoviceSquat], which is the rationale for occasional calibration sets taken to failure (inference).

**Attentional focus** (meta-analysis of experiments plus one [[term:rct|RCT]]; the interference explanation is the field's interpretation)

An external focus, on the effect of a movement, produced more efficient neuromuscular activity on EMG (g = 0.833) alongside better performance and learning [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA]. The field's interpretation is that attending to body parts interferes with automatic motor control. Attending to a target muscle can nonetheless increase its growth in an [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercise]] (one small trial; elbow flexors but not quadriceps) [@Schoenfeld2018_attentionalFocusHypertrophy], so focus can match purpose: external for learning a [[term:compound-exercise|compound lift]], internal for isolation work.

**Pain as a guide to load** (RCT and case series in tendinopathy plus an interpretive model)

In the interpretive model, pain reflects tissue sensitivity and perceived threat rather than a fixed index of damage, and graded loading maintains tissue capacity while avoidance lets it decline. Two observations fit: continued loading within monitored pain limits matched rest without harm in Achilles tendinopathy [@Silbernagel2007_painMonitoringRCT], and fear of movement was associated with poorer recovery in a 5-year case series [@Silbernagel2010_achilles5yr]. The model itself was not directly tested in the studies read; the [[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring model]] puts it into practice.
articles.evidence:
**Do you need medical clearance first?** Probable: not without symptoms or known disease.

The American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) dropped risk-factor counting and now screens on current activity, symptoms or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and intended intensity, because the old process generated excessive referrals that could deter exercise [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening]. The PAR-Q+ applies this logic: 'no' to all seven page-1 questions clears you for unrestricted activity, and any 'yes' leads to follow-up questions and, if needed, the ePARmed-X+ or a qualified exercise professional [@PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus]. In 1,670 people screened this way and cleared for maximal exercise, no adverse events occurred, which puts the upper 95% bound at about 0.18% per test (rule of three; arithmetic). The share cleared ranged from 85.3% to 99.5% depending on the resting blood-pressure cut-point, and the authors recommend below 160/94 mmHg [@Yee2019_PARQplusBPcutpoints].

**How large is the cardiac risk?** Probable: briefly raised during vigorous effort, lower overall with training.

The American Heart Association (AHA) states that vigorous activity, particularly by unfit people, can acutely raise the risk of sudden cardiac death and myocardial infarction in susceptible individuals, while more activity and fitness mean fewer coronary events [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk]. No absolute rates were in the sources read; for a healthy 31-year-old the risk is very low (inference). The listed warning signs are chest pain or pressure lasting minutes or coming and going, discomfort in the jaw, neck, back, arms or shoulders, shortness of breath, and feeling weak, light-headed or faint, sometimes with a cold sweat [@CDC2024_heartAttackSymptoms].

**Exertional rhabdomyolysis** Probable: rare, and concentrated in unaccustomed, excessive sessions.

In a systematic review of 772 athletes, most were young men (mean age 28.7 years); running accounted for 54.3% of cases and weightlifting for 14.8%, and mean creatine kinase at presentation was 31,481 IU/L (range 164-106,488) [@Backer2022_exertionalRhabdoSR]. The authors advise screening anyone who presents with muscle soreness, cramps or dark urine after heavy exertion. A narrative review names improper prescription, exercise as punishment and an inadequate medical history as recurring settings [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]. Case series cannot give a risk per session.

**Heat illness** Probable: largely preventable.

Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency, and most exertional heat illness can be prevented by modifying known risk factors [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness]. Acclimatisation through repeated exercise-heat exposure over 1-2 weeks is the most important single measure, alongside starting sessions well hydrated and scheduling around the heat, especially on the first hot days of the year [@Racinais2015_heatConsensus].

**How often do lifters get hurt, and how?** Probable.

| Source | Finding |
|---|---|
| Review of weight-training sports [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury] | Bodybuilding lowest at 0.24-1 injuries per 1,000 h; strongman 4.5-6.1 and Highland Games 7.5. Mostly strains, tendinitis and sprains of the shoulder, lower back, knee, elbow and wrist |
| US emergency departments, 1990-2007 [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED] | 65.5% from a weight dropping on the person; 90.4% involved free weights; fractures or dislocations made up 23.6% of free-weight vs 9.7% of machine injuries (injury proportion ratio 2.44, 95% [[term:confidence-interval|CI]] 1.92-3.09) |

Neither source follows novices prospectively, and the emergency data lack exposure time and include home lifters and children.

**Breath-holding and blood pressure** Uncertain.

Directly measured arterial pressure reached mean peaks of 320/250 mmHg in a double-leg press to failure (one participant above 480/350) and 255/190 mmHg in a single-arm curl [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting]. Despite such transient peaks, the AHA judges resistance training safe and effective for adults with and without cardiovascular disease [@Paluch2023_AHAresistanceTraining]. No trial has tested breathing instructions against a health outcome.

**How accurate are reps-in-reserve estimates?** Probable: about one rep off on average, with wide individual spread.

Across 12 studies, people under-predicted repetitions to failure by 0.95 reps (95% CI 0.17-1.73; [[term:i2|I²]] 97.9%; between-person SD about 1.5 reps); accuracy was better close to failure, in sets of 12 reps or fewer and in later sets, and training status did not change it [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy]. Trained lifters calling 3 and 1 RIR on the bench press were off by 0.65 ± 0.78 reps [@Refalo2024_RIRaccuracyBench], and two further studies including untrained or novice lifters found no clear effect of experience [@Remmert2023_RIRtrainedUntrained; @Droguett2025_RIRnoviceSquat]. Failure has costs: six bench-press sets to failure cut bar velocity by 25% at 4 minutes, against 13% at 1 RIR and 8% at 3 RIR, and made the session feel worse [@Refalo2023_proximityFatigue]. In trained people, failure and 1-2 RIR gave similar quadriceps growth over 8 weeks (+0.181 vs +0.182 cm) [@Refalo2024_FAILvsRIRhypertrophy], although an exploratory meta-regression found [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] rising as sets ended closer to failure [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression]. Truly untrained samples are scarce.

**Learning technique without a coach** Probable for cueing; uncertain for self-reviewed video.

An external focus beat an internal one for performance (g = 0.264, 95% CI 0.217-0.310), retention (g = 0.583, 0.425-0.741) and transfer (g = 0.584, 0.325-0.842), with no moderation by age, health status or skill level; more distal external cues added a little (g = 0.224) [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA]. Allegiance bias is possible in this literature. In untrained men, an internal focus on the target muscle gave larger elbow-flexor thickness gains (12.4% vs 6.9%), with similar quadriceps gains [@Schoenfeld2018_attentionalFocusHypertrophy]. In a small double-blind randomised trial, watching video of one's own squats after each set improved knee alignment, trunk lean and foot pressure and kept the gains for 3 days to a week, whereas gains from hands-on feedback were not retained; a physical therapist chose what to correct, so unguided self-review remains untested [@Shin2023_videoFeedbackSquat].

**Pain during training** Uncertain: the evidence is indirect.

In a randomised trial in Achilles tendinopathy, continuing running and jumping under a pain-monitoring model improved function as much as 6 weeks of active rest (VISA-A-S score 57 to 85 vs 57 to 91 at 12 months, no significant difference), with no harm detected [@Silbernagel2007_painMonitoringRCT]. At 5 years 80% had fully recovered, and fear of movement correlated with poorer recovery (r = -0.59) [@Silbernagel2010_achilles5yr]. In a pilot trial in patellar tendinopathy, pain-guided activity gave better treatment compliance than pain-free restriction (86% vs 67%) [@Sprague2021_painGuidedActivity]. These were patients with tendon problems, not healthy beginners.
articles.practice:
- **Screen first** ([[dec:D02]]): complete the official PAR-Q+ before your first session, then yearly or when your health changes; any 'yes' means seeing a doctor or qualified exercise professional first. A resting blood-pressure reading is a useful optional baseline.
- **Ramp effort** ([[dec:D07]]): stop sets about 4 RIR short in [[phase:p0]] and 3-4 RIR short in the first two weeks of [[phase:p1]], skip high-rep or eccentric-heavy finishers and keep cardio conversational; then 2-3 RIR on free-weight compound lifts, 1-2 on machines and 0-2 on isolation work. Hard intervals start only in week 7 of [[phase:p1]]. Exercise is never a punishment.
- **Stop and get help** (full card in [[plan:safety]]): chest pain or pressure, faintness or unusual breathlessness: stop and call emergency services. Muscle pain or swelling far beyond normal soreness, marked weakness or dark urine: same-day medical care and no training until cleared. Confusion or collapse in heat: cool the whole body at once and call for help.
- **Solo equipment rules** ([[dec:D15]], [[dec:D08]]): barbell squats and bench presses only in a rack with safety arms set just below the bottom position, or in a Smith machine; otherwise dumbbells or machines. Keep 2-3 RIR on free-weight compound lifts and never take them to failure; failure is allowed only on the last set of machine or cable work. Rehearse bailing out of each lift with an empty bar.
- **Breathing**: exhale through the effort on light and isolation work; brace briefly only on the hardest reps of heavy compound lifts, and release it within the rep.
- **Calibrate RIR** ([[rule:rir-calibration]]): Hevy records [[term:rpe|RPE]], and RPE 8 means 2 RIR (practical convention). In weeks 5 and 9 of [[phase:p1]], then every 4-6 weeks, take the last set of one machine exercise, such as [[ex:leg-extension]], to failure and compare the reps with your prediction.
- **Technique**: external cues for compound lifts, a 'squeeze' focus for isolation work; film each new lift from the side weekly for the first month.
- **Pain** ([[rule:pain]]): discomfort that is mild, settles by the next day and is not rising week to week: modify and continue. Sharp or joint-line pain, limping, swelling, numbness, weakness, or pain worsening over 1-2 weeks: stop that exercise and see a physiotherapist or doctor.
- **Heat**: without air-conditioning at midday, acclimatise over 1-2 weeks at lower intensity, well hydrated.
articles.uncertainties:
- No absolute cardiac or rhabdomyolysis risk per session was available for a healthy, untrained 31-year-old, and how much early volume is too much for a novice is unknown.
- Your resting blood pressure is unknown. An elevated reading, any PAR-Q+ 'yes' or a family history of premature sudden cardiac death (inference) would route you to medical review first.
- Whether your gym is air-conditioned, and the emergency number to display for your location in India, still need confirming.
- The solo-equipment rules rest on injury mechanisms rather than trials, and no trial has tested breathing instructions or bracing in healthy novices.
- RIR evidence comes mostly from trained or mixed samples; whether the calibration routine improves a novice's accuracy is untested, and some people are consistent over- or under-predictors.
- Unguided video self-review is untested, and the internal-focus growth benefit rests on one small trial.
- The pain-monitoring evidence comes from tendinopathy patients and its numeric limits were not verified, so the app uses only qualitative rules.
- The red-flag list is assembled from agency and consensus guidance and has not been reviewed by a clinician.

articles.title: Sticking with it
articles.tagline: What keeps people training, how long a habit takes to form, and how to pursue an aesthetic goal without it turning against you.
articles.summary:
Every adaptation this programme aims for depends on months of consistent training, so whatever keeps you training matters as much as the details of the training (inference). In healthy inactive adults, structured programmes raise activity modestly, and part of the gain lasts beyond six months (effect sizes of about 0.3, falling to 0.2) [@Howlett2019_BCTinactiveAdults]. The technique most strongly linked to success across studies is self-monitoring, keeping a record of what you do, and it was associated with larger effects when paired with a goal and a regular review [@Michie2009_BCTmetaRegression]; your Hevy log and weekly check-in provide both. If-then plans ('when I finish my first meal after waking, I leave for the gym') add a small further effect, mainly in people who already intend to train and feel capable [@Silva2018_implementationIntentionsMA; @Kompf2020_implementationIntentionsModerators], which probably describes you.

How sessions feel matters. Feeling better during moderate exercise predicts more activity later [@Rhodes2015_affectFuturePA], and in trained lifters, sets stopped one or two reps short of [[term:momentary-failure|failure]] felt better than sets taken to failure [@Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual]. A sense of variety helps a little [@Sylvester2015_varietySupportRCT]. A new routine takes about two months on median to become automatic, but anywhere from 4 to 335 days [@Singh2024_habitFormationTime], so lapses are expected and planned for.

On average, exercise improves body image only slightly [@Campbell2009_exerciseBodyImageMA]. Because appearance is your first goal, the programme also watches for signs of muscle dysmorphia: an obsessive preoccupation with muscularity combined with compulsive training, rigid dieting and frequent body checking [@Cinaroglu2025_muscleDysmorphiaMA]. Regular activity reduces symptoms of low mood, anxiety and stress by a moderate amount on average, including in healthy people [@Singh2023_PAmentalHealthUmbrella]; treat this as a benefit to expect, not a treatment.
articles.mechanisms:
**Habit: handing the start of a behaviour to a cue** (systematic review and [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of intervention studies using self-reported automaticity; the neural account is background knowledge, largely from animal studies, not assessed in the sources read)

A habit is a learned link between a context and a response, so that the context starts the behaviour with little deliberation. Repetition in a stable context strengthens the link: frequency, timing, personal choice and how the behaviour feels all influenced habit strength, and morning and self-chosen habits tended to be stronger [@Singh2024_habitFormationTime]. In neural terms, repeated, rewarded actions shift from goal-directed control, which weighs outcomes, towards stimulus-response control centred on the dorsolateral striatum (background). What becomes automatic is the cue-triggered start, such as packing the bag and leaving, not the effortful session itself (inference). Reported medians of 59-66 days sit well below means of 106-154 days, so the distribution has a long right tail and a minority take many months (statistical inference from the reported summaries) [@Singh2024_habitFormationTime].

**Self-monitoring as a feedback loop** (meta-regression across intervention studies; the control-theory framing is the authors')

Control theory treats self-regulation as a loop: set a goal, monitor behaviour, compare the two and adjust. For a biochemist this is negative feedback with a set-point, a sensor and an effector (analogy). Self-monitoring alone is a sensor without a comparator; pairing it with at least one other control-theory technique, such as goal-setting or feedback on performance, was associated with larger effects (0.42 vs 0.26) [@Michie2009_BCTmetaRegression]. The modest effect of activity trackers, which are self-monitoring devices [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA], and the added benefit of accountability in self-weighing trials [@Madigan2015_selfweighingMA] fit the same picture (inference).

**Implementation intentions: closing the gap between intending and doing** (meta-analysis of [[term:rct|RCTs]] plus a narrative review; the mechanism is the field's interpretation)

An if-then plan pre-selects a situational cue and links it to a response, so the decision is made once, in advance, rather than every day. It adds little motivation of its own, which is why it worked best in people who already intended to be active, felt capable and saw the goal as their own (self-concordance) [@Kompf2020_implementationIntentionsModerators], and why its average effect is small [@Silva2018_implementationIntentionsMA].

**Affect: how a session feels shapes the next decision** (systematic review of mostly observational studies plus small randomised trials)

The change in affect during moderate-intensity exercise predicted later activity, whereas post-exercise affect did not; affect related reliably to affective judgements about future activity and negligibly to intention [@Rhodes2015_affectFuturePA]. A plausible reading is that the remembered feel of a session sets how appealing the next one looks, without passing through conscious plans (interpretation). Proximity to failure is one controllable driver: sets to failure raised discomfort, session effort and acute fatigue and lowered pleasure compared with stopping 1-3 reps short [@Refalo2023_proximityFatigue; @Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual].

**Perceived variety and autonomy** (one randomised trial with a mediation analysis; moderator data from two reviews)

Variety support improved adherence through how varied participants perceived the programme to be [@Sylvester2015_varietySupportRCT]. Because the mediator is a perception, small rotations of accessory exercises may supply it while the main lifts stay fixed for tracking (inference). Autonomy has only indirect support: self-chosen habits were stronger [@Singh2024_habitFormationTime], and self-concordance moderated the effect of if-then plans [@Kompf2020_implementationIntentionsModerators]. Both suggest that behaviours you choose and endorse last longer than imposed ones (inference).

**Body checking and compulsive exercise** (cross-sectional meta-analyses and qualitative syntheses; the maintenance loop is background cognitive-behavioural theory, not tested in the sources read)

Muscle dysmorphia combines obsessive preoccupation with muscularity and compulsive behaviours, namely excessive exercise, rigid dieting and frequent body checking; severity correlates with obsessive-compulsive traits (about 0.24) [@Cinaroglu2025_muscleDysmorphiaMA]. In the cognitive-behavioural model, checking briefly relieves anxiety, which reinforces the checking while keeping attention on perceived flaws (background theory). The cognitive component of body image, meaning thoughts and beliefs about one's body, showed the stronger link with exercise-addiction risk [@Guo2025_bodyImageExerciseAddiction]. Causal direction is unknown throughout.

**Mood** (umbrella review; mechanisms not assessed)

The umbrella review did not test mechanisms. Candidate pathways range from neurobiological (neurotrophic and monoaminergic signalling) to psychological (mastery, self-efficacy) and sleep; none was assessed in the sources read (background hypotheses). The larger effects seen at higher intensity [@Singh2023_PAmentalHealthUmbrella] are compatible with several of them.
articles.evidence:
**Do behaviour-change programmes work, and which techniques matter?** Probable: modest, partly lasting effects.

In healthy inactive adults, physical-activity interventions changed behaviour by d = 0.32 (95% [[term:confidence-interval|CI]] 0.16-0.48) after the intervention and by d = 0.21 (0.12-0.30) at 6 months or more. Post-intervention effects were associated with demonstration, practice, graded tasks and biofeedback; maintenance with action planning, instruction on how to perform the behaviour, prompts and cues, practice, graded tasks and self-reward [@Howlett2019_BCTinactiveAdults]. Across 122 evaluations of healthy-eating and activity interventions, the pooled effect was 0.31 (0.26-0.36; [[term:i2|I²]] 69%); self-monitoring explained the most heterogeneity (13%), and interventions pairing it with another control-theory technique outperformed the rest (0.42 vs 0.26) [@Michie2009_BCTmetaRegression]. Both reviews compare techniques across studies rather than in head-to-head trials.

**Does self-monitoring technology help?** Probable: modestly.

Interventions using consumer activity trackers raised daily steps ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.24, 95% CI 0.16-0.33) and moderate-to-vigorous activity (SMD 0.27, 0.15-0.39) compared with interventions without them [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA]. Adding self-weighing to weight-loss programmes gave an extra -1.7 kg (95% CI -2.6 to -0.8), and accountability increased weight loss [@Madigan2015_selfweighingMA]. Self-weighing was not associated overall with anxiety, depression, body attitudes or disordered eating, apart from a small negative association with psychological functioning such as self-esteem [@Benn2016_selfweighingpsych].

**Do if-then plans help?** Probable: a small, conditional effect.

In trials that reinforced implementation intentions, activity rose relative to controls (0.25, 95% CI 0.05-0.45) [@Silva2018_implementationIntentionsMA]. Intention, self-efficacy, perceived behavioural control, habit strength and self-concordance moderated the effect [@Kompf2020_implementationIntentionsModerators].

**Does enjoyment predict adherence?** Probable for in-session affect.

A more positive change in affect during moderate-intensity exercise was linked to more future activity; post-exercise affect showed a null relationship [@Rhodes2015_affectFuturePA]. In an 8-week trial in 18 trained lifters, with one leg trained to failure and the other 1-2 reps short, perceived discomfort averaged 5.1 vs 4.1, session [[term:rpe|RPE]] 5.4 vs 4.3 and the Feeling Scale +0.3 vs +1.2 [@Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual]. No trial in the sources read tested whether such in-session differences change long-term adherence.

**Does variety help?** Probable: a small effect.

In a 6-week randomised trial in inactive adults, high variety support improved adherence (partial η² 0.05), mediated by perceived variety (β = 0.16) [@Sylvester2015_varietySupportRCT]. This is a single, short trial.

**How long does a habit take?** Uncertain on timing; the wide variation is consistent.

Only four studies reported time to habit formation: medians 59-66 days, means 106-154 days, individual times 4-335 days. Habit-strength scores rose with interventions (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.49-0.88) [@Singh2024_habitFormationTime]. Automaticity was self-reported, and the behaviours were health habits in general rather than gym training. No trial in the sources read tested autonomy-supportive programming directly.

**Does training improve body image?** Uncertain: slightly, and not in every group.

Across 57 controlled interventions, exercise improved body image more than control conditions, with a small effect moderated by age, publication year, and exercise frequency and specificity [@Campbell2009_exerciseBodyImageMA]. In a [[term:grade|GRADE]]-rated meta-analysis in women after breast cancer, exercise did not improve body image (very low certainty), although resistance exercise raised self-esteem (SMD 0.31, 0.07-0.55) [@CasusoHolgado2024_exerciseBodyImageBreastCancer]. Neither population resembles a 31-year-old man starting to train.

**What marks muscle dysmorphia?** Uncertain: cross-sectional and qualitative data only.

| Finding | Source |
|---|---|
| Severity correlates with obsessive-compulsive traits (about 0.24); anabolic-steroid users score higher (d about 0.45) and have markedly higher odds of the condition | 5 quantitative and 5 qualitative studies [@Cinaroglu2025_muscleDysmorphiaMA] |
| Body image correlates with exercise-addiction risk (r = 0.26), more strongly for the cognitive component and where compulsive exercise was measured | Three-level meta-analysis [@Guo2025_bodyImageExerciseAddiction] |
| More social-media use is associated with more symptoms; evidence for muscle dysmorphia is preliminary | Systematic review [@VintroAlcaraz2025_socialMediaMD] |

No validated brief screener suitable for an app was evaluated in the sources read.

**Does training improve mental wellbeing?** Probable: moderate average benefits from a low-quality evidence base.

An umbrella review of 97 meta-analysed reviews (1,039 trials) found median effects of -0.43 for depressive symptoms (IQR -0.66 to -0.27) and -0.42 for anxiety (IQR -0.66 to -0.26), and a pooled -0.60 for psychological distress (95% CI -0.78 to -0.42). Healthy individuals were among the groups benefiting most, higher intensity was associated with larger effects, and effects shrank in longer interventions [@Singh2023_PAmentalHealthUmbrella]. Most underlying reviews were rated critically low in quality, and outcomes were unblinded.
articles.practice:
- **Log everything, review weekly** ([[plan:logging]], [[tool:checkin]]): every session goes into Hevy with load, reps, RPE and notes, and the weekly check-in compares the week with explicit goals, pairing self-monitoring with goals and feedback.
- **Write three if-then plans** tied to your fixed day, for example: 'When I finish my first meal after waking, I pack my bag and leave for the gym'; 'If I miss a session, I do it the next day at 13:00'; 'If I am short of time, I do the minimum session', meaning the first two exercises of the day at normal effort (practical convention).
- **Keep early sessions pleasant**: no routine training to failure in the first weeks ([[dec:D07]]), and conversational cardio in a mode you enjoy, which can include a dance class ([[ex:cardio-long]]).
- **Vary the edges, not the core**: main lifts stay fixed for tracking while accessories or formats rotate at block changes ([[rule:substitution]]).
- **Expect about two months** before training feels automatic, and expect lapses; after a gap, return with [[rule:breaks]]. If you miss more than about 1 in 4 planned sessions over a month, simplify the plan and rewrite the if-then plans (inference).
- **Measure appearance on a schedule, not on impulse**: waist weekly and photos monthly under fixed conditions ([[ex:test-girths]], [[sci:sci-bodycomp]]); no daily photo or mirror checks and no comparison with idealised physiques online ([[dec:D26]], [[sci:sci-expectations]]).
- **Every 4-8 weeks, check yourself** for persistent preoccupation with not being muscular enough despite progress, distress or guilt after a missed session, training through injury or illness, rigid dieting that crowds out social life, frequent mirror or photo checking, and interest in steroids or other performance drugs. If several apply, speak to a mental-health professional (practical convention; not a validated screener).
- **Mood**: rate mood, stress and energy in one line each week. Exercise supports wellbeing but is not treatment; persistent low mood is a reason to seek professional help.
- **Long term**: the maintenance phase ([[phase:pm]], [[dec:D18]]) keeps training going once the main phases end.
articles.uncertainties:
- Technique effects come from comparisons across studies; few behaviour-change techniques have been tested head to head, and none in someone with your schedule.
- Habit timing rests on four studies with self-reported automaticity. Whether a session one hour after a 12:00 wake-up behaves like a 'morning' habit is inference.
- Variety evidence is one 6-week trial, and the best rotation interval is unknown.
- Autonomy is supported only by moderator findings, not by direct trials.
- The body-image evidence comes from mixed and clinical populations; whether training will improve your body image or sharpen dissatisfaction cannot be predicted for an individual.
- All muscle-dysmorphia evidence is cross-sectional or qualitative, and the self-check questions are not a validated screener; a validated brief tool would replace them.
- The mental-health benefits rest on reviews mostly rated critically low in quality, with unblinded outcomes.
- Streaks and other gamification were not evaluated; losing a streak may demotivate (inference).
- Your own adherence data will outweigh all of this: repeated missed sessions or distress about your appearance would change the plan.
